BILLY: A NAVVY'S DOG. Be wasn't not much of a dog. no doubt, No points an' no pedigree; , From the tip o' his tail to his grizzly snout But a mongrel bred was he. An' on'y three legs that was sound an' whole, An' one o' his eyes on strike; But he 'd got a heart, an' mebbe a soul, If there's ever a soul in a tike. Picked up a puppy in sixty-eight, I've had him for nigh twelve year, An' it sets me a-thinkin' o' life an' fate When I see a-lyin' theer ; For as we tramp'd it there came a cry, He was nailed by the down express, -An' now there's a cur'ous mist in my eye An' a lump in my tkroat, I guess! You may laugh if you like at *hat I say— Jest look at that crippled limb, That saved my bacon for me one day, An' I ain't goin' back on him. We'd been for a spree to the nighest town— We were on the "Long Drag" then— 'There was me an' Jerry an' big Bill Brown, An' Nobby an' Charlie Slen. We'd laps o' coin an' we'd drunk the lot, We'd all got a fairish load, An' halfway home I fell like a shot Dead-beat on the incline road. An' there they left me—my mates, I mean— 'T was the drink that made them fail, Wi' the snow beginnin' to fall unseen, An' my neck on the nearest rail. But Billy stood by me without a whine All night as I lay an' snored, Till the first loco came no the line Wi' Blazing Benny aboard ; An' then he howled till he made em slow • And stop close to my head; But that foreleg you see twisted so Was mangled and torn instead! So it's kinder rough on a chapiike Me, As is ',tun in want o' a friend, That a matey as saved his life should be Knocked down like this in the end. Yet hap him up wi' a bit o' sod Laid light on his faithful breast; I've had many a mate sin' I took the road, Bat Billy was aye the best ,!

It is beautiful to gather About the domestic fireside, but the fire ought to be on the 'hearthstone: and not in the tem- pers of those who live there. ---:- - --, MN SPANISH PitovEßßS.—Love, a horse, and money carry a man throggh the world. Three things kill a man: a hot sun, supper, and trouble. To shave an ass is a waste of lather. If the gossip is not in her own houseshe is in some- body else's. Don't speak ill of the year till it is over. Men are as grateful for kind deeds as the sea is when you fling it a cup of water.

NED'S SUGGESTION. "Where did you buy her, mamma ?' Asked three-year-old Ned of me, Is he leaned o'er the dainty cradle His "new little sister" to see. "An angel brought her, darling," I answered, and he smiled, Then softly bent his curly head And kissed the sleeping child. But a sudden change came ;over him And he said, "If I'd been you, While I was about it, minima, I'd have caught the angel, too !" TROLLOPE'S VIEW OF HIS LITERARY :CAILEER.—"iAnd so I end the record of my literary performances,—which I think are more in amount than the works of ,any other liv- ing English author. If any English authors not living have written more—as may probably have been the case—l do not know who they are. I find that, taking the books which have appeared under our names, I have published much more than twice m much as !Carlyle. I have also cabliahed considerably more than Voltaire, even including his letters. We are told that Varro, at the age of eighty, had written 480 volumes, and that he went on writing for eight years longer. I wish I knew what was the length of Varro's volumes; I comfort myself by reflecting that the amount of manuscript described as a book in Varro's time was not much. Varro, too, is dead, and Voltaire; whereas I am still living, and may add to the pile."—Autobkirapke of A. Trollop?. A SHIP OF TYRE.—Ltit us follow one of their traders on his way. Slowly he will creep on from island to island, to Rhodes, to Crete to Thera, Melos Samothrace, Leinnos, Tha.sl3; at each he will plant trading stations, to which again and again he may return. In exchange for hie ware he will win copper ore from Cyprus, gold from Thasoa. cap- tive slaves from each and all. And last, on a fateful day, some trader more venturesome than the rest moors his black ship in the Bay of Argos; he unlades his wares—stuffs dyed with Tyrian purple, carved ivory, and amber, and graven ostrich eggs, vessels of pottery, shining armour and ca yen bowls—such bowls as we have seen. Eager natives crowd about the gay bazaar, goodly men and fair tall women; and gladly they barter for these Eastern gauds their home- grown wares, and, most of all, the purple dye-fish on their coasts. Further afield we will not follow the Phenician trader ; we know his ships touched at the coast of Etruria and Latium, for the first of our bowls was found at Pales- Ulna. We know that to the coast ot Africa came the Pheni- cien Queen Dido; and ho a' her colonies held Sicily and Sar- dinia, the Balearic Isles and Spain. We know, too, that the Phenician voyaged even beyond the pillars of Hercules, and that one day he bore for freight the prophet Jonah. But we will pause at Hellas, where the treasures of Mycenee tell of his presence, and Ezekiel lifts his voice, adding yet another woe to "the burden of Tyre." Javan (the lonian, I .e.; the Greek), Tabal, and Meshech, they were their mer- chants, they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in their market.—Jane E. Harrison in the " Magazine of Art." OLIVER WENDELL HOLMES ON LANGUAGE REFORMERS.— Language is a solemn thing, I said. It grows out of life,— lent of its agonies and ecstasies, its wants and its weariness. Every language is a temple, in which the soul of those who speak it is enshrined. Because time softens its outlines and rounds the sharp angles of its cornices, shall a fellow tale a pickaxe to help time? Let me tell you what comes of meddling with things that can take care of themselves. A friend of mine had a watch given him, when he was a boa', —a "bull's eve," with a loose silver case that came off Hie an oyster shell from its contents; you know them,—the oases that you hang on your thumb, while the core, or the Teal watch, lies in your hand as naked as a peeled apple. Well, he began with taking off the case, and so on from one liberty to another, until he got it fairly open, and there were the works, as good as it they -were alive,—crown- wheel, balance-wheel, and all the rest. All right except one thing,—there was a confounded little hair had got tangled round the balance-wheel. So my young Solomon got a pair of tweezers, and caught hold of the hair very, ' :nicely and pulled it right out, without touching any of the wheels,— when,—buzzzZZZ ! and the watch had done up twenty-four hours in double magnetic-telegraph time! The English language was wound up to ran some thousands of years, I trust; bat if everybody is to be pulling at everything he thinks is a hair, our grandchildren will have to make the discovery that it is a hair•spring, and the old Anglo-Norman soul's-timekeeper will run down, as so many other dialects have done before it. I can't stand this meddling any better than your, sir. But we have a great deal to be proud of in the lifelong labours of that old lexicographer, and we mustn't be ungrateful. Besides, don't let us deceive our- selves,—the war of the dictionaries is only a disguised rivalry of cities, colleges, and especially of publishers. After all, it is likely that toe language will shape itself by larger forces than phonography and dictionary-making. You may spade up the ocean as much as you like, and harrow it afterwards, if you can but the moon will still lead the tides, and the winds will form their surface.—The Professor at the Breakfast Table. A YousG ARCTIC SERo.—Bellot, who was of humble origin, rose to position by his own perseverance and in- dustry. His enthusiasm in the cause of the Franklin search was kindled by his ardent admiration of the heroic devotedness of Lady Franklin and lively sympathy with the English people in their Christian philanthropy in the cause. On his first expedition, in the Prince Albert, his conduct was such that he was received in England with en- thusiasm; the British Government made it known to France hew well satisfied it was with the zealous and intelligent be-Operation of the young officer; Lady Franklin expressed her gratitude to him in the most touching terms, and the Royal Geographical Society gave him honours. His second expedition was in the Phoeaix. "lie departed with the glee of a high-sotiled soldier who rushes into the thick of the fight to win his spurs at the risk of his life," says his friend and biographer, M. Julien Lemer. No vulgar calcu- lation sullied his purpose; he refused the pay which Lady Franklin offered him—hecwished to represent hie country worthily among the English by his disinterestedness as well as by his courage. Arrived in the Polar regions, it was im- 'portant that certain deepatches should be conveyed to Sir Edward Belcher without delay, and Bellot, who knew that their transmission was one of the special and urgent objects of the mission of the Phenix, and that it was necessary they should be promptly delivered, himself volunteered to carry them, and with four men, a sledge, and an india-rubber canoe, started • off. When they had been out only a taw days, Bellot, with two of his men, found themselves on a detached mass of ice which was being driven rapidly by a furious gate towards mid-channel. He talked to the men about the danger of the position, when one of them, John- son, reminded him that the American Expedition were drawn up and down this channel by the ice. "I know they were," Ise replied, "and when the Lord protects us not a hair of our head shall be touched." He then went out from the retreat in which they had sheltered themselves from the gale to see how the ice was clriving, and in about five minutes afterwards Johnson followed him. The wind was blowing with terrific fury. Bellot was not to be seen. His name was shouted, but no answer came. On the oppo- site side of a crack about five fathoms wide was his stick. And that was all. There could be no doubt that when he left the shelter to see how the ice was driving, the wind carried him off his feet, and he slipped into the crack from which e he never rose again.—" Heroes of Britain in Peace and War." NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, ann. CULTURE, &c.

COTTAGE GARDENING. PUNTING FRUIT TuEzs.—This work so seldom falls to the lot Of the cottager that he is probably less acquainted with it than any other garden operation. We shall, there- fore, offer a few remarks that will serve as a guide to him. A.t one time the planting or transplan•ing trees was deferred till the foliage was all off the trees. The consequences were that, in cases where the trees were of any size, they made but little progress the succeeding year, and soon entirely succumbed. Experience has taught us that all deciduous trees do best if moved before losing all their foliage; and we have before now commenced the work as early as the last week in September, beginning with cherries and plums, fol- lowed by pears and apples. The latter snffers less than any from late planting, because it is so late in starting to grow in the Spring. The reasons why planting is best done at once are these :—Roots, as a rule, are not formed in the ab- sence of leaves; it is therefore evident that a tree moved after losing them remains in a state of inactivity till called to action by natural agencies in the Spring. The tree pushes forth apparently strong enough up to a certain stage, when it comes to a standstill, because all its stored food is exhausted and the roots are nbt in a position to replenish the store. The shoots and stems assume a half-shrivelled appearance, the sap having been used up; and it is purely a question of weather, how it will go yiifla the plant. A few dull, moist days may turn the balance in its favour, but if dry winds and sun prevail, the consequences will be disas- trous. Early planted trees have this advantage. The tem- perature of the soil is much higher at this time than it will be for some months hence. It averages now, according to soil and localities, from 54 deg. to 62 deg. at two feet below the surface; in March 40 to 43 deg. Consequently the roots are placed in a warmer medium, and they sooner heal over than they would do later on. The roots are further encou- raged by the action of the descending sap from the leaves, and they soon form at the end of the cut roots rootlets or spongioles, which are really the feeding roots of all plants, and these are the ones that get destroyed on moving the tree. The early planted tree may be said to be partially established soon after its removal, and its roots are in a position to respond to the calls that will be made upon them at the proper time. Having proved the best time to plant, we shall give a few directions how to plant :—Deep plant- ing is a mistake frequently committed, at the same time the ground should be moved two feet deep, and, if clayey, simply stir the clay and leave it. To remove the clay and replace it by good soil would be to entice the roots into a clay basin, and as they cannot penetrate beyond its side they will assuredly perish. Under such circumstances the best of the soil should be reserved for the upper nine or twelve inches, and disposed of by placing three to six inches under the roots, and the remainder on the top. Where the ground has been unfavourable, we have planted nearly level with the surface, and conveyed sufficient soil from elsewhere to cover the roots- the necessary depth. Before the soil is trodden down over the roots, it is necessary to see that the plant is upright, which is easily done by one holding it whilst anoper steps a short distance away to view it. It should have been mentioned that the ends of the roots should be nearly on a level with their starting point. This will cause them to travel laterally, instead of taking a downward course, and thus the sooner feel the effects of a cold, wet, or hungry subsoil. Newly planted trees require to be made secure to a stake or two, one on either side. Small trees re- quire only one, and a piece of cloth or leather, or a band of hay, should be placed round the stem where it is tied, to keep it from chafing against the stake and destroy the bark. Tax FRONT GARDENS.—This is a most suitable time of the year to disturb all kinds of bulbous plants. In our peregrinations during the summer and spring, we noticed several 'trout gardens capable of being itpproved by re- arranging this class of plants, which includes Snowdrops, Crocus, Tulips, and Daffodils, or Narcissus as they are called. They are all now in a partially dormant state, and may be moved with impunity; and as they are a class of plants that are not benefited by frequent removals, it is as well to give them a rich spot to grow in. The easiest method to accomplish this is to remove all exhausted or po3r soil, and replace it with fresh soil and decayed manure. To exchange a few spadefulls of soil occupies but little time and it would be madness to plant bulbs in ground that had been occupied by such greedy herbaceous plants as Phloxes or Delphiniums, or others of similar exhausting capacity, without replacing lost fertility. The same rule also applies to any fresh clumps of imported bulbs that may now be made. We think all bulbs should be planted from 41n. to 6in. below the :surface. TRH WINDOW.—An elegant plant suitable for the window is to be found in Dracaana indivisa, a native of New Zea- land. It is grown exclusively for its foliage, which is dark green, and measures if t. to 4ft. in length, actording to the age of the plant, and each leaf is seldom more than one inch in width. It is much easier grown than the Pelargonium or even Fuchsias. It will require to be kept moderately moist at all times, but more especially whilst making its growth.

HOW ARE WE TO KEEP APPLES.—" Store them, as I have done for years, in a damp airy cellar. Handle them as lightly as possible, and place in crates, hampers, or cold cases with holes bored in the sides, so as to prevent the fruit fromheating. On the approach of frost, cover. Fruit thus treated will remain plump and good at least two or three months longer than if stored in a high and dry temperature. Before used, develop the flavour by placing in a high tem- perature for twenty-four hours at least."—Correspondent of the Journal of Horticulture. FOOT AND Mount DISEASE.—Sir Baldwyn Leighton, Bart., writes:—" In view of the continued spread of Foot and Mouth Disease, I think it may be worth your while to publish the enclosed prescription, which I had from Mr. Kearey, of Bridgnorth, who has himself tested it, and found it efficacious. He also tells me that it is most essential that the animals should be fed with linseed gruel ;when at the worst for three or four days."—COPY of Prescription : Dissolve three tablespoonfuls of salicyclic acid in hot water, adding enough lukewarm water to make up a gallon. Wash the mouth and feet of the animal three times a day with this liquid, and powder the hoofs with the dry acid after each washing. To the drinking water of each animal add two tablespoonfuls of the acid dissolved in hot water. HARES AND HABBITS.—A carious game case turned up at Hamilton, on Friday. Mr. M‘Lachlan, farmer, sued the game tenant of his farm, Mr. Donaldson, for the value of a number of rabbit snares alledged to have been removed by defender, and compensation for loss sustained to his crops through the consequent increase of rabbits, and the value of the rabbits he was prevented from catching. The pursuer under his lease has a right to snare rabbits, but has no right to hares. The Sheriff, after hearing the evidence, held the defender's gamekeepers had taken away 150 snares, but that in pursuer's other snares there had been caught 75 hares, of which 22 were found dead. His lordship remarked that it was inevitable that some hares would be caught in the rabbit snares, but, considering that the number caught here was a third or fourth of the stock on the ground, the snares must have been carelessly set. He found the game tenant liable for the price of the 150 snares and of 50 rabbits, which he presumed pursuer would have caught, and 'also for the damage to the crops., On the other hand he held pursuer liable for the extra number of hares destroyed by the rabbit snares, and adjusting the claims,decerned against the defen- der for Els What endless troubles poor hares and rabbits cause. MATTER IN A HORSE'S HEAD.-9 DECAYED TOOTH.— A. correspondent in the North British Agriculturist, in replying ttea letter where a somewhat similar experience had been given, says that some time since he had a horse from which the matter was so offensive at times that he had difficulty in getting the man who worked him to do so, and attend to him, although the veterinary' surgeon assured me that it was no dangerous disesee. At length the horse died, and as I was puzzled about the case, I examined the head carefully by opening up the nostril and following up the matter which was coming down, till above the eye I found a lamp, as large as my closed hand, of the food the horse had been living on, in a state more like dung than anything else, and very hard. How it had got there I could not imagine, but on carefully picking it out I found an opening underneath, about three-quarters of an inch wide, quite full of the same stuff; and on following this downwards I found it to terminate in a small round hole about three-eighths of an inch in diameter in one of the grinders. Evidently this was the cause of the whole affair, as in chewing the food a part had been continuously forced upwards till it could get no further. Of course, around the dirty and decomposed lumps of stuff were in quite a festered condition and full of matter. , PURE WATER FOR CATTLE.—Mr. Jaoez nogg writes to The Times on a want of pure water for cattle, and says it deserves far more occasion from farmers and graziers than it receives. "Soon After an outbreak of contagious fever among cattle I was invited to inspect a number of farms, in some of which the disease then prevailed. On going over all of them I was much struck with the want of atten- tion to the coMmouest matters of sanitltion, and above all to the neglect of good drinking water for the cattle. In almost every case the pond which received the drainage of the farm or district was, the only or principal souree of drinking-water. In some farms a trough fixed in the middle of the yard, and into which water was pumped from a shallow well, and which drained the farm, the fatal buildings, and the middens, was the sole water supple, and this was too often found to be seriously contaminated. I examined mi- croscopically numerous specimens of the water of the farms and also the milk of the cows, and almost invaribly dis- covered in both the same species of bacteria. I saw the wife of a farm labourer who was suffering from a low form of fever, and who was then suckling a sickly-looking infant. I was asked by her medical attendant to examine a specimen of her breast milk, and in this I also discovered the same form of bacteria. This may have been a coincidence, but it must be admitted to be a very remarkaable one—cause and effect, evidently. 'lt might have been expected that the spread of sanitary knowledge was producing a better state of things, but Mr. Bowle3 says it has not yet reached those who dealt with cattle. At all events, I can fully endorse his views with' regard to basl water being a fruitful cuuse of cattle disease. It certainly may be said that bad water and want- of attention to sanitary matters are the cause of cattle disease at all times and in all places. It is equally true that outbreaks of typhoid fever are produced by the milk of cogs drinking sewage-polluted water; and equally true that neither good buttsr nor good cheese can be made from sewage-contaminate I milk. The question of a pure water supply is as pressing for cattle as it is for Londoners. All surburban streams, those especially which border graz- ing grounds, for miles around London are shamefully and dangerously polluted." MR. W. A. GIBBS' DRYING CYLINDEHS.—The climate of this cluntry renders the artificial drying of bay and conn essentially neceAary to successful practice in competition with foreign rivalry ; this is equally true 'of all kinds of corn when separated from the straw, which in the majority of seasons require artificial drying. In a fire season the utility of drying machines is lost sight of, but even in such seasons much corn thrashes out damp and has to be left till the drying winds of March before being fit for the miller. But this is not all, for what was " laid " before cutting is mouldy, and the growth of mould spreads rapidly through the stack. The grain in such cases ought to be separated frem the straw without delay, and dried in order to kill the mould and remove superfluous moisture. The loss which farmers annually sustain in sending damp and mouldy grain to market is enormous, and yet the whole of the loss could be saved. Corn exported from America comparatively dry, reaches our ports damp and mouldy. Messrs. Spiller and Co., millers and corn merchants, Cardiff, to obviate this loss bought one of the cylinders, and have had it in constant use day and, night for two years, drying between 10,000 and 14,000 bushels per week. They find that the grain is not only dried, but the musty smell removed and the colour of the sample improved. Conditioning for market is not the only use for the cylinder—barley, oats, and all light corn for stock feeding should be dried. It is well known that oats undergo a chemical change for the better by kiln•dry- ing. But there are many objections to kiln-drying; the grain near the floor gets roasted, that on the surface is only scalded, and when burned the scorched grain re-absorbs the the steam rising from below. In the cylinder the process is continuous, and scorching and scalding alike impossible. Hence seed corn and barley for malting can both be dried by this process, whilst kilns, though often tried, have always failed. For hops also the cylinder is far better than the old Oast house, and another use for it has just been found in the drying of the pulp of the apple after cider pressing. The cells of Mr. Gibbs' machine thoroughly scatter the grain, so that every berry is separately and equally dried, whilst the louvres have a scouring as well as a drying ac- tion. A far higher temperature and stronger blast can be used than in any other known machine, and this accounts for the unusually large yield of 850 tons per week from one cylinder. Coke is generally used as fuel, the hot air being taken directly from the furnace as in kiln-drying, but the waste heat from any existing furnace can be drawn by the fan through brick flues for even such distances as 50 or 100 feet, so as to dispense with all fuel cost. On the other hand, when preferred the air can be heated by a steam coil. THE DUKE OF SUTHERLAND'S LAND REC LAMATIONS.— The Royal Commissioners at present inquiring into the state of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland paid a visit on Fri- day to the land which the Duke of Sutherland is reclaiming at Kinbrace. His Grace himself, accompanied by Sir Arnold Kemball and Mr. Greig, who has been carrying on the opera- tions, met the Commissioners at Kinhrace station, and showed them over the land. The Duke has reclaimed about 400 acres, which he converted into three farms. The re- claimed land is fitted for crops, and the three farms have between them about 5,000 acres of pasture for grazing sheep. Each farm has been supplied with suitable steadings built of concrete, but when they were advertised no one came for- ward to take them up singly, which was the. Duke's desire, the result being that the three had to be let as one to a gentle- man from the south. This experiment, in its way, proves one thing, that farms of 100 acres, even though they could be had, would not readily be taken up by the crofters, and for smaller farms it is a question if a rental could be ob- tained to repay any proprietor for erecting buildings for human habitations. His Grace afterwards showed the Com- missioners some land in the course of reclamation, the work being done entirely by mechanical instead of manual labour, and the way the immense ploughs turned up the turf to a depth of 2i feet and unrooted large boulders, evoked the keenest interest on the part of the Commissioners. In this Case also the coet of reclamation is very large, and the pro- bability is that the Duke of Sutherlaha may ultimately be compelled to relinquish the task, taking some other means of utilising the enormous tract of land at present useless except for sporting purposes. What direction those efforts may take it is impossible to say, but already experiments have been begun with the planting of trees, and probably it is in this direction that this waste land may be ultimately employed at Kinhrace. The Duke's private saloon and engine were in waiting to take the party down to Helms. dale, and, with his Grace as driver, a smart run took the Commissioners to Helmsdale shortly after six o'clock.

div.head: a............. 111.11............
div.p: Nothing is degrading which a high and graceful purpose ennobles, and offices the most menial cease to be menial the moment they are wrought in love. What services are ren- dered around the bed of sickness which, else considered mean, become at once holy and quite inalienable rights! To smooth the pillow, to proffer nourishment, to soothe or obey the fancies of the delirious will, to sit for hours as a mere sentinel of the feverish sleep—these things are sud- denly erected, by their relation to hope and life, into sacred privileges. ADIES' MECHANICAL TALL—Mr. Mc I think it is, who tells us some very good stories about the way in which two Chinese gentlemen contrive to keep up a long talk without saying a word which has any meaning in it. Something like this is occasionally heard on this side of the Great Wall. The best Chinese talkers I know are some pretty women whom I meet from time to time. Pleasant, airy, complimentary, the little flakes of flattery glimmering in their talk like the bits of gold-leaf in eau-de-vie de Dantzic ; their accents flowing on in a soft ripple,—never a wave, and I never a calm; words nicely fitted, but never a coloured phrase or a high-flavoured epithet; they tarn air into syl- lables so gracefully, that we find meaning for the music they make as we find faces in the coals and fairy palaces in the clouds. There is something very odd, though, about this mechanical talk. You have sometimes been in a train on the railroad when the engine was detached a long way from the station you were approaching? Well, you have noticed how quietly and rapidly the cars kept on, just air if the locomotive were drawing them? Indeed, you would not have suspected that you were travelling on the .strength of a dead fact, if you had not seen the engine running away from you on a side-track. Upon my conscience, I believe , some of these pretty women detach their minds entirely, sometimes, from their talk,—and, what is more, that we never know the difference. Their lips let off the fluty syl- lables just as their fingers would sprinkle the music-drops from their pianos; unconscious habit turns the phrase of thought into words just as it does that of music into notes. Well, they govern the world for all that,—these sweet- lipped women,—tecanse beauty is the index of a larger fact than wisdom.-0. Wendell Holmes in "The Professor at the Breakfast Table." ECONOMY IN THE KITCHEN.—I have mentioned that I believe economy to be the soul of cookery. There is, per- haps, no word in the English language so little understood aS this word economy. Just as political economists are too often considered by the vulgar to be men of hard hearts, so, too, in the art of cookery is. economy often associated with meanness and stinginess. I have no hesitation in saying it will be invariably found that the better the cook the more economy will be practised. There is more waste in the cot- tage than in the palace, for the simple reason that the cottage cook is entirely ignorant of an art which the chef has brought to perfection. What your so-called good plain cooks throw away, an ingenious French artiste will make into entrees. The French are a nation of cooks, and they cannot afford to dine without soup. Probably the contents of the dust-bins of England would more than fill the soup. tureens of France. I will give a very simple instance of what I term economy in the ordinary living of middle-class families. We all know that grand old-fashioned piece de resistance, the British sirloin. Who has not seen it in its last stages ?—the under-cut gone; the upper part dug out, on which some greedy individual has evidently grasped after the under-done piece in the middle, but who, at the same time, has entirely, ignored the end. The kitchen more than follows suit to the dining-room, and what is despised above is scorned below, and perhaps the real destination of the end of the sirloin, which the young housekeeper fondly imagines has done for the servants' supper, has in reality supplied the kennel. Suppose, now, this end had been cut off before the joint was roasted, and placed in a little salt water, a nice, wholesome, and agreeable hot dinner would have been obtainable with the assistance of some boiled greens and potatoes. A little forethought in these matters constitutes real economy. Scraps of meat, fag ends of pieces of bacon, too often wasted, will, with a little judicious management, make nice a dish of rissoles. There can be no doubt that the most economical institution in any kitchen is the stock-pot; and it is in this respect that our French neighbours show their enormous superiority over ourselves. It is obvious that the larger the kitchen, and the greater the number of the persons to be supplied with food, the greater will be the number of odds and ends that find their way back from the dining-room. In private houses it will be too often found that huge plates of what are ingeniously termed "broken victuals" are given to the dog, the greater portion of which, if placed in the stock-pot, would have been converted into most excellent soup. Now, it is un- questionably not agreeable to the English taste to use for culinary purposes bones that have been left upon plates. The economy of boning a joint—for instance, a loin of mutton—before cooking it is very considerable, as the bones, which in one case would have been left only half- scraped upon the plates, are in the other converted into excellent soup. At the call of time each side had scored four goals. so that another match Was rendered necessary. This took place at Ilayflock on Saturday afternoon last, and after a one-side game the Temperance men secured a splendid victory by five goals to none. The weather Was very unfavourable, but this did not deter about 300 spectators assembling to witness the contest. During the first half the home eleven played with the wind and ground in their favour, and to the delight of their supporters severely pressed their opponents. Before the chaege of ends they succeeded in scoring four goals, while tho etacksteads players were unable to secure a single • point. A SEVENTH Smos.—Sir William Thomson, the eminent Professor of Mathematics in the University of Glasgow, in his inaugural address, delivered last week, as President of the Midland Institute at Birmingham, broached the idea of the existence of a magnetic sense. This sense he called the seventh sense, to distinguish it from our other six senses— namely, those of sight, hearing, taste, smell,heat, and force. If there was not a distinct magnetic sense, it was a very great wonder that there was not The study of magnetism was a very recondite subject. One very wonderful discovery that was made in electric magnetism was made by Faraday, and worked out very admirably by Foucauld, an excellent French experimenter,.showinF that a piece of copper, or a piece of silver, let fall between the poles of a magnet, would fall dow2 slowly, as if through mud. Was it conceivable that, U a piece of copper could scarcely move through the air between the poles of an electric magnet,.that a human being or living creature, in the same position, would ex- perience no effect? Lord Lindsay got an enormous mag- nets so large that the head of any person wishing to try the experiment could get well between the poles; and the re- salt of the experiment was marvellous, the marvel being that nothing was perceived. Sir William Thomson, how- ever, was not willing to admit that the investigation was I completed. He could not but think that the quality of I matter in the air, which produced such a prodigious effect on a piece of metal, could be absolutely without any per- ceptible effect whatever on a living body. He thought the experiment was worth repeating; and it was worth 0-mm- -1 ining whether or not an exceedingly powerful magnetic force was without perceptible effect on a living vegetable cz animal body. His own speculations had led him to con- clude that there might be a seventh or magnetic sense; and that it was possible an exceedingly powerful magnetic effect might be Produced on living bodies that could not be ex- plained by heat, force, or any other aensati,on,—British Medical Journal,
