div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

A general strike in the coal trade of Yorkshire and the Midlands is threatened. The Salvation Army Barracks at Yarmsuth have been destroyed by fire, the origin of which is nnkown. SUSPECTED MURDER IN LONDON. - The body of Mr. Bullwinkle, a licensed victualler, of St. GeorFe's-in-the- East, London, was found in the Thames on Friday, under circumstances suggesting that he had died from violence. A lighter, having eight men on board, capsized in Hartle- pool harbour on Saturday whilst in tow of a steam tug. Two of the eight were drowned, one was crushed to death between the vessels, and the others were with some difficulty rescued alive. Ingram Bilbrough, of Poppleton, Yorkshire, was charged at Birmingham Police Court, on Tuesday, with having in his possession two dies for the purpose of producing spu- rious sovereigns. He was committed for trial at the

assizes. Part of the wall of the new board school in course of erection at Stanningley, near Leeds, suddenly fell on Saturday morning, severely injuring Charles Gould, fore- man mason, of Leeds, and Thomas Oltrien, labourer, of Stanningley. , Mr. John Newton Mappin, of Ranmoor, Sheffield, has be- queathed to the town of Sheffield his magnificent collection of pictures, .which are said to be worth £60,000, together With a sum of £15,000 for the erection of a suitable building to contain them. ANOTHER DEFAULTING ACCOUNTANT.—It was reported at a meeting of the General Purposes Committee of the Wol- verhampton Town Council that !lie accounts of the borough accountant, Mr. Bryan, had been examki aud a deficiency of £1,300 discovered. FAILURE OF Barcvmus.—A petition for liquidation has been filed in the Wakefield Bankruptcy Court on behalf of ' William John and Benjamin Mitchell, trading as Mitchell Brothers, brewers, at Whitwood Wakefield. The liabilities are estimated at over £20,000. PRESENTATION TO CAPTAIN SHAW DiE QuErs._ 1 Captain Shaw has a resent tom the Queen of a handsome ' • " P- —.rote clock, with the following inscripticn resznted to Captain Shag, Superintendent of the Metro- Inolitan Fire Brigade, by Victoria It. 1., 1883." CA:rIItRkNE FLANNAGAN AND MARGARET HIGGINS were 01".'Tuesday taken before the Liverpool Stipendiary, charged with poisoning Higgins's husband by the administration of arsenic. The proceedings were purely formal, the prisoners being remanded for a further period of seven days. The towel weavers at Ashton, who have been on strike nine weeks against a proposed reduction of per cent. in Wave, have accepted a reduction of ak per cent., and work has been resumed. This arrangement is to terminate in three months if trade should continue unsatisfactory. On Saturday, a verdict of accidental death was returned at an inquest at Driffield on the body of William Kavanagh, aged 27, a native of Belfast, 'who died from frightful injur- ies sustained by leaping into a deep ehaik pit, which he mistOok for a narrow watercourse, on the estate of Lord

Halifax. The Earl of Leicester (Lord Lieutenant of Norfolk), pre- siding at the annual meeting on Saturday of the Norfolk and Norwich Prisoners' Aid Society, said that crime was steadily decreasing, but not until there was J. prisoners' aid society in connection with every prison would the prison system be efficient Dr. Haffenden, who was last week "charged at Hammer- smith Police Court with procurirq abortion, and was ad- mitted to ball, was found dead ett Tuesday morning in his bedroom at Bath Place, KeasiTtgton. It is believed that the deceased committed suicide by poisoning. He left behind him a written statement -pretesting his innocence. There was a renewal 'on Sunday of the disgraceful scenes 'Which have followed the iniLition of the Rev. Mr. Fitzßoy, incumbent of St. Jude's, Hardwick-street, Liverpool. Not- withstanding the &ace of the bishop, Mr. Fitzßoy held a service in the church, and a row ensued, in the course of Which several of the communion table emblems were destroyed. George Goo av nged 36, dock labourer, was charged at the Stratford Petty Sessions, on Saturday, on four charges of uttering counterfeit coin. The prisoner, who was -proseeuted by the Treasury, was committed for trial. He was at once removed to the cells at the back of the court, but when the commitment had been made out be was found to have escaped. Edward Collins, hairdresser, charged with attempting to murder Benjamin Bass, butler to Mr. Townsend, Harley- street, London, was on Tuesday committed for trial. The injored man stated that on the night of September 29th the prisoner, whom he had known for two years, paid him a viait, and, after making some inquiries about the plate, at- tacked him with a razor. William Sherbourne, a man who said he "could not beg and would not steal," and did not think it right that "in a free country a man should lie down and starve," was on Monday at the Bow-street Police Court, London, fined 103 and costs and the amount of damage done for having on Saturday afternoon wilfully thrown a stone through one of the windows at the Home Office. At a meeting at Wrexham a resolution was passed calling upon the Welsh members of Parliament to press for the removal of Mr. Homersham Cox from the position of County Court judge in Wales. Mr. Cox has given great offence to the Welsh people) by attributing to them a prone- ness to commit perjury; and it is retorted upon him in turn that he is ignorant of the native tongue. TEE GREA.T BASK ROBBERIES.—At the Guildhall Police Coprt, London, on Monday, John Davis Watters, Arundel Villa, West Croydon, stockbroker, was formally brought before Sir Thomas S. Owden, by arrangement, to be formally remanded until the 30th inst., on the charge of being con- cerned with Warden, the late secretary of the London and River Plate Bank, in stealing and converting to their own use over £lOO,OOO worth of securities belonging to the bank. Sesen ex ST. -PAUL'S CATIIEDRAL.—During the servize on Sunday evening at St. Paul's Cathedral, and while the sermon was being preached by the Rev. W. C. Ingram, vicar of St. Matthew's, Leicester, a man in the congregation caused considerable disturbance by shouting and gesticulat- ing wildly. He was at once seized by the police on duty, and conveyed with some difficulty to the police station. The offender, when charged at the police station, said he was a preacher. THE LIVERPOOL MURDER.—Lewis Parry, a labourer, was charged at Liverpool on Tuesday with rue murder of a young woman named Susannah Hutton, who was beaten to death with a large stone and then flung into the Leeds and Liverpool Canal on the night of the 13th inst. The evi- dence against the prisoner was circumstantial, but of the strongest possible character. He was fatly committed for trial at the assizes. SHOCKING OUTRAGE BY AN IRONWORKER —.7 as. Hogan, an ironworker, was brought up at Wednesbury, on Tuesday, on a charge of committing a shocking outrage on his step- 'father, Richard Jackton. Oa Monday night the prisoner went home and threateaed to murder his mother, and upon the prosecutor interfering the prisoner broke a bottle and jumped upon hie head, inflicting frightful injuries. Prose- cutor was found lying in a pool of blood, and for some time was believed to be dead. Mr. ROBERTSON, M.P. for Shrewsbury and a gentleman largely interested in the mineral trade of North Wales has laid before a meeting at Chester a scheme which he has formed for converting the River Dee, between Chester and Connah's Quay, into a canal navigable by vessels of large tonnage. It is stated that the expenditure will not exceed half a million sterling, and that application will be at once made for Parliamentary powers to construct the canal. The proposal is favourably regarded in the city most interested. kremlin. TO WRECK A TRAIN. A dastardly attempt was made on Sunday morning to wreck the South-Western • mail train from London. About two miles from Dorchester Station a heavy iron drag had been placed across the metals, but the train, which was running at a high speed, fortun- ately cut through the obstruction. Some trifling damage was caused to the carriages, and several passengers were shaken. The srfikes of the drag came in contact with the gas cylinder in the postal van, nearly causing an explo- sion. STEALING HUMAN REMAINS.—At Nottingham, on Tues- day, Harriet Hemsley was charged, on remand, with steal- ing a box, containing human remains, the property of a medical student, named William Henry Turton, who was tn .•at&te to Edinburgh from ['canon. The box was left in the cloak-room of the Nottingham Midland Railway Station. on Saturday, and the prisoner made off with It. On discover- ing the nature of the contents she attempted to return it to the railway station, but was apprehended. She was sen- tenced to three months' imprisonment. SETTING FIRE TO A REFORMATORY—At the county ses- sions at Bristol, on Monday, two Youths named Buttery and Jones were charged with setting lire to Kingswood Reform- atory, near Bristol, in which there are about 150 boys. On Wednesday the lads broke open the oil store stole a quan- tity of petroleum with which they saturated the beds in one of the dormitories and set fire to the bedding. Next day they stole two gallons of oil and were about to set fire to the rooms of the assistant masters, when they were detected. The prisoners pleaded that they were tired of the place, and wanted to get away. They were committed for trial. Another dairyman at Dundee has been summoned before the Sheriff for selling milk from his premises whilst cases Of infectious disease were under treatment therein. The defendant, James Henderson, was supplying a large number of residents in the town with nellk whilst three of his c:eil- dren were suffering from typhoid fever. From this criminal recklessness on his pert there followed a general visitation of the epidemic, nearly one hundred persons having been attacked in one district of Dundee where Henderson's "round" was situated. An order was m'ade for the closing Om the dairy for seven weeks, the removal of Henderson's Children to hoepital, and a thorough disinfection of the premises. ANOTHER C.OLVLERY EXPLOSION AT Bans'eLEY.—During Monday afternoon, whilst a band of explorers were seeking to recover the bodies remaining in the Carleton Colliery at Barnsley—the scene,of the diiastrous explosion of Friday laBt—a second explosion of gas occurred. Some of those in the pit were severely burned, and at one time it was ex- pected that three of them, a colliery owner, manager, and Dlr. Lupton, the lecturee on mining at Leeds college, bad lost their lives. A further gallant effort was made by valunteers from the pit bank, and eventually the three gentlemen, who had penetrated to the scene of the first explosion, were rescued alive. Two of them were scorched, DOI not dangerously. The seersh operations were stopped. fjA.TING'S COUGH LOZENGES cures Coughs, AEtluna, Bran- is.-5-Ifedical testimony stales the 110 other meeteine is so errectual in the cure of these dangerous ntalalies. Oae I,..ncru:e !tone gives ease, one or two at bed ti:ne enqurpa For ng ZiffiCalty of breathing th.v. 2.1 e tree:lea e. entemists, tc Sins, 1/11 and 9 ,at'.---I(irt.

Three navvies were buried by a landslip in a railway cut- ting near Andover on Wednesday night. One was killed. The foundation stone of public buildings which are to be erected in Middlesborough at a cost of about £lOO,OOO WAa laid, on Wednesday, by the mayor of that borough. The Mayor of Bradford (Alderman F. rriestman) on Tuesday morning gave a breakfast to about 200 children employed in the street sale of newspapers, matches, J:c. The Corporation of Rochester have just sealed an agree- ment with the Earl of Jersey for purchasing Rochester Castle and the castle grounds for public use for £B,OOO. If has now:been definitely decided that the constables of the Metropolitan Police are to be armed with revolvers. At first the arm will only be issued to trusted men who are stationed upon remote suburban beats. The Huddersfield police have arrested John Shaw, for- merly a railway clerk, and at present out of employment, on a charge of causing the death of his niece, Ann Jane Clarke, wife of a coachman at Slaithwaite. A reward of £lOO has been offered by the Home Secre- tary fcr the apprehension of the murderer or murderers of Mr. Bottomley, of Keighley, who was found killed and robbed at Monkbridge, Leeds, on the 4th inst. A serious fire occurred at West Hartlepool on Thursday evening, on the premises of Mr. Henry Burton, upholsterer, Surtees-street. The building, which had a frontage of 40 feet, was distroyed. The total loss, about £2,000, is

covered by insurance. Her Majesty's troopship Humber arrived at Limassol on Wednesday afternoon, from Malta, with a draft of nine men from Cyprus, and left again during tte night with about 3D convalescents for Egypt. The Mediterranean squadron is expected to visit Cyprus next month. At Leeds quarter sessions, Sam Brook, a deaf mute, pleaded guilty to setting fire to a quantity of gunpowder in Briggate and thus inflicting grevious bodily harm upon Henry iye, labourer. The recorder bound the prisoner over in his own recognisances to come np for judgment when

called upon. A ehort rim- • t..Vvilliarn Smith engine, or Lovirer agc Gornal, threw a dog down a disused pit shaft. Ten. days afterwards the animal was heard moaning iv the shaft, and some men recovered it alive, and it is now well and hearty. Smith was on Wednesday charged with cruelty to the dog, and his defence was that be wanted to kill it expeditiously.

He was fined £5 and costs. Before the Leicester magistrates, on Wednesday, 21 per- sons were summoned for refusing to .have their children vaccinated. The defendants urged conscientious objections on account of death and injury having, occurred in their families through vaccination. It is said that there are several thousand unvaccinated children in the town, and that a thousand parents are to be summoned. Several waggons of a goods train were, on Wednav, thrown off the line in the Summit Tunnel on the Lanc.a- shire and Yorkshire Railway, through a bag of fligtian fall ing off one of the Waggons. About 20 yards of rails 'iNrere torn up, several trucks were much damaged, and the line was eutirely blocked against goods traffic. The 7,assenger traffic was carried on by a single line, aati. was much

delayed. SHOCKING AFFAIR.—On Wednesday night a gentleman farmer named Tomkins., residing at the Ckdars, London-road, Maidstone, attempted to cut ht a wife's throat with a razor, and upon assistance being summoned by the servants cut his own throat in a shocking manner. Mrs. Tonikins received a severe gash across the forehead, and her hands were also cut,. It is Ir.,upposed that Mr. Tomkins is mentally

effected. At a conference at Yorkshire and North Derbyshire miners' delegates, held at Rotherham on Wednesday—there being present 142 delegate, representing 41,000 men—resolutions were passed expressing regret at the refusal of the em- ployers to give an advance of 15 per cent. in waggs, de- claring the intention to prosecute the demand by all legitimate means, and deciding that 41,000 notices should

be printed. An explosion occurred at the gas works belonging to the Bury Corporation. A stoker, named William Hine, was killed, and much damage was done to property. The ex- plosion occurred in a large tank containing ta,r and am- moniacal liquor. The tar evolves a most explosive gas, and it is thought the explosion must •have taken place through this gas coming in contact with the hot cinders, which are slacked in the adjoining retort house. ANOTHER MISTAKE BY A BANK OFFICIAL—A mistake somewhat similar to the one which recently occurred in an English bank has just been made by an official in the Bank of Ireland. In exchanging English for Irish notes he paid over to a cattle dealer i.:700 instead of £5OO. On discovering the mistake he proceeded to Nap fair in the hope of recog- nising the dealer, but this he failed to do, and then the matter was placed in the hands of the police. THE BIRMINGHAM RANK FRAUDS. At a meeting at Birmingham, on Wednesday, the resolutions for the transfer of the liabilities and assets of the Birmingham Union Bank to the Birmingham and Midland Bank, Limited, upon the terms already published were confirmed. The transfer was rendered necessary by the extensive defalcations of the manager of the Union Bank, Mr. Burgan, who is no in custody at Havre awaiting eztradition to England. A Roman Catholic priest, named Father Consuello, was charged at Leicester, on Thursday, with assaulting a lad named Towers, in St. Patrick's Day School. The com- plainant did not attend mass on Sunday, and on Monday refused to kneel in school when directed, whereupon the defendant held him between his knees and flogged him with a cane. The defence was that the lad was disrespectful and violent. The bench cautioned the defendant, but did not impose a fine. THE LrmarooL_CANAL TRAGEDY.—The inquest on the

body of Susannah Halton, the young woman who was mur- dered on the banks of the Liverpool Canal, and whose body was afterwards discovered in the canal on the evening of Saturday, the 13(11 inst., was resumed on Thursday. The evidence was similar to that given at the police court, and the jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against Lewis Parry, Nvho on Tuesday was committed to the assizes by the stipendiary on the capital charge. OUTBREAK OF PLEURO-PNEUMONIA IN LANCASHIRE.— The Inspector under the Cattle Diseases Act for the Wigan district reported to the Clerk of the Peace on Thursday morning that a case of pleuro-pneumonia, one of the most fatal forms of cattle disease, had broken out on the farm of William Gregory, ellorwich, near Wigan. The affected animal has been slaughtered. There are at present about 170 farms affected with the disease in Lancashire, almost 80 being in the Salford and 60 in the West Derby Hundreds. A pensioner of the Royal Engineers, named William James Wilson, was on Thursday committed for trial at Canterbury on a charge 0; perjury, alleged to have been committed in a declaration made in an application for a cer- tificate of identity to enable him to draw his pension. He stated that the original certificate was lost. From subse- quent information it appeared that he had mortgaged the document to a gentleman named Wilson, of the Wellington Hotel, Hunslet, Leeds, for £4. Upon this the Treasury in- stituted proceedings. A DISGRACEFUL HOAX.—Tlie Rev. L. Chamberlin, vicar of Chatburn, is making inquiries to discover the perpetrator or perpetratress 6f a disgraceful hoax. Last week a letter was sent to Chatburn Vicarage asking the vicar to publish the banns of marriage between two individuals residing in Chatburn. Accordingly the vicar made the announcement at the parish church on Suiday, but after service it was dis- covered that the letter was only intended forthe perpetration of a huge joke, it being a forged letter. The discomfiture and indignation of the parties upon whom the hoax was played may be imagined. A SLUR ON THE MODERN SCHOOLBOY. -- The question of the extent to which a schoolmaster may punish his pupils came before the magistrate at Woolwich on Tuesday, when the headmaster of Shooter's-hill National School was summoned for flogging a boy. The father did net object to the boy being punished, but considered he ought not to be flogged in a way the law would not tolerate had he been a pony. The magistrate remarked that the rising generation of boys seemed rather "soft," but, as he considered the punishment had been excessive, he adjourned the summons that the school managers might investigate the case. SEerrEetcE ON A NOTORIOI7S BURGLAR.—At Surrey Ses- sions, on Tuesday, Thomas Webb, a returned convict, was found guilty of being concetned, with two others now under- going imprisonment, in a burglary at Wimbledon, on the 25th May last. When arrested, the police found in the pri- soner's house eighty-three skeleton keys, a loaded revolver, a rope ladder, a number of " jenanoies," and various other housebreaking implements. The prisoner was sentenced in 1852 to ten years' transportation, and in 1860 to twenty years' penal servitude. He was sentenced to a further term of twenty years' penal servitude, and left the dock laughing. A BETTING SALOON FOR BOY S.—An important betting prosecution was heard at Birmingham on Wednesday. Gee. Cale, stationer, was summoned for keeping a house for the purpose of betting. It was proved by three youths under 14 years that they went to the defendant's shop snd backed horses for the Cambridgeshire; that defendant's house was princioallay used for betting transactions, and that it was d` common thing for boys of all ages t 3 go and deposit eix- pences and shillings upon different horses. The magistrates said they could not conceive a more reprehensible practice, and it seemed from the evidence that bstting men as well as boys were In the habit of constantly assembling at the house. Defendant was fined £2O and costs. A DYNAMITE HOA.X.—Shortly after 10 o'clock on Wed- nesday evening the caretaker of the Methodist New Con- nexion Chapel, Woodhouse•lane, Leeds, presented himself before the night inspector at the Town Hall and demanded the assistance of a constable to remove a suspicious-looking parcel which lay on a window-sill in the yard of the chapel. Constable Moor was accordingly sent, and the two nude all speed to Woodhouse-lane. The parcel—eviden`ly a box carefully wrapped in brawn piper—was removed, and con- veyed with great caution to the Town Hall. The inscrip- tion in pencil, "Dynamite, for the love of Ireland," Laving been read, everyone retired to a safe distance except the constable, who carefully cut the string, unfold:l the paper, I opened the box, and diicloscd—a dead cot. SHOCKING SUICIDE ON BOARD THE AL SKA..—AbOUt half-past twelve o'clock on Saturday, as the Union steam- ship Alaska was about to proceed on the voyaae to America it was discovered that a man named Thomas Fleming. second steward, had cut his throat in his berth. He was at once put on board a tender and taken to the stage, whence he was removed to the Northern Hospital, where he died from his injuries., which were so severe that his head was almost severed from his b-ely. In his berth were found a table knife and a memorandum book, in which were written the following words :—" Dear wife and children, forgive me. lam mad. Dear friends, forgive me. Poor Tom Fleming. Drink killed--" Here the writing abruptly ceased; and le the memorandum book was smeared with blood it looked 1a1.,,,0ugh he had contmitte I the injuries while in the act of eerieiele. Decease(' Lad been drinking heavi `y.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27,1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27,1883.
PERSONAL.

• Sir Moses MontefeTre—ias entered upon the huniredth year of his age. The Archbishop of Canterbury is reported to be making satisfactory progress towards recovery. Sir Evelyn and Lady Wood and family arrived in Dover on Saturday, and left for Calais, en route for Egypt. The Bishop of Peterborough is suffering from illness which is pronounced by his medical attendant to he of a serious character. The Rev. Charles B. Langdon, of University College, Oxford, and recently a curate of Plympton, St. Mary, Ply- mouth, hes joined the Roman Catholic Church, and is preparing for the priesthood. Mr. R. C. Woodville, the eminent painter of battle pieces, has, by command of Her Majesty, engaged to execute a large picture representing the battle of Tel-Kebir, as seen from the position in the rear, where Prince Arthur was with his regiment of the Guards. Mr. l'iroodville expects to have the work ready fur next year's academy. Lord and Lady Lansdowne landed on Tuesday at Quebec, and the new Governor General was sworn in with great ceremony by the judges, in the presence of the Marquis of Lorne and the Ministers. His Lordship was received by the people with great enthusiasm. No exceptional incident of any kind occurred. There has not appeared the slightest foundation for the report that a conspiracy had been formed to assassinate the Marquis. DEATH OF CAPTAIN MAYNE Rl.—The death is an- nounced of Captain Mayne Reid, the well-known novelist. He had bean ailing for the past two years, and was in his 67th year, but died in harness, baNlng half comnleted a neW work. Captain Reid had but recently been granted an added pension from the Mexican Government for services rendered. He was London correspondent of the New York Tribune, but better known as the author of dashing stories of travel and adventure. • ~, Mr. CEadstone has written to the secretary of the Liberal tiommittee of the Edinburgh University studenie apres- sing his hopes for the success of Mr. Trevelyan i* the con- test for the Lord Rectorship. While desiring for Professor Blackie every honour which a contest not political cou'd afford him, Mr. Gladstone fears that in this political con- test, while it may be impossible for him to win, his stand- ing may divert votes from what he would wish to 01111 the good cause, and thus impair, or worse than impair, th:„ expression of the ante of the University which he ta4 so long adorned. Ma. CHILDERS.—The Chancellor of tte Exchequer has extended his visit to North Wales. On Monday the right hon. gentler-no, accompanied ty Mrs. and the Misses Chil- ders. ;ad Mr. and Mrs. Rat'- joone, visited the toy railway at driving by coach to Beddgelert, at Pt the t mfoot ovc f. afterwardssn o)n where the pass of Aberglasllyn and Gelert's grave 'were visited. The party afterwards returned to GlanvQ,adw, the residence of Mr. Rathbone, M.P. The Pwlihela -Liberal Committee and Mr. Derbyshire, chairman of the Carnarvonshire Liberal Association, dined with Mr. Childers in the evening.
lUREIGrN INTELLIGENCE.

Count Stefan Batthyany was shot dead on Monday, in a duel, at Temesvar. t, Ten men have lost their lives by an accident in an iron- foundry at Creuzot. Cholera is again spreading in Alexandria. Four deaths occurred in the city on Tuesday. The news that a treaty of peace between Peru and Chili has been signed has been officially continued. It is reportad ir Alexandria that the Egyptian troops have obtained a victory in the Seudan. The Mandi, it is dealared, has been completely defeated. A mining torpEdo factory has exploded at Wilkesbarre, Pennsylvania, and of eight children employed five were killed and the others injured. The convention of 900 electors returned by the paople of Ecuador have nominated Don Jose Matir Placid() Centeno Provisional President of the Republic.

Intelligence received in San Prancieco from Hong Kong states that Sir Harry Parkes, the British Minister, was about to leave for Corea in order to negotiate a new treaty with that country. The steamship Britannic arrived at New York on Sunday, with Mr. Henry Irving and Miss Ellen Terry on board. The distinguished players were both well, and appeared to have enjoyed the voyage. The total number of immigrants who settled in the Dominion of Canada during the nine months ending Sep- tember 30 last, WO3 01,779, as compared with 76,378 in the corresponding period of last year. ESCAPE OF A SOCIALIST LEAbEP,.—According to private advices from Lemburg, one of the leaders of the Socialist party in Galicia has just escaped from prison, with the as- sistance of his friends, in open day. A severe shock of earthquake, lasting some three seconds, was felt on Saturday in the Spanish provinces of Cadiz Huelva, No damage was done. A elialet shot was also felt at Malta on Sunday motiling, and a Trieete, on Mon- day, no damage being done. The accounts traesinitte.:l of the loss of life through the earthquake in Anatol;.,a are declared at Athens to be " enore mously exaggere,*(ed.,, It should be stated, however, that the Vice Consul has informed Lord Dufferin that the kJsfl • and intured number a thousand. It is stated- in a Constantinople telegram that three per- sons were recently captured by brigands near Zipka, in the Egridereh Mountains, and a ransom of £5OO was demanded for each of them. The Military Commander of the dis- trict, however, succeeded in effecting their release. Several days ago it was reported that Midhat Pasha had escaped, or had been permitted to escape, from his place of confinement. The editors of the vernacular papers at Con- stantinople, who republished the report, have been summoned to the palace, and reprimanded. The report was untrue. A Vienna telegram states that a serous fight has occurred between two bands of gipsies in the Hungarian commitat of Weissenburg. The men were mounted and armed with hatchets, and the women and children joined in the fray. Four of the combatants were killed and two severely wounded, while many received serious injuries. A despatch from Tamatave, dated the 4th inst., says there appeared at that time to be no probability of a peaceable settlement of the questions at issue between the Hovas and the French. It was feared that the French ships were about to recommence ihe work of destroying the coast towns, and a "general exodus" of the inhabitants had taken place. FALL OF A TRAIN THROUGH A BRIDGE. A railway train in northern New York, on Monday, fell through a bridge over the Champlain Canal, three persons being killed and 22 wounded, several fatally. Every person in the train, in fact, except a newsboy, was injured, and every coach wrecked, though the locomotive safely passed over the bridge. DISASTERS IN AMERICA. A broken rail on the Louis- ville and Nashville Railroad, near St. Louis, wrecked a pas- senger train, on Tuesday, GO passengers being injured, ten seriously.—A large building was destroyed by fire in St. Louis on Tuesday night, three of the occupants being burned to death.—Two fishing schooners were lost off the Massachusetts coast in Saturday night's gale, and 20 fisher- men were drowned.

PANIC IN A. MENAGERIE.—A Vienna correspondent telegraphs that during a performance in the Grand Menagerie of Kleberg, at Brun, a panic occurred among the audience. Just as the liontamer was ending his perfor- mance someone called out, "The lion has broken loose" The eiltct was instantaneous. All the audience rose and hurried to the doors. The pressure was so great that many persons received injuries. THE DYNAMITE CONSPIRACY.—A despatch from llalifax says :—Among the luggage of the Irishmen arrested there last week are tin boxes exactly answering to the discription of dynamite box used in the explosion of Government build- ings in London, and also a keyhole saw of superior workman- ship, and a set of hooks adapted for the purpose of hauling a man in a swimming suit up a vessel's side.—Mr. Patrick Egan has filed a statement in the District Court, Lincoln, Nebraska, announcing his intention of becoming an American citizen. _

THE ARREST OF SUPPOSED FENIANS IN NOVA SCOTIA.—A Reuter's New York telegram, dated October 20, says : Intelligence received here from Halifax states that since the arrest of the two men named William Bracken and Jas. Holmes, the six British war ships at Halifax have been direfully guarded, particularly at night. Vice-Admiral Sir John Commerell, commander of Northampton, had stated that the articles found on the prisoners were exactly suited to the intentions of which they were suspected. Ife had ordered the chief gun instructor of the Northampton to fully explain to the law officers the serious harm which an improper use of the confiscated explosives and apparatus was capable of causing. EXTRAORDINARY MURDERS AT STRASBUltG.—Telegrams from S:rasburg state that great excitement prevails in the garrison and amongst the German population by the dis- covery of two crimes, committed under most mysterious cir- cumstances. Early on Tuesday morning the b )dy of a young German named •Lienhart, an assistant in the estab- lishment of Herr Reb, an apothecary, was found with f-,ar- ful wounds upon it, which leave no doubt that-he was foully murdered. Hardly had the police time to convey Lienhart's body to the Morgue when news was brought to them of another outrage. In this case the victim was a military -sentinel, who was found lying on the groond near his post, with hie head smashed, and otherwise terribly in- jured.
1 11 ELAND.
Two houses and a large quintity of farm produce were destroyed by lire, on Sunday, at Pilmore, a few miles from Youghal.

George -Philp Stanhope, Earl of Chesterfield, died at the residence of Mr. A. Montgomery Stewart, Killendonagh, near Lifford, connty Donegal, on Friday evening, after a prolonged Michael Watters, 19, who was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude at Belfast assizes in March last for compli- city in the Patriotic Brotherhoo,l conspiracy, died in Mount- joy Prison, Dublin, on Wednesday. At the Dublin Commission Court, on Thursday, Joseph Poole was indicted for the murder of John Kenny in Seville-place. Owing to the illness of Dr. Webb, leading counsel for the defence, the trial was adjourned. The Marquis of Donegal!, who is owner of extensive pro- perty in and around Belfast, died at Brighton on Saturday. lie has not visited Belfast since 1864. Ormeau Parla, in which his residence formerly stood, is now a public park. A SOLDIER SENTENCED TO DEATIL—At the Dublin Com- mission Court, on Thursday, Private Thomas Wilson, of the East Kent Regiment, was found guilty of the murder of Corporal Ernest Hope at the Linenhall Barracks on the 26th July last, by shooting him through the back, and was sentenced to death. • SHOOTING A rOACHEE.—Thomas Caulfield, supposed to be a poacher, was shot on Monday morning, at Thomas- town, near Ballinasloe, by a gamekeeper in the employment of Mrs. Nattair, a lady who for the past two years has been boycotted and under police protection. The gamekeeper observed the man creeping along, and concluding his purpose was evil tiredsit him. The gamekeeper has been arrested. Intelligence has reached Thurles of a murderous assault or a sheriff s officer named Kane, in the mountain district, a few miles from the town. Kane went with some assis- tants to the farm Of a man narnqd Dwyer, and seized some cattle on a decree for non-payment of rent. They were attackel by Dwyer and slime members of his family, and Kane was struck and terribly wounded about the head. He now lies in an uncongcious condition. SHOCKING OCCURRENCE ON AN IRISH RAILWAY.—At Drumquin, near Omagh, on Saturday evening, a middle- aged woman rushed on to the railway in front of an advanc- ing train. ,The gateman on duty at the crossing, seeing the woman's danger, ran to her assistance, and endeavoured to pull her off the line. It is said the woman resisted, and in the midst of the struggle the engine dashed round a curve and struck them both. The woman was decapitated and one _ _ _ .

leg was cut off; and the man was also dreadfully mangled, his body being ripped open by the guard rail in front of the engine. In both cases death was almost instantaneous. AGRARIAN OUTRAGE.—An agrarian outrage of a very daring character was perpetrated on Saturday, at Mushera Mountain, a wild district west of Macroom. It held a great notoriety in connection with the Moonlight outrages during the and agitation. It was in this district the Moonlight band, under Connel, the " captain," who afterwards turned approver, committed their chief depredations. The victim of the present outrage is Daniel Lucy, a bailiff and rent- warner on the estate of Mr. W. 11. Massey. At 11 o'clock he was found on the nvmantain road dangerously wounded in the head and body. He was in an unconscious state, but it was evident he was attacked by an armed party. Three arrests have been made. THE "THGEGHT READER" AND HIS MANACIER.—At the Dublin Police Court, on Tuesday, art application was made on behalf of Mr. living Bishop, the thought realer, against the proprieters of the Antient Concert ROght; for the return of a blackboard and some lithographs detained by the direc- tion of Mr. Bishop's manager, Mr. Gordon. The last-named gentleman appeared in court, and said he had a claim against Mr. Bishop for breach of contract. He had arranged to give Mr. Biskop £1,200 for six week's performaron, but Mr. Bishop had not fulfilled his engagement, and had gone away to Manchester. The magistrates held that the cause assigned was no justification for the detention of the articles in question, and ordered them to be given up.

THE EARLESTOWN COFFEE PALACE.—It is a pleasure to learn that the Coffee Palace, opened on the Market Ground some weeks ago, still continues to be well patronilid. The first quarterly meeting of the shareholders will he held in a few weeks, and it is r xpccted that a favourable report will be presented.

SUSPICIOUS DEATH AT WARRINGTON. SHOCKING REVELATIONS. At the Police Parade-room, Irlam-street, on Tuesday, Mr. T. W. Barker, coroner, held an inquiry touching the death of Elizabeth Turner, wife of Thomas Turner, labourer, of Rose-yard, off Dial-street, who died on Sunday, under sus- picious circumstances.—The facts of the case are shortly these :—On Sunday afternoon, the 14th inst., two of the deceased's neighbours, were attracted by moans to a closet in the yard, and they there found the deceased in an almost unconscious state. Her clothes were completely saturated with water, and her eyes were dreadfully blackened. She had a clog on one foot, and only a stocking on the other. The bruised state of the deceased led one of the neighbours te ask her if they might fetch a policeman or a doctor, but the deceased requested them net to fetch anyone. When asked "who had done it," the deceased replied, "Tom did it." She was helped into a neighbour's, and subsequently taken into her own house. On the following morning two of the neighbours went to the deceased's house to see the woman, but the husband's sister would not allow them to do so. On Sunday morning last, about half-past eight, the deceased died, and no elector bad been called in to eree her. The deceased and her husband were addicted to drink, and I had often quarrelled when drunk. Full particulars of tee I case may be gathered from the following evidence:— Mary Ann Taylor said she was the mother of the deceased, who was 25 years of age.--qieeannah Finn, wife of James Finn, of Cockhedge-lane, said she had known the deceased for some time. She had seen the deceased worse for drink. She saw her on Sunday week last in her own house, when she was so drunk that she could not speak. Her clothes wers. wet and her face was black. She saw her on the fol- leeeitig day lying on a bed on the boards upstairs. She asked her what was the matter, and she said she had fallen downstairs, and had also fallen in coming up the yard on the Saturday night. Tne deceased's husband came upstairs while she was there, but lie said nothing about the matter. She was present when the deceased died, and at that time her husband had gone for a doctor. She never heard the deceased blame her husband about the injuries she had re- ceived. BF the Foreman: When the husband came upstairs be was perfectly sober.—Sarah Flemming, wife of John Flemming, Rose-yard, said she had known the deceased about two years. On Sunday afternoon week, at four o'clock, witness heard moaning, as though someone was in great pain, but she could not tell from whence it proceeded. It continued until six o'clock in the evening, when Mrs. Shaw came into her house and told her that deceased was in a closet in the yard. Witness went with Mrs. Shaw to the place, and there found the deceased leaning against the doer-post. The deceased's chilies were very wet, and her eyes were blackened. They asked her if they might fetch a policeman or a doctor, and she said "No, don't." They took her into Mrs. Shaw's, and from there home. • Witness asked her " Who had done it," and she replied "Tom did it." Witness then proceeded home, acd on the following morning went to see the de- ceased, but Mrs. Whitworth (deceased's sister-in-law) would not allow her to do so, saying that no one should see her until the doctor had seen her.—By the Chief Constable: She heard no disturbance at Turner's on the Sunday after- noon, and had there been one she thought she would have heard it.—By the Foreman: When the deceased said "Tons did it," she did not say when or where.—A Juror: What made you ask her if you might fetch a policeman? There must have been some reason for it.—Witness (who did not appear to have fully comprehended the question): I don't know that there was any reason for it.—ln reply to further questions witness said : I saw deceased's husband when she was in our closet, but be did not give her any assistance. I have seen the deceased run down the yard.—The Coroner: Why has she run down the yard ?—Witness: I suppose to get out of the road of her husband. Mary Ann Shaw, wife of Samuel Shaw, Rose-yard, said sue had known deceased some years. Deceased liked beer, and witness had seen her tipsy. When the deceased and her husband had had beer they sometimes quarrelled. She saw deceased on Sunday afternoon, the 14th inst., and she was then under the influence of drink. In the eveaing she heard moaning proceeding from the direction of Mrs. Chester's closet. She went to the place with Mrs. Flemming, and found the deceased sitting down, with her arms extended and her head leaning back. Witness asked her what she was doing there, but deceased seemed unable to speak. The deceased appeared to be sober but could not walk, and they helped her home. Witness went home, leav- ing Mrs. Whitworth in charge of the deceased. When wit- ness and Mrs. Flemming went to see the deceased On the following morning Mr. Whitworth said "No one shall see her until the doctor has seen her."—By the Chief Constable: Deceased sometimes got drunk and witness did too. She went to the deceased's husbaed and said Whatever is Lizzie doing in the closet? " and be said "I don't know." She heard Mrs. Flemming ask the deceased "Who had done it," and the reply was "Tom did it." She had seen deceased run down the yard out of the way of her husband when the two had been quarrelling, but she had never .seen the deceased struck by her husband.—By the Foreman: She asked deceased if she might fetch a policeman, because she thought it was a shame that she should be bruised in the manner she was.—By deceased's husband: Mrs. Whitworth did not say when Mrs. Flemming and witness went to see deceased that she would not let them see her because they were the worse for drink.—Ann Wilson, wife of William Wilson, Rose Yard, said she had often seen the deceased tipsy. She saw deceased in the Rosa heerhouse on Sunday afternoon, the 14th inst. De- ceaced wanted witness to have a glass of beer there, but , witness said "Come and have a pint in your own house." Deceased replied "No, Tom will beat me." They each then got a glass of beer at the Rose, and shortly after that ' she called deceased's husband to take his wife home, as she was drunk and unable to stand. Witness and the husband then helped deceased home. Deceased's face was then alright. About a quarter-past six the same evening she saw deceased in the closet. Deceased was in " such a fearful 'tate that sne could not have told who she was if she hadn't known her." Witness said, "Some one fetch a bobby to her," am I el.c.-tased said " Let me go to sleep." Deceased had on one foot nothing but a stocking, and a clog was fetched. Witness afterwards said to deceased's husband, "Who has done this? She is killed." He replied, "Let the h---- dee," and then went away and left herd! He then appeared to be sober.—By the fore- man : She did not know how the deceased's clothes became so saturated with water, unless it was with staying out in the rain.—Sarah Chester, 11 yes of age, residing in Rese- yar'd, said that on Sunday night, the 14th inst., between six and seven o'clock, she saw deceased come out of her own house and fall four times in the yard. Deceased fell once near witness' entry door, and said "Oh. Mrs. Chester, do take pity on me and take me in." Witness and another girl helped deceased into witness' house and placed her on a chair. Deceased, while sitting there, said "Oh, I let me run, be is coming," but witness ' did not know to whom else referred. Sarah Bibby, wife of Thomas Bibby, Rose-yard, also gave evidence. Mary Ann Burke, wife of Henry Burke, Rose-yard, said she saw deceased coming out of her own house on the morning of the 14th instant, and she seemed to he in drink; she was very drunk on the pre- vious night. She saw her in the afternoon, about 5 o'clock, and she was then lying in filth on the floor of her own house. There was nobody in the house but deceased, and she was screaming. Witness "felt disgusted to look at her." She 9A)V deceased in the evening, when she had been taken from the closet, and again on the following day (Monday), when she told witness that she was very ill, and that she had been shaken by a fall. On Sunday morning last the husband name to her door, and, bursting into tears, said "Come in ; lam sure Lizzie is dying." She went into the deceased house, and told the husband that he had better fetch a doctor. The husband put his coat on and went out apparently to, fetch one, but deceased died before he returned.—Elizabeth Whitworth, wife of Rebert Whitworth, of Rose-yard, and sister-in-law to the deceased, said she was in attendance on the deceased when the latter died. The reason she did not send for a doctor was that she thought there was no necessity for one. She had asked deceased how she came by her injuries, and she replied that she had fallen on Mrs. Chester's steps. She would not allow the two women to see the deceased because they wanted to bring drink into the house, and she thought drink had done enough there.—By the Chief Constable: She asked deceased if she might fetch a doctor, atfd she replied, "No, don't; for if you do, they will lock Tons up, and say that he has done it."—Dr. StarkeyeSmith stated that he made a post-mortem examina- tion of the body on Monday morning. Both eyes were very black, and there were several discolourations on the arms and forearms, also on the knees and shins. On remov- ing the scalp he found an extravasation of blood in front and likewise behind, which must have been caused by blows or falls. The skull was not fractured. On removing it he found the membranes of the brain a good deal congested, which as attributable to drink. The heart was dilated and fatty, and the air vesicles of the lungs were ruptured, attri- butable to irregular habits. The liver was enlarged and congested, again caused by drink. The kidneys were healthy. The peritonium was very much inflamed, and there was a rupture, about an inch and a half long, in the bladder. He was of opinion that the rupture in the bladder and a shock to the peritonium was the cause of death. An act of violence, such as a kick, applied to the abdomen while the bladder was distended, would, he thought, cause. the rupture. There was no mark externally to show that violence hail been applied to the abdomsn, but he thought that a blow might have been given and no bruises appear. A fall while the bladder was distended might also causs the rupture, but he thought it more likely to have been caused by a blow or by some person kneeling on the stomach. He thought that the rupture must have hap- pened :about two dive before death, because the inflimma- iion of the peritonium had not gone on td the extend he said that the etherwise. The black ewould wouldha e expectedb e caused hbaydbiLi•Vdnealt on the cheek bones.— The ilriceuCmosrtolnneere sea nes ui rnrgouanldeintiggthth' esudmeamtihngweurep very suspicious, but at present there was no evidence showing that, the de- ceased's husband was guilty of any act of violence.—The jury retired, and after the lapse of a few minutes returned with a verdict to the effect that the deceased died from certain injuries received, namely, rupture of the bladder, producing peritonitis, but how or by what means such in- juries were brought about there was not sufficient evidence to show.—A large nureber of persons, mostly women, gathered in front of the parade room to await the reealt o f the inquiry, and the proceedings appeared to have evoked much interest.

div.head: POLITICAL.
div.p: POLITICAL.

Sir Stafford Northc--ote- was pre-sent at a great meeting of Conservatives of North Wales, held at Carnarvon on Monday evening. The Standard understands that steps have been taken to place before the Government the views of these members of the Liberal party who desire that next session should be de- voted to questions of local government, and that the franchise question should be postponed till 1885. The death is announced of the Rev. C. Stove], in his 85th year. He was one of the founders of the Liberation Society, was a distinguished controversialist, and in his time one of the leading ministers of the Baptist denomination. Mr. Stovel took an active part in the movement for the abolition of slavery in the British colonies. Mr. Bright has written a strong condemnation of Mr. Hare's franchise scheme. ' The right hon. gentleman says that the scheme would break Parliament up into "busy cliques led by the political lunatics who would have entrance within its walls," and he roundly intimates that Mr. Hare's supporters are lacking in common sense. Mr. George Elier will be the Liberal candidate for North Ayrshire at the next election, and the Hon. North Dalrymple for South Ayrshire. A Dundee correspondent says that Mr. Carnegie, the American millionaire is anxious to enter the English Parliament, and that he will probably contest the Kirke tidy District of Burghs. Messrs. Fowler and Shield, the members for the borough of Cambridge, addressed a meeting of their constituents on Monday night, and a resolution expressing confidence in the Government was passed. Mr. rowler, referring to the arti- cle of the Marquis of Salisbury on disintegration, said the Conservatives should be the last to talk of disintegration, in- asmuch as they themselves set the example. Addressing his constituents at Huddersfield, on Tuesday night, Mr. E. A. Leatham, M.P., said the Government had met with reverses during last session, but the Opposition had gained nothing from them, and Ministers stood as strongly in the country now as they did three years ago. They had gone in for legislation of a humble rather than heroic kind, but had passed several unsensational though eminently use- ful measures. _ . . .

Sir Henry James, the Attorney-General, writing to a cor- respondent who urged the necessity of reform at municipal elections, says—"l think it probable that the subject of cor- rupt practices at municipal elections may be submitted to the consideration of Parliament during the coming session. Probably it has escaped your attention that, by the Corrupt Practices Municipal Election Act of 1872 (58), paymentfor the conveyance of voters by a candidate or his agent is rendered illegal." The Hon. E. L. Stanley, M.P., speaking at the Liberal meeting on Saturday at Oldham, said one of the great causes of discontent in Ireland was the great poverty there. He advocated the development of the resources of Ireland as a counteracting influence, and as means of staying the development of con,piracy and insurrection. He thought the Corrupt Practie a Act a step in the right direction, and added that he did not see why the cost of Parliamentary elections should not come out of the rates. CABINET COUNCIL.—The first meeting of the Cabinet since the prorogation was held at noon on Thursday in the Prime Minister's official residence, Downing-street. The Ministers present included Mr. Gladstone, Earl Selborne, Mr. Childers. Mr. Dodson, Sir C. Dilke, Earl of Kimberley, Earl of Northbrook, Sir William Harcourt, Earl Spencer, and Mr. Chamberlain. The Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland and the Honig Secretary were attended, as usual, by detectives. Earl Granville, Lord Carlingford, and J ord Hartington entered the Cabinet Council at a quarter to one o'clock. Lord Derby, being at Knowsley entertaining company, did not attend. Mr. G. Osborne Morgan, M.P., spoke at the opening of a Liberal club at Brymbow, near Wrexhana, on Wednesday. He referred principally to the Carnarvon 'speech of Sir Stafford Northcote, who declared that he did not fear the county franchise extension, but what might come alter it. Mr. Morgan's reply was that he fearalenothing from the granting of a piece of justice, and he confidently relied on the intelligence of his countrymen. The Tory leader had said that Conservatism was not in sympathy with the mass of the Welsh people, but the fact was that the mass of the Welsh people was not in sympathy. with Conservatism. A resolution of confidence in the Government was unanimously adopted. At a meeting of the London Municipal Reform League, on Thursday night, Mr. Sidney Buxton, M.P., ,presiding, resolutions were passed approving the steps taken by the executive council for a representative colference at the Memorial Hall, Farrindon-street, on the Bth proximo, pro- testing against any further postponement of the London Government Reform Bill, and expressing the opinion that the abandonment of the measure would be frought with most serious mischief, as well as be a violation of undertakings to which the Government is pledged. Public meetings are to be held in each of the London boroughs in the largest halls available, to be followed by a mass meeting in St. James's Hall. The Press Association, referring to the meeting of the Cabinet Council, says there is reason to believe that the proceedings chiefly concerned matters of foreign policy, upon which it was thought desirable that Ministers should consult preliminary to such authoritative statements as may be shortly expected on the subject from the Premier at the Lord Mayor's banquet, and also from Sir Charles Dilke at the important series of political meetings he has under- taken to address in Scotland next week. Some questions were expected to arise as to the condition of Zululand and the position of Cetewayo •, but this subject was not dealt with in the absence of the Colonial Secretary. Consideration was, however, given to certain arrangements and conditions connected with the approaching withdrawal of the British trooe s from Egypt, a. well as to modifications upon points of minor detail which are likely to be conceded in regard to the Ilbert Bill, without, however, sacrificing the principle of that measure. Lea WORE OF THE COMING SESSION.—The Daily News says :—With respect to domestic legislation the question whinh the Government will have to consider is one rather of tactics than of policy. The order of measures must be fixed by the Government on full consideration of the par- liamentary position, as well as of the desire outside, and the decision, whatever it is, will be received generally with the acquiescence which Mr. Bright has expressed beforehand. Supposing, however, that the Government should adopt Mr. Bright's suggestion and bring in a Franchise Bill and a London Municipal Bill, next year, it may be asked what will become of the yet larger question of redistribution. This is the most important part of the reform which this Parliament is expected to accomplish. It seems to be granted that a apprehensive and efficient redistribution could scarcely be put forward next year, and must neces- sarily stand over to the session -of 1855. The proposal to deal with the county franchise next year consequently in- volves the passing of the Reform Bill in two parts. The precedents of 1832 and 1867 are against this division, but there is scarcely any other reason why it should not take place. The point on which it is needful to insist is that the same Mtnistry and the same Parliament which undertake the one shall carry out the other.

A PAINTER'S LESSON.—Mr. Fielding on one occasion lent him a drawing and told him to try his hand at copying it. It appeared wonderfully simple th execution, and he thought he would have little difficulty with it. The sky looked to him as if it had been all done by one wash. But when he came to try he was much disappointed. He brought his copy to Mr. Fielding and told him how hard he had tried, and yet had made so little of it. "Yes," he said, "I went over that sky six times." " Ah, there it is," said Fielding; 1" you think it looks very simple because it does not show any labour in it. You say you went over the sky six times. I believe lam wiin the mark when I say that I went over .mine sixty timt.. •—God Words.

ASHTON. " CHINA AND Taa ClliivESE.”—Thie was the title of a magic lantern exhibitiou given in the uslngregationel School. Ashton, on Monday evening, under the auspices of the Band of Hope. The views were shown by Mr. Thomas Rigby, and the descriptive readings were given by Mr. Henry Winstanley. There was a good attendance, and everyone thoroughly .enjoyed the entertainment. • HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICES AT STUBSIIA.W CROSS' —Special harvest thanksgiving services were held in St. Luke's Mission Church, Stubshaw Cross, Aeliton, on Sunday last. The interior of the building had been very neatly and attractively decorated by the teachers and members of the congregation, the pulpit, communion, lectern, and reading- desk being objects of admiration in their temporary garbs of wheat, corn, flowers, and fruit. The preacher in the after- noon was the Rev. W. J. Melville, M.A., Rector of Ashton, and in the evening the Rev. T. Williamson, Vicar of Thel- wall. On the former occasion the choir effectively sang the anthem, "Praise ye the Lord," and in the evening gave "Rejoice in the Lord." The attendances were large; and I the collections, in aid of the Church expenses, realised alient ,E 74 MEETI/•14 OF MINERS AT ASIITON.—A meeting of the miners of Ashton and district was held in the lower room of the Cave Browne Protestant Institute, Heath-lane, Ashton, on Tuesday evening. There was a good attendance, and Mr. Thomas Dix presided.—ln the course of his address the ! Chairman explained that the object of the meeting was to discuss the wages question' a matter whicn was of great I importance to miners at the present time. The present agitation, he said, was spread over the whole North of Eng- land, and the miners of each separate district were at liberty to make the best terms they could with theiri'employers.— Mr. Samuel Woods, of Park-lane, miners' agent, gave a long address on various matters affecting the collier& He drew attention to the recent strike in North Staffordshire, and I pointed out that there had been a great increase in the out- ! put of ceal dulling the last 20 years, while its cost and price ! had been almost trebled. Still the wages of the men were I no better than they were 20 years ago; and the only way by which the men could protect themselves or better their position was by organisation. The prices of coal were too I low, and the wages of the men were too low. He hoped! the men would look better after their interests in the future ' than they had done in the past. Proceeding to allude to the Land Laws, he maintained that the land ought to be cultivated so as to prodece sufE:ient food to keep the work- men of the country; and, if such a method could be estab- lished, it would help to make the nation still more prosperous—Hearty votes of thanks were accorded to Mr. Woods and the chairman at the close of the meeting. MINERS' ANNIVERSARY AT ASHTO,N.—On Saturday last the members of the No. 11 Hope of Ashton Lodge of the Ashton and Haydock District of the Miners' Federation, held their anniversary at the Caledonian Inn, Ashton. Nearly 40 members and their wives sat down to an excellent repast, served up in the usual good style of Mr. and Mrs. Causev ; after which Mr. T. Dix was called to the chair. In a few remarks he pointed out the benefits of unionism, and said it was the duty of every miner to be in the society; to think out those questions affectink his social position, and to try to improve his position and that of his fellow- man. Aft.. S. Woods, of Park-lane, also addressed the meeting. The health of the host and hostess was received with musical honoure, and suitably responded to by.the host. The Chairman next gave "Success to the Ashton aud Haydock District," and coupled with it the 'mime of Mr. W. Greenall. The latter, in responding, said a society was what its members made it, and urged unou them the neces- sity of looking after the interests of the society. "'nese should try to place it upon a more permanent basis, and he hoped the time was not far distant when they would have in connection with their society a superannuation fund. The rest of the evening was spent in singing and dancing, the following songs being sung at intervals :—" Life is a river," Mr. W. Greenall (encore. " Ere the rose will cease to blow ") ; " Jolly miller," Mr. D. Pilling; " The thorn," Mr. W. Johnson (encore, A flower from my aged mother's grave ") ; " Farmer's boy," Mr. T. Dix; " Awfully naughty," Mr. J. Ogden ; "Cheshire Cheese," Mr. W. Greenall (encore, "The Englishman.") Votes of thanks to the promoter of the evening's entertainment, Mr. Airey, and the chairman, with the singing of the National Anthem, brought a very enjoyable meeting to a close. ASHTON CHURCH ASSOCIATION PENNY SAVINHS BANK.— The governing body of the above institution having deemed it desirable that at the end of the fourth financial veer a printed statement of the bank's past business and progress should be circulated amongst the depositors, Sunday scholarc, teachers, and parents, have prepared a statement which will doubtless be read with interest. The bank was instituted in May, 1879, its objects being "to provide frequent opportunities to the Sunday scholars, relatives, and friends, of depositing their small savings in a place of security until they have need to use them, and thus to create amongst them thrifty and provident habits." In the first year ending June, 1880, 69 depositors opened accounts with the Penny Savings' Bank, and made a total of 1,321 deposits, amounting to £2B 3s. 9.1. 48 withdrawals, amouting to £ll 10e. 11d., took place, leaving a balance of £l6 121.101 to the credit of depositors, exclusive of interest earned by accounts of 10s. and upwards. In the second year to June, 1881, new accounts were opened by 46 depositors, and 910 deposits were made in these and former accounts, amounting to £57 16s. 11d., and 80 withdrawals occurred of a total of £35 12s. lid., leaving a balance to the credit of depositors, including interest £1 3s. 11., allowed to them in this aisa previous year, of £4O O. Pd. In tha third year ending June, 1882,18 new accounts were opened, and in the whole 860 deposits were made, amounting to £4l 19s. 11d., whilst the number of withdrawals were 83 of a total sum of £45 12s. 10.1. Thus the balance due to depositors, after crediting interest earned, £1 2s. 11d., was at this year's end reduced to £37 10s. 91 In the fourth year of the bank's existence, enclitics on the 30th June last, 20 new accounts were opened arid 539 deposits were made, amounting to £52 17s. 21, whilst 94 withdrawals of a total of £56 12s. 3d. took place—and thus the balance left to credit of depositors, including inzerest £1 3s. 2d. awed by accounts of 103. and . upwards, was again reduced to £34 183. 103., evidencing that the humble penny bank had been truly a place of security for large as well as small sums " until the deposi- tors had need to use them," for re-investment or other pur- poses Since its institution 153 accounts have been opened with the bank, 3,630 deposits have been made, amounting in the aggregate to £lBO 17s. 93., and the sum of £149 Ss. 11d, has been repaid in 305 withdrawals, and thus almost 4,000 transactions have been entered twice over. The interest allowed to depositors has averaged £3 153. per cent per annum, or 50 per cent in excess of the rate allowed in the Post Office Savings' Bank, and a reserve fund of £1 103. is held by the governing body to keep up the rate of interest. The governing body urged upon the depositors, Sunday scholars, and teachers to make the bank and its ad- vantages more generally known, and induce their relatives and friends to become depositors, thus extending the general 'utility of the institution. BROAD GREEN. BROST) GRE2N CRICKET CLUB—The second annual dinner of the above club was held on S aturday, at the Stork Hotel, Mr. S. W. Doyle in the chair. After the usual toasts the secretary read his annual statemeet, which showed that the rezalt of metches played during the season was highly creditahle te so young a club. A pleasing part of the pro- ceedings was reached when Messrs. A. Unsworth and M. E. Kearney were presented w ilk bats, the former for the highest anerage and the latter for the highest individual score of the season. A humorous duet, composed for the occasion, was effectively rendered by Messrs. Hargreaves and Green, after whin a vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceedings to a close. BURTON WOOD. BURTONWOOD CITURCII 'HARVEST FESTIVAL. Sdeei it thanksgiving services for the ingathering of the harvest were held in Buttonwood Church on Sund iy last. The in- terior of the sacred edifice was most elaborately and artisti- cally bedecked in honour of the occasion, the thanks of the congregation for this being due to Mr. Sefton, Mr. Wood- ward, Miss Atherton, Miss Woodward, Miss Appleton, and , other members of the choir and congregation. The vicinity of the communion had received the greatest attention. The altar table was literally laden with flowers and fruits, arranged in a pleasing iumres, while canspicueus at each end were two large bunches of wheat. The wiadow spaces. behind the communion were filled with ivy leaves, &c., two handsome floral wreaths attrecting perticular attention. The ' communion rails were almost lavisihle in their garb of corn ; the dullness being broken by an abundance of ivy leaves running along the top of the rail& From the top of the pulpit NVIS suspended a fringe of corn, interspersed with bunches of luscious grapes and three magnificent pears. The stave, by which the interior of the church is warmed, when necessary, WAS altogether hid from view by a skil- fully-worked covering of ears of wheat, surmounted with a bunch of flowers and ivy leaves. At the foot of the stove were a quantity of splendid potatoes. Each Of the window sills had been bedecked with fruit, ivy leaves, and plants, while at intervals along the walls of the church were bring floral wreaths, for ni crosae,s, and other artistica' devices. The organ gallery cline in for a fair share of at- tention, and the front of it was capitally " set cut " with borders and fringes of corn, wheat, and various floral orna- ments. Altogether the seemed edifice presented a very pleasing appearance, and it was evident that much paies and great care had been taken in the task of decoration. The preacher in the morning was the Rev. H. E. Smith, curate of St. John's, Earlestown ; and in the afternoon the Pulpit was occupied by the Rev. 'l'. R. Matthews, vicar of Earlestown. The congregations were large, and collections were made at the close of each service in aid of the schael funds.

W. Preston, M.A , of Runcorn, the '

(subject being entitled "OT to America." The chair was taken by Mr. E. A. Wright J.['., but there v.-as only a very moderate attendance, widch the chairman accounted for by , the short notice which bad 13,?en giveti of the meeting. The Rev. lecturer met with a lie4rty rec?ption, and the lecture was much enjoyed. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Pres- ton, proposed by Mr. Linaker and seconded by Mr. Peter Riley. div.p: GOLBORNE.

MAGIC LANTERN ENTERTAINMENT.. Mr. R:gby, of Ashton, gave a magic lantern entertainment in the Congre- gational school, Golborne, en Wednesday evening. The subject was "War in Egypt," and the views consisted of a representation of the principle battles ad incidents in that campaign. At the close a number of ccmiie slides were reflected on the screen, the. children being greatly amused therewith. Considering the very unfavourable weather they! W.:5 a fair attendance.

HAYDOCK. ACCIDENT TO A COLLIER AT HAYDOCX. On Tuesday night, abont seven o'clock, John Bate, a collier employed in No. 1 Ram Pit, met with a serious accident. While Bate was following his customary occupation, a large stone fell from the roof, and unfortunately alighted upon Bate. Be had one of his legs badly smashed in two places, and it was found necessary to convey him to his home, where he haF, since been medically attended.

TEL PARTY AT HAYDOCK PRIMITIVE METHODIST —.The first tea party in connec!dou with the Tonic..23l.fa Ciass at Haydock Primitive Methodist Sunday c:-‘ ,ai was held in that school-room on Saturd:7 -g last. A. goodly number of membe:s'and frieuds partook of an excel- lent tea, after which an enj:yabie entertainment was held. Interesting addresses were given by Messrs James Livesley and William Harrison ; and a selection of music by the choir, conducted by Mr. J. Livesloy, junr., was much appre- ciated. A number of recitations, e., were very nicely given a very pleasant gathering concluding with the cult. tornary vote of thanks. WESLEYAN MISSIONS: MEETING AT HAYDOCK.—The annual sermons in aid of the Wesleyan Foreign Mission fund were preached in Haydock Wesleyan Methodist Chapel on Sunday last, when Mr. J. London, of Padgate, preached to a fairly large congregatiot, both in tho morning and in the evening. In the afternoon a missionary meeting was held in the Sunday school, addresses being given by Messrs. T. Wedgewood, J. Briscoe, and C. H. Brazendale. The annual ,public meeting was held in the chapel on Tuesday evening. when Mr. John Fairhurst presided. Thera was a good 1 attendance. Interesting addresses on mission work were, given by the Revs. J. M. Fairbourno (Earlestown) and House (Newcastle), and Mr. R i-rley ; and extracts from the annual report were read by Mr. Brown (the circuit steward). At the close of each service and meeting, a cAlection in aid of the mission funds was made.

HAYROCII COLLIERS AND THEIR WAO7S.—A deputation of the colliers and day-wagernen employed by Messrs. Rd. Evans and Co., waited upon Mr. B. 13_ Glover (agent for the firm), at the Colliery Offices, on Tuesdiv afternoon last. The deputation asked for an opinion from the firm as to the prospects of an advance of the, men's wagcs ; and Mr. Glover, in reply, observed that the 11i-in could not see their way clear to give an advance at the present moment. He, however, advised the men to keep at work, and said the firm would do whit they could in the course of time. The result of the interview was brou.,,lit b.ifore a meeting of the colliers, held at the Rain's Ilud, Iliydock, last (Thursday) evening, and the men's :lel2gite3 were instruc- ted to bring the views of the firm before a conference of Miners' delegates, to be held in Witu to-morrow (Satur- day).

THE SANITARY STATE OF THE LEIGH WORKHORSE STRANGE REVELATIONS.—An outbreak of scarlet lever has caused the Guardians to obtain a report on the condition of the Leigh Workhouse, the result being smne surprising revelations. Messrs. Banks, Fairclough, and Stephen report that the house is situate at the higVst part of the Leigh Local Board systena of sewers, and al these are practically unventilated, the workhouse is liable to receive sewer gas

from them. There are no :m ins of ins?ection of the work- house sewers, there being neither manholes nor lampholes provided, nor any arrangemeot for flushing, on accJunt of the roof water being diverted into cisterns. The sewers arc: common earthenware pipes, without sockets, and laid in a manner similar to field draining tiles. In 13 different places the sewers are carried directly unier the building. The cook'uouse has been built over a settling tank receiving the sink water from the kitchen and scullery, with no means of clean:sing or inspection. The smoke test has been applicd to all the drains running under the builditio. and sewer air direct from the sewer was escaping into the interior of the house in twenty different plac,s, including the fever hos- pital, men and women's hospitals and several lavatories. Sewer air in large quintities was even finding its way into the boardroom. The report stites that to put the house in a proper sanitary condition a new drainage system should be carried out, and the Guardians have ordered an estimate of the cost to be prepared. 'LA.NDLORD AND TENANT.— rhe Middlewich magisttate, have been called upon to settle a dispute between a landlord aud his tenant. Joseph iloole, greengrocer, S:c., Micicilewich, was summoned for removing his goods for ihe• purpose of avoioling a distraint, he being a tenant of Mr. David Harding, and in arrear with his rent to the amount Li' 10s. Mr. Cooke defended.—Mr. Hirding said defendant WIS his tenant, and occupied a Ilcusa in Kinderton-strccti. Middlewich, the rent being £lO per annum, payable quar- terly. On the 12th S2ptetnb last be on..ed Li 103 for rent, and had not yet paid it. The goods bad t.),,en removed fr;rn the house, and defendant still held the key —Goo. Fairhurzt, , clerk to Mr. Harding, gave evid..nce for 111, prosecution.— Mr. Cooke, for the defence, contended that it was nrft his client's intention to remove the goods to avoid payment, anl that they were removed in open daylight.—Defenclant, Hannah 'Buckley, and Mrs. Morris gave evidence in support of the defence.—The Bench dismssed the Case for want of corroborative evidence.

uARVFST THANKSGIVING. - On Sunday last harvest thanksgiving services were held in the Congregational Church, Over, when sermons were preached by Alderman Ainsworth, of Crewe, to large congregations, especially in the evening. The chapel was neat,ly decorated with corn, fruit, flowers, moss, and texts, the chief decorators being Mrs. Maxwell, Mrs. J. .H Cooke, and the Misses Cooke, Wood, Walker, Vernon, and M. E. Stu ha. On Monday a tea meeting was held in the Marshall Memorial Schools, which were also suitably decorated by the young men of trio congregation. Tables were given by Mesdames Leigh, J. IL Cooke, Vernon, Pickering, Jos. Wood, Philip Wood, and Hulse, and the Misses Leng, Cooke, and Marsey. Thera- was a very large attendance. After tea a meeting was held in the chapel, when Mr. W. H. Verdin, J.P., officiated as chairman in the unavoidable absence of Mr. R. Verdin, of the Brockhurst. Addresses were given by the Rev. W. Lees, of Crewe, and other gentlemen. Some anthems, &c., were well rendered by the choir, Mr. J. H. Cook r presidin,r, at the ori.j,,ats. The collections on Sahlay and Monday aMounted to £lO 18.1. 41-d., and were to be devoted to the incidental expenses. The proceeds of the tea were given to the Pastor; the Rey. J. T. Maxwell.
