THE RE-VALUATION OF THE COUNTY —We take the fol- lowing from the list of new assessments for the West Derby Hundred, with previous values for comparison :—Warring- ton: 1872, £96,254; 1877, £ll6 350 ; 1883, £156,312. Widnes: 1872, £56,736; 1877, £91,692; 1883, £131,212. Prescot : 1872, £9,502; 1877, £10,966; 1883, £12,950.

„ WARRINGTON TOTAL ABSTINENCE LEAGUE OF THE CROSS. —On Sunday evening a meeting of the members of the above society was held in the hall, when the chaplain (Father Beauvoiein) addressed those present, and announced that the arrangements for the brass band were now com- plete. Mr. J. Mullins (seceetary) also addressed the meet- ing, after which the chaplain administered the pledge. NARROW ESCAPE OF Two BOYS FROM DROWNING.—A narrow escape from drowning in the canal at Wilderspool occurred on Sunday afternoon. Four boys were playing with a large dog, when two of their number, named Tilling and Plumpton, fell into the water. Nothing was seen of the lads for a few moments, but soon the hands and head of Tilling appeared on the surface of the water. An attempt was made to reach him by means of a stick, but this failed, when a young man named Joseph Nixon, who lives near Black Bear Bridge, came up, and without any hesitation threw off his coat and went into the water, and succeeded in getting hold of Ming, and pushed him to the side of the canal, when he was taken out by the bystanders. The back of the other lad, Plumptou, now showed itself above water, a considerable distance further out, but Nixon at once made for him and seized lihn by the coat, and on lifting his head above water, it was seen that his fee° was livid, and be was quite unconscious. The lads were taken home as early as possible by a gentleman who witnessed their rescue, and. prompt measures for restoration having been applied, both lads have almost recovered from their accident. Nixon's pluck deserves recognition from the Royal Humane Society. THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE. So far as actual business is concerned the maiket is quiet. Fair in- quiries for pig iron from the local forge proprietors were reported on 'Change on Tuesday, but the low prices at which Scotch and north country iron is being sold has a tendency to influence buyers of the local and district brands, and the offers made were at under the present quoted rates. In meet cases both local and district makers are so well sold over the next few months that they show little or no dis- position to entertain business except at their full rates, and if anything there is a slightly firmer tone in Lancashire pig iron. For delivery equal to Manchester the quoted prices are about as under :—Lancashire forge and foundry, 45s Gd ; Lincelnshire forge, 44, 6d to 44s 103; foundry, 45s 6d to 45s 103, lees 2e, but only a very limited business is being done at these figures. There are afew sellers in the market willing to take less money, and they are able to- secure orders where makers are not prepared with conces- sions. In the finished iron trade there are indications of decreasing activity. The leading makers still report a fair trade coming in, and as a rule they are fully supplied with work, but some of the Lancashire furnaces are now getting on to short time. Quoted prices remain at £6 2s 63 to £6 5s for bars, £6 12s 63 to id 15s for hoops, and .E 8 to £8 5s per ton for sheets delivered into the Manchester district. S. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION: WARRINGTON CENTRE.—On Monday the classes for instruction in first aid to the injured were commenced in the Lecture-room, Museum-street. The evening lecturer is Mr. A. H. Young, M.B„ F.R C.S. The lecturer in the course of his observa;„ tions said what they wanted to do was to teach them how Or render efficient aid when it was needed in cases of emer- gency. In many cases people did not know what to do, and it would be his dray to teach them to do nothing some- times, rather than do something and do it wrong. When. a person fell down in a fit or fainted, a crowd of people gathered with a crowd of suggestions, which amounted to this, after people had satisfied their curiosity, "Stand back, fresh air and plenty of water,” which might be put down as the ordinary formula in cases of accidents, no matter what they were. The best treatment for fainting was to place the patient's head as low as possible, to allow the blcod to run in that direction. The lecturer described the anatomy of the human frame, and briefly deseribed the functions per- formed by some of the organs of the body. He showed by means of a skeleton the different bones that were more liable than others to injury, these being the bones of the arms and legs, and the clavicle or collar bone, the frequent -fracture of the latter being often caused by a violent shock to the arm. In the case of a broken rib the greatest care should be exercised to avoid plashing the broken end into the lungs, or into other organs which the limbs were sup- posed to protect, or death might be the result. In the case of the arm a patient's suffering might be intensified and prolonged by one of the points being pushed into the muscles and flesh. He then etplained the application ref bandages, and showed the difference between a bad and. a good knot. The lecturer, who assisted himself by chalk drawings on the black board and diagrams in the wall, war, listened to with attention.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1553.

The important meeting held this week in zonnection with the Manchester branch of the Liberation Society combined with the sPeech of Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, at Carnarvon, in which he incidentally alluded to the proposed Disestablishment of the Church in Wales, will serve to direct public attention to a question which is too often lost Sight of in the desire for other and probably' lore pressing reforms. That the Disestab- tishment of the Church not only in Wales, but in Scotland and England as well, will very soon come "within the range of prac- tical politics," there cannot be any reasonable doubt, In fact, in the next session of Parlia- kerit resolutions, we are iold, will be sub- Mitted in favour of the Disestablishment of the three churches, and it is well that in the rh, eanwhile the Liberation Society should, by lectures and all other means, educate not °ray the people, but, we regret to think it Should be necessary, some of their Liberal representatives also, in the necessity of the Church as a State establishment being swept Way. However well suited the Church may utave been in previous ages to the circum- tarices of the times, its existence is no longer ltoOked'upon in such a light by the thought- ttll people of this country. We notice that It STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, in his Carnarvon Speech, pays, for obvious reasons, a fitting ~tribute to the work the Nonconformists of Wales have accomplished. but he deprecates the Disestablishment andDisendowment— c spoliation" he terms it—of the Church. ,` he famous letter of the Rector of Merthyr- Ydvil must surely have escaped Sir STAF- tORD'S attention, otherwise he would not, we think, be so anxious to maintain an institution Which is indefensible. The Rector of oterthyr-Tydvil is able to speak with authority, and his experience of the Church in Wales is this, that it "is not a Church for neighbours and equals. It is a rich man's Church: the Poor man has turned his back upon it a hun- dred years ago." Nay more, the Rector adds this—" that it is a sin for any Government to aIIDNy such a church to continue." More con- ,clerrinatory evidence of the evils of the Estab- lishment could scarcely have been penned; and seeing that the Nonconformists of Wales are doing, as Sir S. NORTHCOTE admits, SO 41l1Ch good, would it not be well, we ask, that Lthe Church there should be relieved from her ,uondage in order that she may join 41 the good work of the Nonconformists 411 d make it still more effective. In the re- Port of the meeting of the Manchester branch 0f the Liberation Society it is impossible to °,verlook the powerful arguments in support of oisestablishment brought forward by one of t,l;.e principal speakers; the Rev. ALEXANDER ;I. SMITH now a Congregational minister, Out formerly curate of St. Mary's, Stockport. he rev, gentleman's observations were thoroughly practical and bristled with sound c°rnmonsense,emanating from honest and out- SPoken purpose and opposed to that spirit of 111eaness and worldliness which is the chief Characteristic of the Church of to-day. He referred chiefly to the "vested interests" of the Established Church, by which she is ob- tl,ged to take merely a one-sided view of ques- ,'°ns affecting the people, for whom she Should act as a mother. So handicapped is that with the trammels of the State control ,nat she holds aloof from many excellent Movements having " for their object the bene- tting of the masses, and in which her voice should be heard. The political side of the qUestion is regarded by her in far too great a degree, and hence arises her laxity and luke- arnmess in grappling with great social re- ;Prins. Briefly, she lacks a wide religious liberty of her own and, consequently, is un- 'able to display that activity in the spiritual 'ants of the nation that she could if she were tree from State influence. To quote the Rev. 14.LExta,,NDER SMITH'S words, "He did not oe,lieve there was a single clergyman in the whatever his position, who could oriestly and conscientiously say that he ac- 'tePted unreservedly every principle of the Toyer Book and of the Articles. With all.), I.lall that would be weakening, but with tihristian ministers, in whose lives should be Lite Words of truth, it was almost ruinous—he tqtad felt it to be so—to their influence to find tlvisat they could not altogether accept what ,:;ey had professed to believe." The plain I'.`eaning of this is—that the present constitu- ,l°ll of the Church promotes hypocrisy and fekves encouragement to careless and thought- men to enter it. Our greatest hope for fr e bisestablishment of the Church comes s °,rh within her own pale. The injudicious oeflection of ministers to livings is productive se the gravest scandals; whilst the various tbetions and shades of thought into which 4e_irninistry is split up points to a process hisinteo-ration going on within which tne s t sooner or later result in the Of urch's collapse, without the aid even need any extraneous assistance. We only refer to the disgraceful ti;'.-eedings recently enacted at St. Jude's, 10'4erp001, to disprove the assertion often rd that the Establishment promotes unity,

THE NEW PCILIC OFFICES FOR RIINCORIC—FrOaI Our advertising columns it will be seen that the Board of Com- missioners will transact their business at Waterloo House on and after the 7th November. The opening of the new offices will be celebrated by some appropriate ceremony. WIDNES SEWERAGE SCHEME.—At a special meeting of Widnes Local Board, on Tuesday, a letter was read from Mr. Robert Davies with reference to the No. 1 sewerage con- tract, and stated that an offer had been made on behalf of Mr. Jeffries tantamount to another offer of arbitration. On the motion of Mr. Carey, seconded by Mr. Midwood, it was unanimously resolved that the course already adopted be carried out. This course is to terminate Mr. Jeffries con- tract.

ASSAULT AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. J. L. Davies, Edwin Cook was charged with assaulting Mary Bostock, a single woman living with her parents.—From the evidence of the prosecutrix and P.S. \Valley, it appeared that Bosteck was standing in Church-street with a number of other women, when the prisoner threw her to the ground-and behaved in a most indecent manner.—The Bench fincd the prisoner I.os and costs is. 4d.

A RUNCORN GENTLEMAN IN WINNIPEG. A Winnipeg newspaper has the following paragraph with reference to Mr. Wm. Walker, late of Runcorn :—" Mr. William Walker, advertising agent of the Winnipeg Conzniercial, left this week to occupy a similar position on the London Advertiser. What is the Commercial's loss is the Advertiser's gain, for as an advertising agent Mr. Walker has no rival in Canada, if, indeed, on the continent. He had made hews of friends in this city, one and all of whom are regretting his departure." THE OPEN-AIR CONCERTS AT RUNCORN.—MT. C. Dutton, the Market Superintendent, who PTAS the chief organiser of the open-air concerts which were the C 11133 of much enjoy- ment to thousands of persons last summer, has shown us a statement of his receipts and expenditure in connection therewith. The expenses amounted to £6 4s. 3d, the largest item having been paid to Mr. Henry White for music-stands, Ice. Tele su'ee.criptione only amount to £5 165. 9.1., thus leaving a deficiency of Ti 111. We trust that some generous advocate of music for the people will come forward, and not allow Mr. Dutton to be a loser by his enterprising conduct. PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN GENTLEITAN.—On Mon- day night, at the Bee Hotel, Liverpool, Mr. Thomas Tom- linson, of Higher Runcorn, who for the past 14 years has occupied the post of cashier at the Runcorn Soap and .Alkali Company's works, was presented with a purse of gaid, a pair of gold sleeve links, and an illuminated address as a mark of esteem. Mr. Tomlinson has just relinqaished the position which he has held with so much credit to him- self, and his late confreres embraced the opportunity of tes- tifying their regard. The address contained the names of upwards of one hundred subscribers to the testimonial. The presentation was preceded by several suitable speeches, and the gift was feelingly acknowledged by Mr. Tomlinson. THE ALLEGED HOUSEBREAKING AT RUNCORN.—Joseph Rowlands, alias Porter, Peter Wilkinson, and Peter Leah were brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. W. Bankes, charged with having, on the 16th, attempted to commit a rape on Eliza Garnett, the wife of a flatsuan.—The prosecutrix now contradicted the evidence which has appeared in The Examiner, stating that when she previously appeared in the witness box she was drunk. She also stated that on the night of the alleged assault she and Mrs. Hicks, the occupier of the house where she was, and John Rowlands were all in a state of intoxication. Mrs. Hicks and Jahn Rowlands were also sworn, and whilst con- tradicting each other, contradicted Garnett, and his Wor- ship, on the ground that the evidence was not credible, discharged the prisoners on this charge.—They were then charged with breaking into the house and stealing a pair of boots and 2s 6.1, the property of Garnett. The evidence being of a similar nature in this instance, his Worship discharged the prisoners. Mr. flitchen appeared for Wil- kinson. Tun RUNCORN SOAP AND ALLALI COMPANY.—At the Liverpool Court of Passage on Monday, the case of Evans v. the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company was heard. Mr. Seger was for the plaintiff, George Evans, a labourer, who sought to recover damages for personal injuries sustained by him through the neglect of the servants of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Works, for whom Mr. Walton appeared. The plaintiff was a labourer in the employment of the Dominion Steamship Company, and on the 17th February last he was engaged discharging some soda ash from the flat Major, the property of the defendants, in the Alexandra Dock. The ash was discharged by means of a gaff on the mast, and when about 20 tierces had been discharged, the ring securing the gaff gave way, and something fell upon the plaintiff. He was seriously injured, and his left arm was now permanently paralyzed. He was 40 years of age, and had been in the receipt of 30s per week. The defence WAS that the gaff was rigged up by the men in the employ- ment of the Dominion Company, and not by the men belong- ing to the defendant company. The leery, after a long hearing, awarded £250 damages. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES.—An enter- taiment in aid of the circuit funds of the above church was held on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of the Rev. W. Valise, who -delivered a short address to the good and'. Nice which had assembled. Then followed the chorus, "Christ arose," given in capital style by the choir under the leadership of Mr. John Betney. he following programme was gone throueii :—" Recitation, "Violets," Miss Ada Hughes ; solo and chorus, "Meet me at the fountain," Mies Alice Betney; solo and chorus, "I shall be satisfied," Mr. Price; recitation, "The snow prayer," Miss Jane Summer- bell- solo and chorus, "Benlah Land," Miss Robinson; solo and chorus, "Wonderful wards," Mr. Bushell ; recitation, "Is it worth while?" Miss Jessie Betney; solo and chorus, "Leaning on Thee," Miss Cawsey ; recitation," Casablanca," Miss Jessie Hughes; solo and chorus, "Peace, be still," Mrs. Lock- recitation, "The dying child," Miss Alice Betney; solo and chorus, "Where is my wandering bay," Mrs. Betney; solo and cherus, " Hiding in Thee," Miss Alice Betney ; chorus, "Follow on," choir. The audience testified their appreciation of the entertainment provided .by warmly applauding each performer. DEATH OF A WESLEYAN LOCAL PRECHER.—AIX)Rt ten days ago Mr. Thomas Gill, a respected member of the Wesleyan Methodist Society, residing in Gladstone-street, was at- tacked with smallpox in one of its most violent forms, and on Tuesday succumbed to the decease. The deceased, who was only 36 years ofeage, had made plans to depart for Australia in a short time. He was a local preacher and class leader in connection with the Wesleyan body, and was a successful conductor of mission services. His death is much deplored by his numerous friends and acquaint- ances. To-morrow Mr. Gill should have preached at the Hartlaud Memorial Chapel, and in the height of his de- lirium he addressed to an imaginary congregation an im- pressive discourse. The body was interred at the Fern- worth Parish Church on Wednesday afternoon. Amongst others who represented the Wesleyan body were Messrs. S. B. Stringer, J. Shaw, J. Houghton, T. S. Swale, G. Davies, Reap, E. Wright, W. Rigby, A. Poulson, T. Hughes, W. Taylor, E. Martley. and Jenkins. The Rev. George Bond performed the burial service, and the hymn commencing ' " Give me the wings of faith " was sung at the grave side with impressive effect.

and this and other similar scandals conclu- sively shows that in the interests of the church itself it ought to be Disestablished We do not find that the report of the Royal Commission on the Ecclesiastical Courts has done anything whatever to mitigate the evils arising from the prosecutions of the clergy, than which nothing could be more fruitful of harm to the cause of re- ligion; on the contrary, the Commission seems rather to have aggravated those evils. The Commissioners insist that the Bishop of the diocese shall continue to have absolute power of refusing leave for the institution of i legal proceedings against a clergyman for either misconduct, neglect of duty, or doc- trinal, or ritual offences ; this, too, in direct contradiction to the opinion of Lord Chief jllStiCe COLERIDGE, one of the Commissioners, "that the active interference of the Bishop to prevent the law of the land being enforced against those who have deliberately broken it is as indefensible in thory as, I must con- fess, it seems to me to be fast becoming in- tolerable in practice." The Commission, on the otlier hand, elicited one fact which ought to be remembered by Liberationists, viz , that in regard to the systems of ecclesiastical pro- cedure, the non-established churches con- nected with the Church of England in Ire- land, Scotland, America, Canada, and else- where maintain discipline without any coer- cive jurisdiction simply bymeans of voluntary compact. Why not, therefore, extend a system which is proved to be productive of incalculable good? We can only hope with the Liberationist Society and other ardent advocates of church reform that the question of Disestablishment will be agitated again and again, and that the Government will ere long see their way to coincide with the ex- pressed views of the majority on this subject. "If the Church is unable to hold her own withbut State support, it proves she is rotten to the core—and if rotten, she ought to be swept away."
The Examiner of Saturday next, November 3rd, will contain a SYNOPSLS of the new and iu- teresting tale
ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL," so far as it has been published in these columns, so that subsequent readers of the Story will be able to follow the further development of the plot.

div.head: EXAMINER, SA TURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1883. OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA TURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1883. OUR LONDON LETTER.
RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY will be closed on the 30th October to the Bth November, whelk it will be opened in its

new location at Waterloo House. The montiily meeting of Widnes Church of England Temperance Society took place on Thursday evening, when an interesting and varied programme was gone through. The Rev. JlPWright-Williams, the vicar, presided. WEsToN POINT READING-ROOM.—It has Ip:en decided to re open the above useful institution on November Ist. Cap- tain Clark is president, and Mr. J. Musgrove lion. sec. The committtee consists of the Rev. J. J. Bryant, Messrs. L. Rosenberg, Riding, Ham, J. Rees, Harvey, and Cowley. Mr. W. Mather is hon. librarian. Newspapers and periodi- cals will be supplied. • CHRISTY MINSTRELS AT RUNCORN.—On Thursday and last evenings Messrs. Carpenter and Lorraine's troupe of Christy Minstrels occupied Runcorn Public Hall, and at- tracted large audiences on each occasion. The troupe, which is of transatlantic fame, has only bet-n in England a few weeks. The performance was a capital one, the singing, being being above the average, while the band is everything that could be desired.

THE SALTATION ARMY AT RUNCORN.—The members of the Army have been holding a special series of services dur- ing the past week. It has been announced that the Army intended to erect a building for the meetings of the Army in Runcorn, at a cost of about £1,500. They hope to raise 500 by voluntary subscriptions, and propose to borrow £l,OOO, mortgaging the building as security. It is stated that the site selected is the plot of land on which the " Old Hell" now stands.

A)IeOWNEDINAMUG AT WIDNES. child named Eliza- beth Eleanor Jameson, aged 18 months, living with its parents at 3, Bank-street, Widnes, was drowned on Thurs- day. Tne mother was engaged in %milling, and using a wringing machine, under which was placed a mug to rece!ve the waste water. She left the child playing in the place while she attended to some other matter, and on her return she found the child in the mug with its legs in the air. She palled it out aud sent for Dr. Richards, who pronounced life extinct.

GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MEEIING AT RUNCORN.—A Gospel Temperance Mission has recently been formed in Runcorn, and the first of a series of meetings intended to be held during the corning winter took place in Bethesda Schoolroom on Thursday evening. Mr. James Kirkham presided, and delivered an earnest address, while the Rev. George Hack, Mr. S. C. Beckett, and Mr. W. Leach also delivered stirring speeches. The choirs of the various places of worship have undertaken to assist at the meetings, and the choir, under the conductorship of Mr. F. Fairhurst, rendered several selections in good style on Thursday even- ing. Mill Brow Brass Band also played selections of music, and the proceeding passed off most successfully. ROBBERY FROM A RUNCORN PUBLIC-HOUSE.—OH Thurs- day, at Runcorn Police Court, Mary Spencer was brought up in custody charged with stealing a purse containing Ps. fid., and a cake of tobacco, from the person of Michael McGrath, a sailor. McGrath lodges at the Slope lan beer- house, Lock-street, and about nine o'clock on Wednesday night he was in the taproom, where he fell asleep. He had then in his pocket a purse containing Ps. Gd. and several cakes of tobacco. When he awoke the prisoner left the room, and from what was said to him by William Ramsdale he felt in his pocket, and missed a cake of tobacco and the purse containing the money. Ramsden stated that he saw the woman put her hand in his pocket and take something which she put in her own, but he could not say what it was. It appeared that the prisoner the same night went to the Blue Ball Inn, and gave Dwyer, the landlord, a cake of tobacco, which she said a sailor had given her for him. Subsequently P.C. Smith apprehended the prisoner, who ad- mitted stealing the tobacco, but denied taking the money. She now pleaded guilty to stealing the tobacco, and Mr. Brundrit spoke to the prisoner on the fearful mode of her life, and said as there was no previous conviction against ; her, the Bench would deal lightly with her, and fine her I 10s. and costs 21s, or in default 14 days. THE LATE MR. War. HOPKINS, OF WIDNES. At the Milton Congregational Chapel, on Sunday evening, the Rev. R. G. Hughes preached the funeral sermon of Mr. W. Hopkins, who died suddenly at the Tharsis copper works on the previous Tuesday. There was a good attendance. The preacher said it was a cause of bitter grief to many of them that one who was so beloved and honoured should have been so suddenly snatched away. The suddenness of death was becoming more terrible day by day. Although he had only known Mr. Hopkins for a short time, he had learned to honour and respect him as though he had known him for many years. Those who may have worked under him, and i had seen and heard a great deal of him would not hesitate to give their evidence of his trustworthiness, straightfor- wardness, and impartiality. He was always kind to his workers. There was no other way better calculated to se- cure good, honest, and conscientious work than b/ the master being attentive and reasonable to those underSaim.l The preacher characterised the deceased as a man humble in temper, respectful in demeanour, commercially honest in all his transactions, regular in the discharge af religious , duties, and a liberal subscriber to the cause of Christ. If ' these were not pre-eminent qualities in the Christian life he ' should like to know what they were. He impressively des- ! cribed the felicities of the future existence of the Christian, and exhorted the bereaved ones to gather consolation from ; the promise of the Divine Word. „,, Sr. EDWARD'S CATHOLIC AMATEURS, RUNCIORN.—.I.IIIS company of local amateur dramatists gave their annual per- formance in the Public Hall, on Monday evening, before a crowded audience. The piece chosen for representation was Mr. Amherst's drama, "Ireland as it was ; or, the eviction," and the delineations of Irish character were greatly enjoyed by the audience, which was demonstrative in its tokens of appreciation. The cast was as follows :—Dan O'Carolan, Mr. T. Mulvaney; Neil O'Carolan, Mr. W. Corless; Connor OTlalierty, Mr. J. Williamson; Ibe Stranger, Mr. J. Cole- man; Stone, Mr. J. Bird; Slang, Mr. J. Gordon; Magistrate, Mr J. Parker; Ragged Pat, Mr. T. Williamson; Boy, Mr. R. Williamson ; Judy O'Trott, Mr. T. Stoner; Honor, Mrs. Mutch ; Florence O'Carolan, Miss Parker. Mr. T. Mul- vaney,as the aged Irishman, created a favourable impression, while as humorous characters Mr. T. Williamson and Mr. T. Stone w-re eminently successful. Mr. Coleman's imper- sonation of The Stranger, a Frenchman, was clever, while Mrs. Mitch and Miss Parker sustained the reputation they gained at the last performance of the amateurs. The mounting of the piece was all that could be desired. A musical pro- gramme, in which Miss L. Jameson, Miss C. Hewitt, and Messrs. Mulvaney and Stoner took part, was gone through in creditable style. This was followed by a laughable negro sketch, "The troublesame servant," the characters being taken by Messrs. Mulvaney and Stoner. The audience was highly amused. During the evening the Irish National Brass Band, Widnes, in aid of whose funds the performance was given, played a capital selection of music under the , conductorship of Mr. M. Ryan. Mr, J. Ravenscroft presided.' at the piano.

ROBERT BROWNING AND HIS CRITICS.-HIS OWN INTERPRETATION OF HIS "LOST LEADER"- CHANGES AT THE NATIONAL GALLERY-FAIR COPYISTS-MISS momrsoN's WAR PICTURE- " OURS " AT TOOLE'S-STATUES FOR THE LON- DON BRIDG ES-TEMPLE CH RI: SANT HEM UM6 AND TEMPLE HOSPITALITIES-BALL DRESSES- THE BISHOP OF LONDON.

The Browning Society still survives. It has not exhaus- ted its labours, an what is perhaps stranger, its labours have not exhausted it. To-morrow its members re-assemble . possibly re-invigorated by two months freedom from active, labour in solving literary cruxes. Mr. Browning meanwhile still lingers in Italy; and, as I suppose he is himself the uin.ilt of appeal, where his critics all hold different opinions as to what their poet intends to mean, his return must be attended with consider- able interest. The society is taking up the Ring and the Book for study, which certainly shows that three sessions of hard work have not cooled their courage. When "Babil and Bijou" was brought out some years ago, to the utter bewilderment of all dramatic critics, it was said there was only one human being who had ever been able to make out the plot, and that hr. had died soon after its dis- covery. Wishing long life to the Browning Society, I can but regret it has taken up the Ring and the- Book for its special study By the.way, let rue myself solve one crux which appears in the early works of the poet when he was less obscure and mare imaginative. Nearly everyone who reads him knows his fine poem called "The Lost Leader." It must have been written about 20 years ago. Most people knew the "Lost Leader;" but very few knew who he WAS. The lines appear to apply to Goethe, but they are intended for another poet. I have it on the authority of Browning him- self that the "Lost Leader " was Wordsworth. •

We have been saturated with portraits of Mary Andersen. She has been more photographed than any other London favourite, and she has suffered frOm her photographs. With a statuesque figure and a beautiful bat certainly not a fault- less face—the chin is weak and the mouth defective—she has little variety, and not much expression. The resnit is that one portrait is as good as another. She wants what Maud Branscombe pre-eminently has, or rather had—sug- gestiveness. And now we are to have a fresh inundation of photographs. The Lady of Lyons comes out at the Lyceum to-morrow, and in all the show windows next week.

The National Gallery has gone through may changes in the course of the past month. In some respects it looks like a new collection of pictures, such a difference does new hanging make. The old friends seen in a new light are practically new acquaintances. The truth is our gallery is congested, and a little blood-letting will be very good for it. Twenty or thirty years ago the trustees, having much more wall space than wall furniture, accepted all kinds of bequests. It was very hard to be uncourteous, and very unwise to be over-fastidious. The result is that the nation now possesses a number of pictures of great merit and interest, but not of supreme excellence. Now, for the first time, the director has power to lend them to the great towns and to provincial museums. Thus he is enabled to classify and to re-arrange. It must not be thought that the capital is getting rid of its rubbish. There are many pictures which have a real interest, and they are being sent to the towns where the interest arises. There are some masters of whom we have more than our share. We are dividing for the general benefit. I strolled through the gallery to-day; and can speak of the great improvement wrought by the new system. A strange perversity had lodged the Peel collection in a gallery of enormous height. It consisted chiefly of Dutch cabinet pictures that to be seen to advantage should be hung in a series of c tbinets. It is so the Dutch picture 3 are treated, in Berlin and Munich and Florence. UnfortunaHy, it was one of. the conditions of the purchase from the 1,10 owner that for a certain number of years they shonld be all in the same gallery; the idea was, of course, that the public should see they all belonged to the same collection. Mr. Burton has relegated them to a room which holds them all, and shows them in a better light, and the big room is now free for important gallery pictures. Mr. Burton has also been very active in protecting fugitive surfaces with glass. The pictures are not seen so well, but Loy undnrihtpcilY gain a fresh lease of life. The National Gallery is well worth a sixpenny visit on a students' day. It is amusing to see the popularity of some works, and to try to account for it.

It is curious also to notice a difference between the Lon- don gallery and every other gallery in which pupils are constantly at work. Here most of the students are women, and most of the women are young and pretty. The profes- sional copyist, the manufacturer of feeble replicas, is scarcely to be met with. In the Louvre, in the Uffizzi, in the Dresden, you meet melancholy plodlers who year after year go on manufacturing c)pies of the same work with a mechanical and hopeless fidelity. But here, in Trafalgar- square, Thursdays and Fridays are quite fashionable d ays There is a kind ef costume for the lAy copyist which is very becominsr. You see a constellation of young girls grouped, not inappropriately, round Sir Joshua's "Angel Heads ;" or, what seems a little"strange, round some of Etty's compositions, in which flesh painting may be studied with greater advantage than drapery. Turner alone—that cynical old bachelor—seems in his work to be as unattractive to ladies as he was in his life. There is an immeasurable distance between the copies of 9C sthetic young beauties and such work as the Storm in the Alps or the Death of Nelson.

The winter art season has not yet begun, but we have had at least a forerunner of it. An old friend has re-appeared in, certainly, unexpected surroundings. Miss Thompson's, I should say Mrs. Batler's, war picture of the charge of the Second Scots Greys at Waterloo, after going a circuit of all the big towns, has come back, and is now located and on view—of all places in the world—at White's. For two years more it will remain in the hands of its present proprietors, and then Miss Thompson will resume the ownership of her own work. ‘Vken I tell the term she bas- received for this picture I think you will not say that good art is underpaid. I hear the owners of the copyright handed her a cheque for 3,000 guineas, they to have the right of publishing the engravings, and of taking the pic- ture about with them, and of exhibiting for a space of four years. About two years of that time has already gone by, land the artist has been offered 2,000 guineas for her rever- sionar tight. But she has wisely refused it.

At the theatres there is more in the sh Apa of novelty to anticipate than to record. At Toole's Theatre " M.P." has made way for " Ours." The crafts are getting qnite melan- choly—as indeed they may—over the comparison of the hrst caste and the last. When the play was first produced we were not so very far removed from the Crimean War. Mrs. Bancroft was then Marie Wilton, and appeared in the burlesque which followed it in tights as little Don Gio- vanni. These were the days when H. J. Byron was the burlesque writer; poor Byron! who is now so ill as "to cause his friends considerable anxiety," and I think the audience expected more from the burlesque than they did from the p'ay. The whole Robertson school of acting dates from this production, and its success was quite phenomenal. Seen now, the play seems a little thin. Some of the points that used to be so fresh have lost their sharpness, and even seem a little forced. But the acting is good. Miss Amy Rostlle's contribution is really very good, but then for years she has been one of the Baacroft troupe. The play cannot run very. long. Mr. Toole will be back. Before he opens work he will have to pay a visit to the Haymarket for the purpose of studying Mr. Bancroft's ren- dering of Coghlan's part. His fresh mimicry will give a new lease to Stage Dora.

Some agitation is being got up at the proposal to decorate Blackfriars Bridge with statues. The ground for the agita- tion is, not that the bridge does not want statires—f:”- that it does I think would be admitted.- nor that the proposed statue is unworthy of its place, but that it is the work of a foreign artist. I may as well say what is proposed before I discuss the objection to it. The Crystal Palace has in its sculpture gallery a cast of a statue by Clesinger, and .it is proposei that a reproduction of this should be put up experimentally in one of the pedestals of Blickfriars Bridge. I cannot see that the fact of Clesinger not being an Englishman, or that the work of reproducing his statue being confided to Italians, is a fatal objection. If the work is bad let it be taken down. We have statues by Englishmen in London, as the Byron Memorial, George IV. in a dressing gown on horse back in Trafalgar-spare, and a Temple Bar Griffin

abundantly prove, to say nothing of the poor Duke of Wellington who is now, I hear, irrevocably doomed to the melting pot. The bridges over the Tharov, except West- minster Bridge, are, perhaps, the u4liost sp,:tc.ntrris of pon- tine architecture in any capital iu Europe. Itio tv tnt them to I,e made less umittractive, and shall he obi ig-:!ti to any sculptor of any natonality who can do it for tai,

Yesterday the gardens of the Inner Tem2le were gay with ladies who had cons to see ne ehrysanthem t It was the first day that the exhibition was open to the pqblic. The Middle Temple show is a week liter. The latter society sticks to the conservative observance of what used to be the first day of term. It will be a gala day for the Temple, as the procession of the judges up the great hall of the new Law Courts will attract crowds of visitors, and now that there , is a subterranean passage by which the Temple is actually next door to the Courts, we may count on a full "assist- ance" of ladies. I have noticed within the last three years that the Temple has become much more popular than it used to be. I attribute this to the splendid sets of chambers recently erected. The upper so-is have been used as residence chambers, not by waifs and strays of literary men who used to colonise this stratum of rooms under the slabs in the dingier courts, but by bachelor members of the inn, who pay a great rent for roomy and well-built quarters. The Temple is getting quite fashionable, and whenever special attractions make an exduse for ladies to visit it, there are stare to be luncheon parties, and even afternoon dane ?s. There were two or three luncheon narties yesterday, and there are safe to be several on Friday, if only the weather is bright.

In dress I have seen this weel: a singular novelty. All through the year there has been a tendency to make the flower trimmings on ball dresses as important as possible. The latest fashion is to wear them very large indeed. Water lilies and Victoria regias, rhododendrons, and hydrangias cross the body of the dress not so much in sprays as in branches, and the leaves are made even larger than the flowers. They are so large that they would be intolerably heavy and stiff, and to obviate this feature are used for the foliage. The effect is fantastic enough ; but in a ball room the difficulties of a waltzer are increased. He has to pro- tect his partner and her dress.

I mentioned in my last letter that I thought there was little foundation for the rumour that the Bishop of Exeter was about to be made Bishop of London? I believe there is no foundation for it. It is time enough to fill vacancies when they arise. Bishop Jackson is still Bishop of London, and I hear is likely for some time to remain so. He is not at all in so great a burry to resign as some of his brethren are to see his successor appointed. There are plenty of other prelates on the bench who are less active ar.d more ad- vanced in years. Resignation is not a specially episcopal virtue.

DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. JOHN JOHNSON, LATE OF RUNCORN. At his residence, Weetcliffe-road, Southport, on Saturday morning last, there died Mr. John Johnson, whose name is intimately connected with the commercial prosperity of Runcorn. Mr. Johnson, who comes of an old Runcorn family, was born at the beginning of the present century, and tied attained the ripe old age of 83 when he died. About 90 years ago his father founded the Runcorn Soap Works, which have now become the Rancorn Soap and Alkali Company, and on his death, his seals, John and Thomas, conducted the business. By accident a mottled brown soap was invented, and afterwards became one of the chief manufactures of the firm. The extent and success of the undertaking may be gathered from the fact that when the works were at their highest point of prosperity upwards of 700 men were employed, and the annual duty on the soap manufactured amounted to the enormous sum of £50,000. Extensions were rapidly made. Weston chemical works were purchased, and operations were also conducted at Widnes, Winsford, and Liverpool. During .the American war the firm were trading largely with that country, and entered into speculations of vast magnitude. Steamers were purchased for the purpose of running the blockade to the southern ports, and one of the vessels succeeding in accomplishing the journey, the owners cleared the enormous sum of £70,000. Subsequently, however, the speculations which promised the source of *great wealth, proved the ruin of the firm, and the downfall of the house of Johnson. All the vessels in attempting to break through the blockade at Charlestown were destroyed, and with their destruction the fortune of the house were irretrievably lost. The works were formed into a limited liability compeny, and the family property was disposed of. Through the kind generosity of Lord Derby Mr. John John- son, the subject of this mem&r, was permitted to retain an interest in a coal mine at St. Helens, and trade at that period being exceedingly good, he was enabled to amass a conskterabte fmtune, and cco, et all the family pr,perty. 'The deceased, who was a justice of tha peece for the cOunties of Lancashire and Cheshire, was an active public character, and he took part in every important movement for a great number of years. He was the chief promoter of the establishment of the Runcorn Gaslight Company in 1836. and when the first act was repealed in 1817, he was one of the proprietors incorporated with the Runcorn Gas Com- pany. He was a member of the old Highway Board, the body which preceded the Improvement Commissioners, and during his term of office, he, in conjunction with Whiteway and Mr. John Rigby, successfully agitated for the removal of an unsightly narrow bridge in Halton-read, and Delph Bridge was erected in its place. In 1832 the town suffered from an epidemic of cholera, and Mr. Johnson was appointed a member of the Board of Health in order to cope with the spread of the dire disease. The duties of the Board were exceedingly arduous, and great tact and judgment were required in dealing with the matters brought under their notice. To aid in stamping out the disease, the Bridgewater Trustees placed at the disposal of the Board a building, which was fitted up as a hospital, and subscriptions were received amounting to £l3O. From the 18th June to the 26th October, 1832, there were 36 people stricken with cholera, 40 per cent, of whom recovered, and it was acknowledged that if it had not been for the prompti- tude displayed in dealing with the epidemic, the town would have been decimated by the ravages of the disease. The members of the Beard were publicly thenkal for their efforts. The Runcorn Improvement Act was passed in 1852, and Mr. Johnson was elected one of the first members of the Board of Commissioners. He, however, resigned his position two years later, hiving during his term of office served the public as chairman of the Finance Com- mittee. Mr. Johnson was an earnest believer in educating the people in religious and secular subjects, and at one time he founded a Sunday school in the works for boys in the employment of the firm. He himself acted as the teacher. He was partly instrumental in the erection of, Holy Trinity Church, which when finished he and his brother *Thom is endowed, thus becoming the patrons of the living. The deceased gentleman also built and maintained at some expense Trinity Ragged School, Heath-road, which has now become the property of the School Board. He also built Trinity Infant School. Mr. Johnson's views on the drinking customs of the country coincided with those of the temperance societies, and on the Bench he was always opposed to the increase of the drink- ing facilities of the town. In the days of his greatest pro`sperity the deceased gentleman was raised almost to the height of a demi-god by the inhabitants of the little town, and it is to his everlasting credit that he s used his power as to win the respect and esteem of all'those with whom he came in contact. He was a man of honourable intentions and strict integrity, and since he left Runcorn to take up his residence at Southport 12 veers ago his name has been cherished in many a household, and his memory will be kept green long after the corroding hand of time has de- faced the carved capitals of his name on the tombstone in the ancient parish churchyard. The funeral ceremony took place on Thursday. The body, in charge of the relatives of the deceased, arrived at Runcorn by the 12-5 noon train from Southport, and a hearse and three mourning coaches were waiting in readi- ness to convey them to the Parish Church. There was also a large assemblage of public men, and men who had for Years been employed in the service of the deceased, who de- sired to pay homage and respect to the departed. They formed a double line in front of the railway .station, being headed by a force of 10 constables in full dress, in command of Superintendent Williamson, Inspector Hollingworth, and Sergeants Whalley and McMichael. In this order they walked in front of the conveyances along Lowlands-road, across Savage's Bridge, and down Bridgewater-street to the , church. Spectators lined the entire route, and many out- ward signs of respect were visible. Flags were flying half- mast from the Town Hall, Holy Trinity Church, and other places; a large number of shops were closed, and as the funeral cortege neared the church the bell rung a mournful note. The carriages were occupied by the following rela- tives of the deceased :—Mr. John A lcock Johnson (son), Mr. Ernest Johnson (nephew), Mr. Hignett (nephew), Dr. Bagnall, Major Bateman. Mr. Gayman, Mr. Freeman Bag- nail (brother-in-law). The following gentlemen, whose name a are given promiscuously, walke in the processior! Rev. NV. Preston, Rev. D. Llevrllyn, Messrs. W. THE SMALL-PDX EPEDEMIC AT WIDNES. VISIT OF THE GOVERNMENT INSPECTOR: LIVELY BOARD MEETING. On Monday afternoon a special meeting of NS idnes Local Board was held for the purpose of receiving Dr. Parsons, the Local Government Board Inspector, who had arrived with the object of viewing the proposed site and others for an infectious diseases hospital, and also to have , an interview with Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington, respect- ing No. 1 sewerage contract. Mr. F. 11. Gossage presided, and there were present : Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. E. Carey, F. H. Pankhurst, D. Wright, J. Midwood, B. Dutton, W. H, Kershaw R. Webster, S. Sadler, J. Houghton' J. E. JohE- son, J. T. Allen (clerk), Dr. Cooper (medical officer), Hig- ginson (surveyor), Copeland (resident engineer), and Dick: sou (nuisance inspector) The CHAIRMAN said he had seen Dr. Parsons, and he said there was no objection in the world to any member or mem- bers of the BJard accompanying him in his tour of the sites. Those who were going would please give Mr. Allen their names so that he might order a carriage of sufficient size.

Mr. KERSHAW thought that before they went round to select a site, they ought to havy the opinion of Dr. Parsons, whether an infec:ious diseases hospital was required. Ttie CHAIRMAN : It is not to select a site, it is to view sites.

Mr. KERSHAW: To view sites is to increase the price of land some 200 or 300 per cent. The CHAIRMAN: It is the action of the Board that has caused that—yourself as much as anybody. Mr. KERSHAW : I quite disagree with you on that point. My action has not caused that, and I think it is very dis- respectful of you to say so. The CHAIRMAN: 1 cannot help saying so because you come here to waste an immense quantity of time. Mr. KERSHAW : I came here as a ratepayer to protect the interests of the town. The CHAIRMAN: So do I, Mr. Kershaw. Mr. KERSHAW : Then if you keep these remarks in per- haps I shall not have to complain. Mr. Deerroe; : Are you going with the inspector, Mr. Chairman? The CHAIRMAN: No, I am not going. If you want my opinion, I think it is very improper to go. 'The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board, dated the 13 h lost, which informed the Board of Dr. Parsons visit to inspect the site or sites for an infectious diseases hospital, and report on their suitability to the Local Government Board. His present visit was merely a pre- liminary one, and before the Board sanctioned the erection of a hospital a formal inquiry would be held, of which due notice would be given, and at which any objection would be heard. Mr. KERSHAW desired to know why the notices of the meeting were not sent out earlier. Mr. ALLEN replied be- cause the letter did not arrive until Saturday. The letter was Entered in the book.—Mr. KERSHAW : I should like to see the envelope.—Mr. ALLEN said that was impossible: Mr. ALLEN asked the Chairman if he should order a trap for 10. The CHAIRMAN: I don't care what you order. Mr. 'AMON : Are we going to visit all these (meaning a list of 26 sites with which each member had been supplied). The CHAIRMAN: I don't know anything about that. I only act as chairman of the Board. Mr. DUTTON: Who will answer that question, sir? Our clerk? The CHAIRMAN: I cannot tell you. Mr. CAREY observed that the Surveyor had put them down in order to be visited. Mr. WEBSTER : Can all the land be taken? It was explained by the Chairman that several of the sites had been offered, and the Board had compulsory power to take the others. The CLERK then read a letter from the Local Govern- ment Board informing the Local Board that a conference of the Guardians of the Prescot Union and the Sanitary Authorities in their district with reference to the inadequate provision 3 for the isolation of infectious disease. The Board spent about an hour in appointing a deputation to attend this conference, amendment after amendment being pro- posed, Mr. Carey several times protesting against the dread- ful waste of time. Eventually it was decided that the Chairman (Mr. Gossage), Dr. O'Keeffe, Mr. Carey, Mr. Dutton, and Mr. Houghton form the deputation, with Mr. Allen (clerk), and Iligginson (surveyor). Mr. CAREY: I must protest against the afternoon being lost. Dr. Parsons is here to investigate the matter of sites for a hospital, and I think we ought really to abandon any other business be allow this matter to go on. I beg to pro- pose that those gentlemen who wish to go round with Dr. Parsons start at once w.th him. Mr. DterroN: I second that. Mr. CAREY said the sewerage business was very important, an I he was only giving it up because so much time had been lost over these -foolish squabbles. Mr. WEBsTER: What time will they get back?—Mr. CAREY: I suppose some time after dark. Dr. Parsons then entered the room, and Mr. Kershaw in- timated his intention of proposing a motion. The Chair- man replied that he ought to have given notice before. Mr. Kershaw retorted that he differed with the chairman's mode of procdure, ending by saying, "Keep your remarks within yourself." In answer to the chairman, Dr. PARSONS said the site behind the market for the temporary erection of tents seemed to him a very undesirable site if any other coma oe obtained. It was much too near the houses, with a fre- queotld building on the other side. If a more isolated site could be obtained it would be much better. He had seen the memorial with reference to the site at Halton-view, and he might explain that the Local Government Board could not relieve the Widnes Local Board of the responsi- bility of choesing a site. If they bad selected any sites he should be happy to see them, and make his report to the Local Government Board, who would then communicate with them as to whether they considered it suitable or not. Mr. KERSHAW said they were not proceeding in the right way to select a site. 'They ought to have had the price fixed in some measure before visiting any of the sites, and he alleged that the Board had not endeavoured to secure sites before asking the inspector to come down. Dr. O'Keeffe refuted this assertion by quoting from the minutes of the Board and Health Committee. Dr. O'Keeffe also stated that another case of small-pox had been reported that morning, and Dr. Cooper said another had broken out since, making two that thy. Dr. PARSONS said he might make one or two general re- marks upon the question of a hospital for Widnes. With regard to the site for the hospital, it should be of adequate size. The Local Government Board considered that no site should be taken which was under an acre, and for a town of theisize of Widnes, where extensions might be required, an acre would not be sufficient. He thought two acres would be necessary, so that any site under that acreage would not be satisfactory. The site should be sufficiently near to be convenient of access, bec muse people would not take their relatives or ftiends a considerable distance, and it was also injurious to the patients if they were very ill, if they had to be removed to a hospital an inconvenient dis- tance away. It was desirable, therefore, that the hospital I should be in a convenient and accessible situation. At the same time it must not be too near other buildings, but have an open situation consistent with an accessible position. It must not be erected in a damp, marshy situation, or near any offensive works. It must be in a locality where good water could be procured. The Local Government Board consi- dered that a hospital, or that part of the building in which infection might be conveyed, should be at least 40 feet diAant from the boundary, so that the site must be of such size that at least 40 feet margin could be secured all round the building. It was of the areatest importance that the hospital should be in readi- ness before needed. One gentleman seemed to think that the matter was not one that ought to be undertaken unless fthe epidemic had reached certain proportions. The experi- ence of the Local Government Board was that a hospital was useful in proportion as it was provided before any epi- demic broke out. Hospitals which were put up hurriedly under the influence of a panic, were found to be always ill arranged and ill adapted for the purposes required, and very speedily fell into disuse; whereas hospitals got up leisurely and with due consideration were found to be more useful, and was far more likely to be of benefit to the neigh- bourhood. Answering a question by Mr. KERSHAW with regard to Prescot workhouse, Dr. Pansozes said the Local Government Board held very firm views that the Guardians had nothing to do as Guardians with the isolation of cases of disease for the purpose of public health. It was for the Sanitary Authority to deal with such cases. The itmoend- ing conference need not alter the position of the Widnes Local Board, and they might consider that no sanction would be given for the workhouse at Prescet to be enlarged for the purpose of enabling them to send their patients who were not paupers. The CHAIRMAN asked if:the attendance of a deputation at that conference would in any way relieve the Board from their duty of providing an infectious diseases hospital when they knew that a disease like amell-pox was raging amongst them. I Dr. PARSONS: Certainly not. I sliould advise you to go on with the present arrangements as if a conference were not to be held. Mr. KERSHAW asked if the Board could erect a hospital outside the township boundary, Dr. PARSONS replied in the adirmative, but if the hospital caused a nuisance they could be compelled to abate it. Mr. KERSHAW: If that is the case I think it is desirable that Dr. Parsons should be shown Pex Hill. Dr. PARSONS said time would not permit him to ge round to see sites. It was not his business to choose a site for the Board. If they had settled upon a site he would see if it was a likely place. OuTTON asked if the urban authorities in the district would join the Board In the cost of a hospital independent of the Preecot authori- ties. He understood that the urban authorities would have to provide accommodation independent of rural authorities. —The CHAIRMAN replied that the Guardians could do nothing towards the expenses of a hospital.—Dr. O'KEEFFE pointed out that the:e was no urban authority in the im- mediate neighbourhood orWidnes, and said from what he knew of the Prescot Union-and the Guardians he did not think they would unite with the Board. Therefore, the sooner Widnes Board took action with the Local Govern- ment Board to separate itself from Prescot Union, both as regarded an infectious diseases hospital and their paupers, and the better. It would be less expensive tei the ratepayers if they got a hospital of their own in Widnes.—Mr. WEBSTER thought as they would have to contribute to the expenses of the hospital at i'Vhiston, it would ba better for them to erect a hospital of their own.— The CHAIRMAN said it was the duty of the Board to have their own hospital, and so not lose control of their patients. It could not cost very much. They must remember that smallpox was not the only disease they had to deal with ; there was always something going on that would be better isolated.—Mr. 'KERSHAW observed that Mr. Hartley seemed to think that the Guardians would be in favour of Ditton and Crouton joining Widnes —The CHAIRMAN thought it would be a far superior way if the Board erected a hospital and let those townships use it. The smaller ought to come to the greater in this matter. After erecting a hospital, it was competent for the Board to permit others to join by sharing the expense. (Hear, hear.)—Dr. O'KEEFFE repented that Dr. Parsons ,viewed a few sites for a hospital on the previous day, and said he would report to the Local Govern- ment Board. Seeing that the chairman of the Board was not present at that inspection, he thought that at the very least the Inspector ought to have bad accompanying him the chairman of the Health Committee, who took a great deal of trouble to visit every part of the township. Whether it was discourtesy on the part of the Inspector or the part of anybody else, he cared not who it was—discourtesy was shown to him (the speaker), and he resented it accordingly. The surveyor, toe, who ought to know the sanitary aspects of the place, was kept out of the plan com- pletely; the medical officer of health was kept out of tbe society of the Inspector, and was never invited to offer an opinion or give his views, or anything else. He was not consulted at all. The Sanitary Inspector, who was formerly not only a mem- ber but chairman of the Board, was treated with supreme content to a certain extent, by the Inspector. The Inspector said he would send his report independently of my consideration. Let him do so by all moans, and then they would perhaps know by what motives he had been actuated.—The CHAIRMAN: Then I understand that the Inspector did not express any opinion about one site or another ?—Dr. O'NEEFFE: No, sir—Mr. MIDWOOD: He didn't, sir, but Dr. Cooper tried to push his opinion down his throat.—Mr. KEB,HAW said if Dr. O'Keeffe had any charge to make against a member of the Board let him make it.—Dr. O'KEEFFE I aril not laying any charge.—Mr. KERSHAW : lam on my legs sir. If he has any charge as to the conduct of the proceedings with the Inspector, I hope he will make the charge openly that we may be able to meet it fairly and tionestly.—Dr. O'KEEFFE: If I had a charge I would lay it before a court of law instead of here, I say it distinctly.—The CEaruktas You don't get on with the business tif the Board by such conduct. If this is to continue I shall certainly leave the chair, I don't wish to sit here if we- are to have scenes of this description.—Mr. KERSHAW': I hope you don't make that remark to me?—The Chairman's reply was inaudible. —Mr. KERSHAw : If you don't like to listen to me, I don't care about it. I will be listened to I have a right. The assertion is made here by Dr. O'Keeffe that some person went to the side of the Inspector simply to influence him in what he may do.—Dr. O'KEEFFE : If the cip fits you may take it.—Mr. KERsHA.W (excitedly): I challenge you-- The CHAIRMAN : I think you ought to settle this outside and not here. If you won't support my authority I will leave the chair. I have no desire to sit here as Chairman.—Mr. Durroti : I think we ought not to allow this sort of thing to go on at all. I think D. O'Keeffe ougnt not to nave introduced the matter.—Dr. O'KEEFFE: You have not to dictate to me, sir.—The CHAIRMAN: I think we had better break up the meeting. Mr. CAREY was perfectly surprised. He begged to propose, if no one had anything to say about Dr. Parsons' inspection, that they proceed to the next business.—Mr. SADLER said the statement that the medical officer was not allowed to express any opinion to the inspector was untrue. He tried to push his opinion down the inspector's throat while in the car- riage. (Hear, hear.)—Dr. O'KEEFFE: I am very sorry he is not here to speak for himself.—Mr. CAREY: This doesn't help us. We never get any nearer to dealing with the in- fectious cases. Where have we to put the temporary tents for that is our business. What we want to deal with is the disease.—Dr. O'KEEFFE said a member present offered a site for the tents behind Dr. Cooper's house. Mr. KERSHAW stated the inspector on the previous day visited Mr. Ireland's property, a site at Halton View, belonging to Mr. Shaw Leigh, with which he seemed favourably impressed, and from there he was driven to the Pex Hill, which be said was too far from the town for a hospital. The site at Ap- pleton, belonging to the Board, was inspected, but the inspector said be did not think the Local Government Board would approve it.--Mr. KERSHAW announced that he was the member who had offered the temporary site.—lt was proposed by Mr. CAREY, seconded by Mr. Hononrox, that the Clerk be requested to ask Mr. Shelmerdine, agent to Mr. Shaw Leigh, to permit the Board the temporary use of a piece of land off Moorfield-lane to erect tents upon it, the purchase of the land to be left for subsequent negotiation. Mr. Durros moved an amendment that the Board at once place the tents on their own land at Pea ; and that they engage a duly qualified medical Practitioner for three months to take small- pox specially in hand, and stamp it out. The land was ready and it was important they should take immediate action.—Mr. MIDWOOD seconded.—After some discussion the original proposition was carried.—lt was then decided that the Health Committee meet on the following day to re- ceive Mr. Allen's repot, and act upon it. That was to say, if the report was favourable, proceed to erect the tents at once upon that ground, and if not to take the next best site they could so as not to trouble the Board any longer.—Mr. WRIGHT seconded.—Carried.—In answer to Mr. Houghton Dr. O'KEEFFE said it was almost impossible now to prevent the families of diseased persons mixing with one another, ' and it was pointed out that persons so exposing themselves were liable to be brought before the magistrates and fined in. the penalty of .£2O.

MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT A WIDNES WORKS. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, James Roach, employed at Widnes Alkali Company's Works, was charged with unlawfully wounding a labourer named Patrick Mannion. From the statement of Inspector Wood and the witnesses it appeared that the prisoner was the " gaffer " of a set of men, amongst whom was Mannion, at the Widnes Alkali Works. They were working there at seven o'clock on Saturday night, when the prisoner requested Mannion to pull some tiring out of a barrow with a spade. Mannion re the np i or is ot n pickeds r struck him u p thei the spades f c fused to do so, and a wrangle took place, the prisoner us- bsa iwnigt he ohmi s fit, e d wl ahnegr tia gp eo 'n Mt ha n h ee rn which was lying by the side of the barrow, and with it struck 'Mannion a heavy blow on the face, felling him t 4 the ground "like a bullock." A workman named Murray said "Roach, you have killed the man," and the prisoner I replied "Let him bleed there." Several men then took up Mannion's unconscious form and carried him home, after washing the blood from his face. Mannion remained un- conscious for a considerable time. On Sunday Dr. O'Keeffe examined the injured man and found a wound on the left cheek, which was dressed, and he did not disturb it. That morning he ascertained that there was an incised wound about 2. inches long on the prominent portion of the left ceek. Ile could not say how deep it was as it was healing nicely. It was dressed with adhesive plaster. The danger was from erysipelas. The spade produced might cause such a wound as that from which Mannion suffered, but considerable violence would have to be used. It would be unwise for Mannion to follow his employment for about a week. P.C. McGuinneal arrested the prisoner at take Alkali Works shortly after the occurrence. On the way „lo the station the prisoner said "I did hit him with gelnp spade. It was in my own defence, and I did not strike any other man." At the police station he was charged, with un- lawfully wounding the prosecutor. He replied" He hit me On the face. I had the spade in my hand and I hit him on the head with it. That is all I have got to say, and that is all I will say."—Evidence having been given by the prose- cutor, who lives at 2, Elizabeth-street; Dr. O'Keefe; Thos. Smith, 12, Timperley-street ; and William Murray, 44, Margaret-street, the prisoner was formally committcd to take ' his trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions. He was admitted to bail, himself in £4O and two sureties of £25 each.

div.head: SMALL-PDX EPIDEMIC AT WIDNES.
div.p: THE SMALL-PDX EPIDEMIC AT WIDNES.

Small-pox shows no signs of decreasing in Widnes. On the contrary, it is extending in a most alarming manner• Up till nesday the disease had ben confined to the higher parts of the town, mainly at Simm's Cress, but on Wednes- day two cases broke out in the populous district of West Bank. At a special meeting of the Health Committee, on Wednesday, it was reported by Mr. Allen, the clerk, that he had been unsuccessful in obtaining from the agent of the Leigh estate a plot of land upon which to erect the two hospital tents purchased by the Board from the Stafford Corporation. Major Cross, however, hearing of the serious difficulty in which the Board was placed, saw a member of the Board, whom he told that the Board were perfectly at liberty to use a piece of his land near to Morrside-terrace, a most suitable spot. The committee at once accepted the kind offer, and passed a unanimous vote of thanks to Major Cross. It was decided to erect the tents on the land with all possible speed. They will accommodate twenty patients. Last evening it was rumoured that several deaths bad oc- curred from smallpox during the day, but we are glad to say that the rumour is entirely groundless. A fresh case was reported during„the afternoon. The hospital tents are expected to be ready for use to-day. There are several per- sons suffering from sctrlet fever and scarletina.

Phe afternoon preacher was the Rev. W. C. Tayler (Baptist), and in the evening the pulpit was occupied by Mr. J. Jones- On Tuesday evening the weekly temperance meeting was held. div.head: ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL,
div.p: ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL,
BY JOHN SAU"OERs, Author of " HIBELL ; OR, BORN OF STRIFE," "ABEL DRLICE'S WIFE," "ISEL hi OVEALNIAN," etC.

cii!....-eTER xxix.—TlLE LAST PAUSE. Stepheo. was no politician, and in that respect resembled most -youths of his rank and prospects. But he had strong IP:ariotic feeling if only circumstances were sufficiently in- feresting to bring it out. Ile had also sagacity—it might almost be called an instinctive power—of insight into men and their motives, when he came personally into contact with them. Now patriotism, such as he bad been led to shape it in England, as directed towards Ireland, prompted so strong a feeling of abhorrence towards everything bearing the taint of Fenianism, that he had been surprised to find himself listening to one who had actually been in its ranks, with a sympathy for the man, whish he was only able to justify when he fouad at the end of his narrative that he had also very quickly left the ranks for ever. They parted at Holyhead with mutual good wishes, Stephen feeling half-ashamed that while hearing so much of his companion's life and views, he had not in return con- fided one sidgle fact that might enable the former to guess . as to his position and object in Ireland; or to obtain the slightest clue as to the character of the man to whom he had been so lavish in self .revelation. " Ah, well," thought Stephen, "we may some day meet again, and I'll pay him back jri his:own coin 1" So while the three days' Fenian and his wife went to the hotel for the night, after a fresh attempt to induce their young fellow-traveller to accompany them, and so all go across the Channel together comfortably the next morning, Stephen hurried to the steamboat, and again brought home to him the contrast between his former as Compared with

his nreseut state, - 'de n(.l pau;d- to glance into the luikurious saloon, and there thought for a moment—should he pay the.differenee, rest there, and let that be his last extravagance ? or should he go on to his proper third-class quarters, and so continua to prepare himself step by step for the inevitable downfall, perhaps degradation, that awaited him in all that concerned his habits of life, and tendencies to personal indulgence? He turned and strode away, and had immediate reason to congratulate himself, for as he moved about—now In the darkness of the night, now in the g'eams oC the lamps of the packet—he passed a tall, stern-looking man on his way to the saloon, who was addressed as "Colonel," by a ser- vant behind him loaded with rugs and small matters of baggage. As he passed a heavy portmanteau that was lying near one of the lamps, he read the officer's name—Hot son. " Colonel ! Going to Ireland! Perhaps to the Curragh. Nice introduction if we had happened to get into talk before I knew his rank and vocation, and I then had to appear before him as one of the humblest of his Tommy Atkinses ! Thank goodness I have escaped, and must rola no such risk

again." lie sought, therefore, his proper place as a representative of the Tommy Atkius class, and found it among a miscel- laneous crowd of men, women, and children, half-buried among their luggage, :most of which could be carried by band, and was no doubt thougkt too valuable to be tfusted elsewhere. The children were crying. Their mothers soothing or islapping, the men noisily discussing, and in some cases -hotly differing about a variety of subjects in which Stephen found it impossible to take any interest, and so unconsciously allowed his thoughts to fly back to home. Painfully now he wondered how his mother was bear- ing his departure ; whether his brother" was using the ad- vantages of his position to secure Miss Vandeleur ; and above all whether that young lady was still exciting her- self from time to time by the reading or recollection of the fatal verse? Out of all this tangled web he could draw but one conclusion—that he abhorred himself for writing that verse, even though he had never dreamed of her seeing it. He was a good sailor, so no sea sickness troubled him. And by the time he reached Dublin, between ten and eleven at night, the conflict that like an undercurrent had been going on, whatever else might appear uppermost, from the moment he left London to the moment when he stepped upon the quay at North Wail, there ended; and he felt and said to himself with something of peace and satisfac- tion. "The die is Cast. I will not return." Yet it had been a trying struggle between pride and humiliation ; self-indulgence, and self-cho3en hardship; the power to go back, handsomely apologise to Miss Vande- leur, then leave her to do and feel as she liked, and the very different power that must be evoked to go forward, while knowing that he thus sacrificed his only chance of winning a charming, if somewhat faulty, girl—and with it independence in his own sphere, and a future that might be almost whatever he chose to make it. But he did now finally decide to go ore; and that so sin- cerely, while thoroughly prepared for whatever might happen, that the consciousness iutused peace of mind and strength of will. He was interrupted by a vice crying from the top of a car, "Shure, an' your honour will Lie wanting to go to --! ' naming one of the most aristocratic Dublin hotels. " And here's the car ready. Wait, s'r, till I get down!" "Thank you—no;" quickly responded Stephen, as he ; shouldered his portmanteau, and walked away into the ob- scurity of the night, followed by the loud remark of the trman, "That young fellow is a haul' imposthure ! I took him for a gintleinan." Stephen heard, and laughed, but became uncomfortable about his appearance. He did not want to be taken for a gentleman: it would greatly add to his annoyance and diffi- culty. lie must think of that! When he lay down that night it was in One of the humblest inns of the neighbonrhood of the quay. After counting his money, and finding that he had more than four pounds in his possession, he could not help saying to himself with a laugh— " Did ever mill enlist before with such a fortune in his pocket!" CHAPTER XXX.—TetE DISPOSAL OF TUE ronTMANTEAU. Perhaps it was the consciousness of a little money to spare that caused Stephen, as he dressed in the morning and looked down into a dingy, miserable street below, to ask hirneelf whether he wee going to let his one glinuese of the city that he had read of AS One of the flmst iti,•2urope, be only a glimpse of her back alums. He could live very cheaply for two or three days in the lodgings he had got to, though the accommodation was wretched in the extreme ; but then the poor old landlady didn't pretend it wee any othee, and begged his honour's pardon that 3119 W. 15 ;o badly able to entertain him. I The plea Was irresistible while he did stop. So he began I ()nee mere to retrace the old ground—this last indulgence— this last bit of freedom—and then— But his pleasure of former days—the baffling men in their excuses for indulgence by strokes of satire that operated like an electric flash on the darkness of the motive alleged—now returned to plague, or benefit, the inventor. With a smile of unusual bitterness, as though full of half a hundred recollections that were galling him, he suddenly called for and paid his little bill, and was ready for the last stage of his momentous journey. What was he to do with his portmenteau ? There were in it the choicest and most useful articles of his wardrobe, carefully selected before leaving home, besides many elegant and soma costly appliances of a dressing case and a writing case. There were still more precious things among We con- tents—letters from his deceased father, letters from his mother, and letters from Miss Vandeleur, each chosen from a iarge ef the most precious of his small wery stock of goods. He attempted tf, glance over them. The admirable good sense that -made every touch a permanent intellectual effect in those of his father; the delicious outpouring of love in his mother's, but always accompanied by some fear, sugges- tive of danger against which he must be warned, conveyed in language so sweet—it seemed to read like a strain of poetry to Stephen even while he was trying to nurse the feeling of his own wrongs from her ; and lastly, the ever short notes of Miss Vandeleur, which irresistibly tempted the reader to ask, " Why doesn't she go on ?" All mese now moved him more deeply than ever, though only catch- ing here and there; in his rapid survey, sentences that told him the nature of the context. These, at least, could qgt possibly be risked in the camp. He did not know but theTe would be a place and persons appointed to take possession of any property belonging to a recruit, to be returned to him at a suitable future time. All else he might Wee risked, but not these letters. So he took out suck few articles as were likely to be most use- ful to him, and which he might carry about with him un- noticed, then repacked tipe remainder. Not knowing what he was to do with the 'portmanteau for secrecy and safety during possibly a lengthened period, he at once shouldered the burden, and pledged it at the nearest pawnbroker's for a pound. after showing the cen- tents, and paving the clerk extra for making out a list. As no robbery could be in question, apart from the ap- pearance of the bringer, and as the latter explained that he was travelling on foot to see the country, and did not' want to move his luggage about, the pawnbroker asked no ques- tions; but volunteered to lend five pounds instead of one, whietewas politely declined. This accomplished he reached the station, took his ticket for Newhridge, and waited the coming of the train, wonder- ing if he should have any companions bent on the same errand. ,

CHAPTER XXXI.—A BIRD'S EYE :VIEW. A curious thought occurred to Stephen as he watched with curiosity every station he passed through ; and between the stations gazed from side to side upon the open country with eager interest. It seemed to him he was looking with new eyes upon everything, and that the weary feeling of life that had of late often overcome him was giving place to something like zest, though whether it was to bring him more of pain than enjoyment, he could not tell. The fact, however, was pleasant m itself, and helped with the beauty of the morning, to greatly raise his spirits; so that it was with a decidedly cheerful aspect and manner he leaped lightly out of the train at Newbridge, which was the stopping place for the camp. A group of soldiers, mostly in Highland uniform. were on the platform. They were all very young men like himself
