—mostly with with gend-looking feces, radiant with fun and frolic, whisking thOr fancy -sticks about, and addressing jokes to the newly-arrif*Vassengers. One of their num- ber began to challenge to 4'etephen, who was pausing a little • apart to notice them. " Well, old fellow, how do You like us, eh? We're a jolly lot, ain't we, now ?" Then turning to a comrade he added pointing with his thumb at Stephen, "More grist to the old mill, eh? Will he stand treat?" Here he was stopped by a whisper from his comrade, which caused him to become suddenly serious, and to look at Stephen with mingled fear and respect. Stephen understood the eenarade thought he might be an officer, and that it were well to be on the safe side, so had warned the jocular man, whom he drew away. This was annoying. And as Stephen left the station he questioned himself whether he bad not better at once find some sheltered corner, and begin the work of outward per- sonal degradation. And yet it seemed too absurd. A crazy vehicle waited outside that had been brought to the station on its way to fetch some luggage from the camp; and of which by some strange conjunction of events the pre- sent regular omnibus almost seems to be a humble imitator and representative. Once more he was appealed to as "his honour " to take a place for the Curragh. Stephen did look into it—as if in doubt, but reilly from a sense of amusement at the sight of the wondrous interior. The original fabric had become so delapidated that it could only be kept together aad made endurable for travellers by patching on a large scale—with leather on one side—through which already had been worn or made somehow a hole that an arm might go through, while over other and still larger , gaps were plates of tin—the supply of leather having failed. In the bottom lay a mass of straw, so dirty that it could only be likened to the contents of a stable that had been long forgotten to be cleaned out. "Will yer honour get in? Going directly." "No, thanksi I want a walk. How far is it to the cimp?" "About three miles." "Along that road in front of us ? ' "Yes." . "Easy to find?" . 1 " Hard to miss." I "All right !" And then putting twopence in the driver's I hand, and taking another longing, lingering view of the in- terior, Stephen walked off. He s3on found himself in a cbarming road, bordered by trees most of the way, and winding picturesquely in parts. A road that in winter becomes as dilapidated in its own fashion as the omnibus is at all times. But now it was revelling in sunshine, in embowering foliage, and in the songs of birds; and Stephen's heart seemed to become vocal in sympathy. He felt as if all things around and within him were Sanc- tioning and confirming his purpose, and he was too content with the result to give way to any of his ordinary specu- ' latiye bantering incredulities. At last a glimpse of the Curragh and of the camp broke upon his sight. How be would like to get a good view before he went far- ther! There was a tree beside him, with a fork at a con- venient height. In a few seconds he had mounted, and could then command a tolerable view of the whole. The Curragla he saw, formed a wide stretch of undulating country, green under foot but treeless, though once a forest; circled in the distance by hills, in places rising to the height and dignity of mountains—one of them being the second only in altitude of all the mountains in Ireland. Occupying the centre of this expanse, for the space of a mile or so in every direction, he saw the camp formed by lines of low wooden huts, their dull character relieved by the white tents of the soldiery brought here for the summer only. lasses of reel-coats were marching in the distance; and from other parts rose the sound of military music, which always inspiring, came to Stephen's ear and soul like the sound of that trumpet which he remembered to have read of in Sir Philip Sidney. On he went, thinking only now how he must act, how shape out a military character worthy of his own position and prospects, if once he righted himself in the manful conquest of a commission, obtained through every obstacle, and perfectly unaided in the getting. That was now his ambition—his sole aim. To it he re- signed for a time every other aspiration and hope. He soon reached what was evidently the front road of the'eamp—got so near that he could see the soldiers in their varying uniforms—passed the officers' huts, divided by a road from the men's, and marked by low white stones on the ground ; and at last came opposite a square space, where recruits in different squads were being drilled. Every detail interested Stephen. Some of the men had not yet got their uniforms. Eagerly he tried to make out if there were any at all like himself—possible future companions—with whom to make a little oasis in the desert of military life, such as he expected for a time to find it. He saw not one that by any stretch of fancy he could sup- pose ever to have supposed himself a gentleman. Noticing their weapons, lie perceived only a few had rifles; others were carrying large clubs, one in each hand ; while yet others bore small boards, which from time to time they lifted over their heads and brought down behind their backs. Many were mar ching ; more fortunate than their com- rades, who were only permitted to pretend to march, by prac- tising the goose step. While Stephen's eyes and thoughts were thus deeply en- grossed—ca deeply that he quite forgot he might himself be in the way of notice from others, that he was not exactly pre- pared for, a Sergeant came up and entered into conversation with him. In the Course of this he told him the police would presently he demanding his business. The camp, he said, was private property, belonging to the Secretary of State for War—no one was allowed there without a pass, and ' trespassers were liable to be prosecuted. He ended by point- ing to the hut of the Provost-Marshall. 'This was not exactly the kind of introduction to the c imp Stephen had planned. However, he smiled, apologised for his ignorance, which he hoped would be excused, for he had come from England to enlist. Marvellous became the change in the Sergeant's behaviour. He looked at Stephen's dress and attitude—as if to realise his mistake in thinking he was simply an impudent amateur gentlemaa, who thought he had only to walk in, look about, and walk out again. Then seeing he was at all events a good-looking, well- dressed, and altogether likely recruit, he smiled in response, shook Stephen's hand warmly, and thus began an acquaint- ance which was destined to colour seriously our young hero's military life.

purse, "Put out your right hand, my fine lad, and I will give you the Queen's bbiliing—the best you ever bad, I'll be bound Stephen put out his hand. "Before I give yJII this, you must answer akw ques- tions." He then, after asking Stephen his name (which he gave as Stephen Shand), his place of business, his age, and about other comparatively unimportant matters, proceeded as follows : "Are you free, willing and able to serve her Majesty the , Queen for a perical of ten years ?" "Yes," said Stephen firmly. "Will you also serve her Majesty for a further period of two years if a state of war exists between her Majesty and any foreign or colonial power ?" " Yes,' responded Stephen, c.lmefuily weighing the Ser. geant-Ma.jor's words. "Do yo belong to any other regiment ?" " Certainly not !'' "Say No—that's enough," remarked the Sergeant-Major, irritably. "No." "Do you belong to the militia or any other corps ?" "I do not." "Can't you say simply—No ?" No." "Are you married?" "No." The Sergeant Major lire condescended to explain that married men were not enlisted, but marriage was granted as a privilege to good old soldiers after so many years ser- vice. For the life of him Stephen could not help ironic illy connecting this inestimable privilege for himself with the image of Miss Vandeleur, but only to his own extreme an- noyance. "Do you know anything the matter with you to prevent your"h?ining the army ?" "There, then, is the shilling. You are now enlisted. This done the Sergeant-Major gave Stephen a notic: paper containing the foregoing questions and the aneretSfq their side; and told him he would have to go to the hospital the next morning at nine to pus the doctor, in company with the Orderly-Corporal, who conducted the sick. Finally, he was informed that if he failed to attend, or had made false answers to any of the questions put to him, he would be treated as a rogue and a vagabond, and prose- cuted accordingly as the law directs. And with that brief and sharp warning that he was, in- deed, committed beyond recall to the life, duties, and dis- agreeables, however heavy, of the private soldier, Stephen was dismissed to his next experience—the barrack room of .he Sergeant's company, whither he was now taken. LTo be continued.)

CiIIAPTER QCEEN+B "Come along with me," said the Sergeant, "And I'll put you straight through. So, like many other men, you want to try your chance for glory?" "I'm afraid there's not much of that falling to the share of the private soldier," said Stephen, with a smile. • "Oh, I don't know, great men have come out of the ranks."
Would you kindly mention

"That's interesting. them ?" "Oh, I don't remember now. But if glory Droves scarce there's nice pickings to be got." "By the private?" " Well, not often. Beauty and booty did fall to his lot now and then. But tkoso were in the old times." "Then. by the non-commissioned officers ?" " Well, here's a case in point. lam a nen-commissioned officer, and I shall get half-a-guinea for the pleasure of taking a first-rate recruit to enter into the service of Her Majesty." 'But that's an accident." • "Well, we have many privileges. Our quarters are good. We may get to be sergeant-Ea ajors, and still better—quarter- masters." " Is that the routine through which a lucky private may hope to pass ultimately to a commission ?" asked Stephen, in tone that was carefully modulated to imply no special interest in the answer. Sergeant Grabble, for that -was his rank and name, turned, and looked in Stephen's face, as though he had made a dis- covery. The latter met the look so well that the sergeant appeared satisfied, and merely said— "You are a young man. I like the look of you. But have a care. Neither officers or men take kindly to a fellow who thinks himself above his station." " I think myself below mine," said Stephen, very humbly, but with a certain enjoyment of the double meaning. "Oh, you'll do. And now, will you join my regiment, the th, the best-dressed corps in the whole camp! Good officers." "Certainly, I should not think of choosing any other," said Stephen, with a half bow. "Come, then, to our Sergeant-Major, get through some business with him, and then you shall join my company. I I am engaged for a time on special duty, but shall be rejoin- ing in a day or two, and will look after you." Wondering how much of this making things pleasant be- longed to the period before enlistment, and would disappear afterwards, Stephen trudged on by the Sergeant's side to the hut of the Sergeant-Major, which stood nearly alone in an open square in the centre of the camp. The Sergeant knocked at the door, and was answered in a , loud stern voice from the Sergeant-Nlajor

'Come in!" If you please, sir," said the Sergeant, as he entered with Stephen, " I have brought a recruit to be enlisted." "Let him stand forward," was the response, in still harsher tones, which, however, evidently came as the natural expression of the man's habit, meaning nothing in particular, except some shadowy idea of discipline. For Stephen as he advanced saw he looked placidly enough, and therefore recovered his own equanimity. "So, my bay, you have COI= to enlist? You want to serve her Majesty. Ah, that's something like an ambition. I enlisted in the same way—and you see me here ! lam glad you have chosen the —th Regiment. You'll find you're in luck in so doing. Pay attention to your drill, behave yourself like a man who respects his superiors, and you'll get promotion. Now, come with me to the orderly room." Stephen followed him, studying on the way his character by the few indications given. He bresaw how important might be a right understanding of the temper, disposition, and ways of thinking of both the men he bad now come in contact with his sergeant, and the still more important sergeant-major, the virtual commandant of the company under, and in the absence of, the commissioned officers. But he again he reminded himself—all this must be a mat- ter of course till the recruit was fast bound ; and it would be as well for him to watch, and be prepared for a disagree- able change thereafter. The Sergeant-Major led the way into a room, where some clerks were sitting at their desks; and Stephen could

DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES. The annual distribution of the prizes and certificates to the successful students in connection with the above classes was made on Friday evening last by the Rev. Chas. Beard, 8.A., of Liverpool, in the Town Hall, St. Helens. The Mayor (Lieutenant-Colonel Gamble) presided, and there were also on the platform, besides Mr. Beard and the suc- cessful students, the Revs. Canon Carr, J. M. Wamslev. and R. J. Ward; Alderman Harrison, Major W. W. Pilkington, Dr. MeNicoll, Messrs. J. C. Gamble, A. J. Speeder!, E. J. Simpson (head master of Cawley Schools), and other gentlemen. There was a large attendance of parents and friends in the body of the hall. The MAYOR, who was received with applause, said he need not tell them that they were met that evening for the purpose of presenting the prizes subscribed for by the peo- ple of St. Helens to be given to the better class of students who had obtained the prizes in the examination of the Science and Art Department of the Government. That was the fifth meeting they had had of that kind, but as most of them knew the classes had been carried on for a great many more years than that; but these subscriptions for prizes and that society for the purpose of having them I distributed publicly had existed for the last five years. They I believed that those prizes, not only those which were given by the Government Science and Art Department, but those which were sub- ' scribed for by the people of St. Helens, derived increased advantage by Whig distributed in the presence of the sub- scribers, and of the people of St. Helens, and of the parents and friends of the young men who had won these prizes. They had thought that when they obtained gentlemen of standing—which they had never failed to ace mplish—to distribute the prizes, their words would not only add some- thing to the value of the prizes, but would add something to the knowledge and enthusiasm of those who were en- deavouring to wits them. (Applause.) He had nothing more to say but would introduce to them hie friend, Mr. Beard, who would distribute the prizes. Before they were distributed, however, he would cell upon the hon. sec., Mr. Culshaw, who had worked very hard at the work for some years, and he would give them an account of their proceed- ings for the year. He would tell them the amount of work that had been done, the number of the students who had been working in those classes, and the number of those who had won certificates. They had not given local prizes to all 1 the students who had won Government certificates, but only ' to those who were recommended by the teachers as being ' the highest of those who obtained Government certificateCa (Applause.) 1..‘11.-. I...•'aSitiva, previous to reading thit report, read \letters of apology for inability to attend from the following gentlemen namely, the Rev. A. A. Nunn, vicar of Parr; Mr. A. Walmsley, Springfield, Eccleston • Councillor Wil- cock ; and Mr. George Daglish, of St. Helens foundry. He might say, Mr. Culshaw added, that Major Ogle, who was also one ef the committee, was unwell? sad consequently unable to attend. He then read ate following report : "St. Helens Science and Art Classes.—Central Committee's Report for the year 1882-83.—At the commencement of the year the classes were placed at a disadvantage throagh Mr. Abbott (a former teacher) leaving the town. Mr. Abbott had instructed classes of one kind and another for six years, and during the year preceding this had taught no less than four science and four art classes, the number of his pupils examined being 48, of whom 39 passed. The loss of a teacher so well known was sure to be felt; but the com- mittee were successful in securing the services of other qualified masters to fill the vacancy thus created. Con- sidering this drawback, the committee think the classes have succeeded satisfactorily, the number of certificates obtained being about the same as in the previous year. The silver medal offered by the committee has been won by , John B. C. Kershaw, the most successful candidate at the May examinations. Mr. Kershaw's Government awards were—lst class certificate and Queen's prize in the advanced , stage of sound, light, and heat; Ist class certificate and Queen's prize for mathematics; Ist class certificate and Queen's prize for chemistry. The committee view , with very great satisfaction the fact that a most com- plete chemical laboratory has been fitted up at Cowley's Middle Schools. Classes in connection with this committee are being held at the laboratory. Feeling convinced that the work in which they are engaged will soon assume such proportions as will be creditable to the town, the committee have had a special die cut, from which this year's medal has been struck. The medal bears the borough arms and the words 'St. Helens Science and Art Classes' on the obverse, and a laurel wreath and suitable inscription an the reverse. The authorities at South Ken- sington have decided to discontinue giving prizes to candi- date who obtain first class passes in an elementary science examination. In place of the prizes, thirty-six National scholarships are now offered for competition, any of which are only likely to be obtained by one town at rare intervals. The committee have therefore decided to give a prize, value 75. 6d., to each candidate who passes first class in the ele- mentary stage of a science subject. In addition to these prizes they will award the following class prizes :—ln any class in which ten or more students pass; three prizes of the respective values of 20s. 15s. and 103., to those who pass the Government examination, and are most attentive and painstaking in their preparatory studies. Where less than ten, but five or more students pass, two primes will be given. And where three or four pass, one prize. A silver medal will be awarded to the candidate who obtains the most and highest passes at the Government examinations." • Mr. BEARD then distributed the prizes to the students as fol- lows :—Sound, Light, and Heat: Class at Cowley's Element- ary Schools. Sheffield, Janet Gardner, Thomas Glover, Samuel Glover, Margaret Fitzpatrick, George Dutton, Government certifi- cate ; William Hodkinson, Herbert Anderton, Edward B. Sherlock, Government certificate and local class prize. Advanced: Sarah Forshaw, Government certificite.—Silver medal, John B. C. Kershaw. The Rev. Mr. BEARD then gave his address. He hardly knew, he said, to what he owed the very great honours of being permitted to dirgribute those prizes to the members of the science and art classes. It was, perhaps, to the fact that ha alWays had had a very deep interest in higher edu- cation and endeavour in a neighbouring city, and showed that interest by every means in his power. (Hear, heir.) He could only say that it would be a source of very pure pleasure to see the exertions which had been made by these boys and young men, increase their enthusiasm as they stood- upon the threshold of the temple of science and predict for them a proud and prosperous futere. (Applause.) And that pleasure was enhanced, at least to him by the fact that the certificates and prizes they had distributed were not simply a recogni- tion on the part of their townsmen of the labours which they had passed, and the conquests they had won, but also a recognition of the same facts at the hands of the Gavern- ment of this great country. (Hear, hear.) If they would go back 100 yeare*in their thoughts they would be able, to some extent, to measure the progress that had been made. National education, not merely of tbe primary kind but of the scientific kind, was ROW a matter of national concern, and here in St. Helens as in Liverpool, and every way else they were able to bear their part in the great onward mar& of scientific thought which was se characteristic of our age. The LECTURER, in commencing, said that he had been called upon rather suddenly that night, but the subject upon which he was going to speak he had spoken about some 18 months ago, when considerable attention was heirsc paid to the question of free trade, or fair trade. At that time he put together some thoughtsand facts on the subject, and there- fore it was in no way new to him. His chief subject, he said, was peace, but there might be some present who were not quite in favour of free trade, and therefore before he showed that free trade was favourable to peace Ilte must first show that free trade was good in itself. If there wax anyone present who doubted for a moment whether free trade had been a good or a bad thing for this country, he should think there was no way more easy to settle that doubt than to appeal to facts. Plainly, a way to tiecide the question would be to look at the stafe of the country before the c..rn Lesee were abolished, and then at the condition of the country since: and if it could be shown by facts that in every point bf view we had progressed; if all good things had increased and bad things decreased, then surely those facts would show that free trade had ben beneficial to the country. Then let them take a fact or two respecting the state of the country before the Corn Laws were abolished.' The lecturer mentioned Hinckley, in Leicestershire, where the poor-rates were 52, in the £, and another town' in Dasetshire where t co-thirds of the population were re- ceiving relief; families in Yorkshire had to live on bran ; in Huddersfield 13,000 people were reduced to the very verge of starvation; atSheffield there were 20,000, and at Leeds 30,000 of the inhabitants on the rates; at Accrington only one-ninth of the people were fully employed; and in many parts of the country there were millions of people who did not know the taste of wheaten bread. Some of these things he himself could remember. To turn to the other side of the picture, he might give them a few figures from a speech made by Lord Derby some few years ago. They all knew that Lord Derby was an exceedingly cautious man. He noted the progress that had been made in the countly in 10 years, gut! gaYe us a few facts. In 18, he said) Oar le."llPorts were 303 !millions of -Founds a year; in 1860-10 -years after—those unpile had increased to 411 millions of pounds a year. Then take the exports. In 1870 the exports were 244 mil- lions of pounds per annum, but in 1880 they were 286 mil- lions 01 pounds. They had been higher than that, but daring the 10 years mentioned there had been an increase in our exports of 42 millions per year. Then his lordship referred to tlse Savings' Bank, and stated in his remarks that it was a very safe criterion to judge by as to the con- dition of the better portion of the working class population of this country. and he said that in 1870 the Savings' Bank held 53 millions of the people's money, and in 1880 it held 78 millions an increase, as they would see, of nearly one-half. Hie lordship also referred to another sriterion by means of which they could judge very fairly of the condition of the peeple generally. Asa proof of the increased comforts of the people he gave the consumption of tea, and said that in 1870 1171 millions of pounds of tea were consumed, but in 1880 158 millions were used by the people. The consumption of sugar had in- creased at about the same rate. During the same 10 years the population had increased more rapidly than during any other period of our history. On the other band crime had greatly decreased, and perhaps the most striking fact was that although the population had enormously increased dur- ing the 10 years pauperism lead decreased by a quarter of a million. It had been asked several times that if free trade had done so much good to this country, how was it that the &amens did not adopt it? He had no doubt in his own mind-that free trade would be good for Germany—(hear, hear)—and it was what the Germans wanted. But why did they have such high tariffs upon goods going into Germany? Not because the Emperor or Prince Bismarck believed it to be for the good of trade and ge the people an that country, but because they were under the necessity of raising a large revenue to support their vast military armaments. What was the result upon the people? Simply that the people of aormany were being so thoroughly protected that they were emigrating to America by thousands. (Hear, hear.) The lecturer then went on to refer to fair trade, which, he said, was only another name for protection. Those styling themselves fair traders argued that as the imports of this country were increasing faster than the exports we were buying at a greater rate than we were selling, and therefore parting with our money—that we were going the wrong way, and would be ruined. But the lecturer gave an illustration showing that although our imports might appear larger than our exports we were the gainers by it, and not the losers. Sup- pose, he said, that a ship load of cotton worth a certain sum was taken from Manchester to India: when it got there it would have to be sold for a large- sum. If the money received for the cotton was spent in buying• jute, the jute when brought to Manchester weuld be sold for a larger sum than was given for it. Therefore the load which came in would be worth ever so much more than the load which went out. He maintained that everybody was benefited by that transection, and what had so alarmed people turned out to be a gain instead of a loss. They would never, he slid, in- crease our exports by putting a tax on our corn. It had been stated as a powerful argument at the time that the Bradford woollen manufacturers were suffering owing to the importa- tation of French goods into this country. No doubt it was 8). The ladies of this country had a preference far French woollens over English woollens, because the French woollens were a much lighter and better material altogether. Would it, he asked, be a right principle to put such a tax upon those goods as to make it almost impossible for people to huy them, and in a manner compel them to buy what they dida7t want It would be Wrong. The proper remedy bad now been adopted. They had begun to adapt their machinery to the requirements of the market, and he believed were now nearly up to the French. (Applause.) If the French got a little ahead of U 3 by their industry let them reap the fruits of it. In refer- ring again to our imports and exports, he said that one of the things which made imports seem so much more than exports was that we had gentlemen who had money in- vested abroad. They did not get the interest for that money in money but in goods, and. there was at least 100 million pounds a year brought into this country in value for interest on money invested abroad. Turning to what he called his own part of the subject—peace—he said that the Treaty of Commerce which was formed between England and France was a very fine illustration that free trade was the handmaid of peace. Before that treaty was formed there was the greatest jealousy between the two countries, but when that treaty was passed, and just in degree as they began to trade with and know more of each other just so mach had their jealousy lessened until it had almost passed away. They ought to rejoice that the old feeling was almost completely conquered. It had been conquered by the good feeling which had been brought about by Com- merce. Before the recent discussion as to free trade and fair trade, and when referring to the fact of the ships of England going across the seas in all directions, and from nation to nation, Mr. Gladstone said that they were like the weaver's shuttle going backwards and forwards, between nation and nation, weaving the web of concord between nations. (Applause.) What difference could there be, the lecturer asked, between the people who were on this or the ()tiles side of a range of mountains? They were still members of the human race and their Interests were identical with our interests. Perhaps he ought to allude to the rule that it was to the interest of countries to be as independent as possible. He believed that just the reverse was the case, that.it was titot well for a country to be independent. How unwise it was to go and shoot-down our customers as we had often done in needless wars—men who would have been our customers, purchasing our manu- factured articles. Interemrse between the different nations of the earth, commercial intercourse, must lead to more wisdom and good feeling, and that would lead to peace. Sometimes commerce would promote peace, and sometimes peace would promote commerce. There was no greater dis- grace to Europe than her vast armaments. Each nation was armed to the teeth, ready to fly at each other on small 'occasions as they bad done. He could give them facts to show that we had entered into wars with nations when it was not in the slightest degree to the interests of the country, but because we had large arms and wanted to fight, and gentlemen wanted to distinguish themselves in battle, and therefore we bad entered into war when there was ni occa- sion for it.. He believed it would come about as a natural consequence that as commerce increased we should have international chambers of commerce in place of military tri- bunals. It was considered a disgrace for two gentlemen to settle a dispute by fighting, but when two nations fought they spoke of the honour and dignity of two great nations. (Applause.) If it was wrong for two gentlemen to settle a dispute by fighting. it was a still greater, wrong for two nations to do so, because the injury was greater. In con- clusion he urged upon them to try to spread free trade, good- will towards the people of every country, and bring about that glorious doctrine and teaching of our Great Master— " Peace on earth and goed-will towards men." (Ap- plause.) A discussion followed, in which Mr. F. Wright, Mr. A. Bennett, Mr. Jenkins, and Mr. Richardson took part, and a vote of thanks to the Lecturer, proposed by Mr. A. BEN- NETT, seconded by Mr. T. C. LONDON, brought the proceed- ings to a close.

CONSERVATISM IN MID-CHESHIRE.

Sir,—At the Conservative tea party at Lymm on Monday night some remarks were made by Mr. John Brooks as to the triumphant position of the party in that locality. The same tone always pervades Conservative gatherings at Lynam, but it strikes lookers-on as remarkable that with so very secure a position they should so censtantly harp upon it, and that whether during an election contest, or in ordinary times, they should show, as they do, more nervous anxiety to get up influential public meetings at Lyman than at almost any other place in Mid-Ohqshire.—l am, Sze., October 23, 1883. A LYMM RESIDENE

div.head: ACCIDENT PAY AT THE VULCAN.
div.p: ACCIDENT PAY AT THE VULCAN.

Sir,—Excuse me trespassing upon your space, but I wish to offer a few remarks upon a subject which is at present agitating the minds of the workmen employed at the foundry, Vulcan. lam not one of those who are desirous of forcing opinions down the throats of others, but I feel compelled to say something when I see a great injustice being committed upon any man or upon any number of men. We workmen have many puzzling questions with which to trouble our heads, and more seems to crop up almost daily. The workingmen residing in the Vulcan dis- trict have recently been asked to say whether or not they agree to any benefit being given to a man who may be acci- dentally injured outside his customary round of duties. Of course, I refer to the duties affecting the Vulcan foundry. The men working at this place are members of a sick and accident society, and one portion of. the men seek to elreinde an3ther portion from the benefits which, I firmly believe, they have a right. Supposing a man meets with an un- avoidable accident outside the works, has he to receive any assistance. Everyone cries " Yes." But then supposing the same person goes on a football field and meets with an accident which stops him from working; what about the relief then? Is he to have any? A raw persons say "No," while othe-s say "Yes." This is in reality the root of the matter which his caused all the bol3er about here. It appears to me as if a few old fogies, past enjoying themselves far an hour or two each Saturday afternoon, wish to debar everyone else from doing so IT holding over their heads the threat that if they do so and get injured they shall not receive any benefit. This, to me, seems a very mean and despicable act. Surely our young men can be permitted to indulge in a few hours amusement without the fear of being unsupported in case of an accident. "But," cry our opponents, "they run into danger." Run into danger! Why the iti.m is a ridiculous one. Supposing Igo for a week's out to Blackpool, and one day venture out to sea in a boat. Do I not then expose myself to danger? How manifold are the dangers and ac- cidents which might happen at any moment, and yet, sup- posing by any possibility I was neatly drowned and rendered incapable of following my occupation, who would say that I was net entitled to assistance from the accident fund? I question if anybody will be found to say so. But there are a few cantankerous fellows who can- not enjoy anything themselves, and are determined if they can to stop everybody else from doing se. We all have different ways and means of spending our leisure hours, aid in whatever manner we occupy them we are always liable to accidents. If young men chose to indulge in a healthful and invigoratine exercise, surely no one with any common sense or any t espect for others will say they should not re- ceive benefits in case of "an accident. I should like to hear what others have to sty upon the matter, and one or two abler pens than mine take the question in hand.—Yours, tte., A WATCHER. Vulcan, 24th October, 1883.

MAGIC LANTERN ENTERTAINMENTS AT EARLESTOWN.— On Monday evening a magic lantern entertainment was given in St. Mary's Catholic School, crow-lane. There was a pretty fair attendance. The views were shown by Mr. A. L. Evans, of Haydock, who also gave a description of each. On Tuesday evening a similar entertainment was given in the Vulcan School; • and on Wednesday evening Mr. Evans showed the views in St. John's school, Market-street. Those present were highly pleased with the entertainment, a number of comic sketches creating much amusement. TEACHERS' MEETING.—Sanday last being a day of special intercession for Sunday schools, a meeting of teachers, scholars and friends, was held in the Houghton- street Sunday School. The Rev. H. A. Macnaghten, vicar, addressed the meeting, taking the subject of his discussion from St. John 21, and mentioned the discOuragements and encouragements of teachers. In the evening the rev. gentle- man in the course of his sermon alluded to Sunday schools —their importance and usefulness—and that the Rev. Samuel Sewel, vicar of Prescot, commenced the first Sunday school in the diocese of Liverpool on March 21st, 1784. A ST. HELENS TRADESMAN COMMITTED. Andrew ilawkseye a furniture itaier St. Helens, sued James Jacques, who carriee on a business as a glass stainer in St. Helens, for :lie balance of the price of a picture supplied; ' and the same defendant was sued by Mr. Mearnes for the sum of £9, money lent. Mr. J. 0. Swift represented the first-named plaintiff and Mr. Mawdsley appeared for the defendant. The defendant did not appear, but Mr. Malkin said that unfortunately he (defendant) was very " hard up" and had nothing with which to pay the debt. A commit- ment was asked for against defendant in both cases and these were granted. • ROBBERIES FROM THE MARKET. At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, a lad named John FaEep was charged with havine stolen a number of knives, forks, and spoons from the stall of Matthew Burnby, a general dealer, who lives at 44, Cropper's• Hill, -Liverpool. Burnby's stall, it seemed, had been erected in the St. Helens market-place on the Monday previous, and the prisoner had been seen to take the articles named from under the stall and walk away with them. Burnby followed and caught him and took the articles from him, afterwards handing him over to the police. The prisoner, it appeared, had thrice before been conv:cted of rebberies from the market-place, and he was sent to gaol for two months. .ROW AT THE RAILWAY STATION. A young man named Jchn Daley, who said he lived at 164, Higher Parr- street, was charged at the St. Helens Police Court, on Mon- dgy, with having been drunk and dis.orderly at the St. Helens railway station on Saturday night, and also with having assaulted the stationmaster 4Mr. Moss) and a porter named James Harvey. It seemed that on Saturday nights it is customary at the railway station to pievent anyone going on to the platform excepting those who had tickets. The prisoner went to the station on Saturday night, and be- cause he was prevented going on to the platform he com- menced a violent assault on Harvey, and afterwards struck Mr. Moss also. By the assistance of Detective Wilkinson prisoner was taken into the stationmaster's office, where he renewed his assault on Harvey. A policeman was in conse- quence sent for and Daley was given into custody. The charge with regard to the assault on the stationmaster was withdrawn, and prisoner was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk and disorderly, and is 6d and costs for the as- emit on Harvey, or severr days in default of payment in each case.

The CHAIR:JAN observed that Mr. PasCdel WAS about to aPaain to them of a period in English history with which every Englishman ought to be fully acquainted, a period to Which we owed the civil and religious liberty of to-day. It ' Was a matter for gratitude to God that in that period men were found, who loved law but at the same time loved indi- •Tiduality ; who felt that not only should law lee regarded but that there should be the individual life regarded; that While there was law, every man should be able to think for himself, and no one tyrannise over him and say that he Should have such and such thoughts, or at any rate that those thoughts should be manifested in Such and such a way. We had to-day to thank gcod Oliver Cromwell. (Applause.) Aftee his death .a very short time sufficed to teach England the magnitude of her loss. He began his great Work at 40 years of age, and finished it before he was 60, Yet he filled the earth with his fame, ruled England with a dignity which caused the greatest monarchs on the earth to - fear, and secured freedom in Church and State; simplify- ing the processes of law, and securing equal justice to all Classes. He enthroned virtue in the highest places in the land; took off the oppressive burdens of taxation; en- couraged equally learning and commerce; in fact his People declared him to be Lord Protector of the Common- wealth of England. The proudest chapters of English his- tory recorded his fame; his name had more honour even to it ,vith each succeeding generation; the thrilling story of his life was now made more clear, and he rose to a prouder eminence than any king. That night they felt in the vigour of their Protestant institutions ; in the substantial civil and religious liberty they enjoyed ; in the trenchant cppesition tO priestly assumption and rule they were much indebted to Oliver Cromwell, yet at • the same time it was but the s'mple, solid faith of Lena of thousands of others in the godly home life Of this dear old country, England. He believed English- were prepared to lift up the standard for God and the tight, and to copy the spirit, temper, and example of the , peat protector of English homes and virtues, the uncrowned king of a glorious country, the friend of piety and truth, tthe founder of religious liberty and the champion of Pro- teetautism, the ever-gloricus Oliver Cromwell. (Loud ap- • IPlause.) . The Rev. J. M. FAIRDOURNE, in moving a hearty vote of

thanks to the Lecturer, said he submitted the Lecturer had proved the point with which he started, that Oliver Crom- well was a king—a man who said he could do a thing and did it. (Applause.) The Rev. JAMES ALIA:I'T seconded the motion. He said he did so with a feeling of gratitude for the splendid justice Mr. Pascoe had done to that stern old true Independent, who from his love of libuty became the uncrowned king of Eng- land. Mr. Allatt proceeded as follows: We in this neigh- bourhood have some kind of a connection with him. I suppose if he never Was beaten in his conflicts he was as pearly as possible beaten between here and Winwick. The Scots turned him back from Winwick, somewhere near to Newton Park; and the name of Red Bank Farm takes its name from Oliver Cromwell's bloody and sanguinary con- flict in that neighbourhood. There is something else to show it. Otte of the finest men—spiritual and intelligent of that great age was John Howe, through so many years the chaplain to Oliver Cromwell. John Howe as a small boy was educated in Winwick Grammar School, and after his education at Cambridge and Oxford he returned, and was ordained minister of Christ in Winwick Chutch, so that I, not personally as an Independent, but we all, as inhabitants of this place, have some reason to feel proud of that noble character which his been put before us so ably by the lec- turer to•night. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN, in supporting the motion, said that not only as inhabitants of that neighboarhoOd, but also as Eng- lishmen, who loved the freedom and right of being able to think for themselves, they could rejoice in Oliver Cromwell. The motion was then carried with hearty enthusiasm ; and the LECTURER, in responding, moved a similar compli- ment to the Chairman, which was seconded by Mr. ASHTON, and carried with acclamation. The proceedings then concluded.

HELENS COLLIERY.—An accident of an unusual character, fortunately not attended by any loss of life, occurred at the No. 9 pit belonging to the St. Helens Collieries Company, on Sunday evening. Pumping operations had been going on during the day as usual, when about five o'clock-as a tank full of water and weighing about four tons had been raised half way up the shaft the side- valve of the engine came off with the result that the eitgine- man lost control of the engine. The tank at once began to descend the shaft at a great velocity, and as it did so it raised with great rapidity an empty tank which had pre- viously been descending. This empty tank was drawn to the hp with such force that it was jerked over the puller and was precipitated upon the engine house beneath, which , it wrecked completely. The eegineman, guessing what would be the result of the defective action of the engine, sprang through the window of the engine-house and also gave a timely warning to some children who were near. The engine, which was only a small one and occupied only a corner of .the engine-house, was not damaged, but of the building nothing but a portion of the walls was left. The damage done was estimated at LSO or £lOO. The working of the colliery was not interfered with.
" CONN OLLY' S TICKETS:' AND THEIR VENDORS,

PROSECUTION AT ST. Ig.:LENS. At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, before MT. J, C. Gamble and Mr. H. Baxter, Thomas Fairclough, a tobacconist carrying on business in Liverpod-road, was charged with unlawfully keeping open on his premises lottery called the Cesarewitch lottery, in which lottery cer- tain prizes were allowed to subscribers by or for whom lotteries should be drawn.—Mr. H. L. Riley prosecuted on behalf of the county authorities, and Mr. J. 0. Swift de- fended.—ln his opening statement Mr. Riley said the pro- ceedings were taken under an Act passed in 1802 fqr the supprassion of certain games and lotteries not authorised by law. The facts were that on the afternoon of Saturday, the oth inst., two constables, P.C.'s Brooks and Caunce, went to the defendant's tobacco shop in Liverpool-road. Caunce asked for half an ounce of tobacco, and after being supplied with that Brooks asked for a Connolly's ticket. He was supplied with a ticket which the defendant took from a pile of similar tickets which he had behind the counter. Brooks paid Is for the ticket, after which Caunce also asked for a ticket, and after receiving one paid is for it. , Brooks asked the defendant where, supposing they won a £5O prize, they were to get the money, to which the defendant replied that they would get the money at his shop, and in answer to their inquiries he also told them that they would learn the winning numbers from a sheet which would be issued on the Tuesday following. On the Tuesday following Brooks went to defendant's shop, and got a sheet containing the winning numbers, for which they paid a halfpenny. This list was I headed, like the tickets he had previously bought, the " Cesarewitch Stakes," and referred to the day on which it ; was suggested that that race would be run. The prizes re- ferred to in the list ranged from £lOO to 15. He (Mr. Riley) said be thought he ought also to mention that while the officers were in the shop buying the tickets, they saw several people buy and go out with similar tickets; and when Brookes went to buy lists be also saw a consider number of people buy lists.—P.C's Brookes and Caunce were called in corroboration. of this statement, and both officers in answer to Mr. Swift said they knew that the tickets were called " Connolly's tickets," but they did not know whether there was such a man as " Connolly."—Mr. Swift in defence sub- mitted that the offence with which the defendant was charged was not sufficiently described in the information, and there- fore that the case ought to fall through. After some ex- planation, however, from Mr. Riley, the clerk (Mr. Brewis) said he thought the offence was sufficiently described in the information.—Mr. Swift then contended that there was not proof sufficient to sAtain the charge, and said that the Bench must not merely be satisfied that tickets had been sold, but also that there had been an actual drawing on the defendant's premises before they could convict. He also pointed out that the Act under which the charge was laid was passed 81 years ago, while the scheme with which the defendant was charged was cf modern growth, and could not therefore have been contemplated when the Act was passed. In conclusion, Mr. Swift said their Worships must have known that the busi- ness connected with these tickets had been carried on for a long time by many respectable peole in St. Helens, and many respectable men had bought them. Fer his own part he did not see any moral wrong in the matter, and he certain- ly did not see any more harm in it than betting on a horse• - race or investing a shilling in a charitable raffle. He also thought the people carrying on the business ought to have had some warning before they were d'ropped upon in the un- ceremonious way in which the defendant had been.—After a short retirement the Bench returned, and the chairman said they were of opinion that these lotteries were distinctly ; illegal, and that defendant had been guilty of the charge laid against him. They would, therefore, impose a fine of £5 and costs.—Mr. Riley said he was requested by the county authorities to ask for solicitor's costs to be allowed.—Mr. Swift objected to this being done as unusual, and said it was paltry for the county authorities to ask for costs when they could spend money in order to entrap people.—The costs applied for were not allowed.—Mr. Swift also intimated that he was instructed to appeal against the decision.

GALE IN THE NORTH.—A terrific galn from the north- west broke over Kirkwall on Thursday morning. H.M.S. Firm, which was anchored in the bay, dragged her anchors, and was driven ashore at 10-30 on the point of Mount, a short distance from the pier. H.M.S. Lord Warden also dragged her anchors. A violent gale from the west pre- vailed in the north of Scotland, and considerable damage bas been done to property. There were no disasters on the Aberdeenshire coast, owing to the direction of the wind. At Kirkwall much alarm was caused, and her Majesty's gun- boat Firm, which, along with the Lord Warden, was lying in the roadstead, drove from her anchorage and went ashore in spite of energetic efforts to keep her off. div.p: - CONSERVATISNI IN RUNCORN. Alta party, organised by the Runcorn Conservative As- teditfean, was held in the Public Hall on Tuesday evening. The sttendance was a fair index of the position the party Occupies in the town, and the heaps of provisions left after the repast, however pleasing an omen to the Liberals, who bad the privilege at a glance, was a sorrowful sight to the assembled Tories. At the subsequent public meeting, which was free to voters, the body of the hall was !scarcely more than half filled, whilst the gallery presented a cheerless array of empty benches. Sir Rd. Broeke, Bart., presided, and he was supported by the Hon. Alande Tatton Egerton, M.P., Mr. Jahn Brooks, of Brooklands (Conservative can- didate for Mid-Cheshire), the Revs. W. Preston. J. Lock- wood, D. Llewellyn, Dr. Steele, Dr. Mouritz, Messrs. A. Thomas, J.P., James Reynolds, J.P , John Brundrit,J.P., J. Ashton, W. Fisher, W. Whittaker, J. J. Speakman, W. Wigg, L. Brooke,T. Guest, W. J. Shone, C. R. H. Harrison, T. Glover, Evans, and J. W. Lightburn (local Conservative agent). Letters of apology were read from the Hon. H. C. Raikes, M.P., Rev. Canon Barclay, and Captain C. W. Haalehurst.—The Cilmaicarr commenced the proceedings by the announcement that he could not make a speech, and called upon the Rev. W. Preston to move a resolution of un- abated confidence in Mr. Piers Egerton Warburton, and the Hon. De Totten Egerton, the members for Mid-Che- shire. The rev, gentleman in doing so said that if they, loyalists and constitationalists, were to venture to call the existing Government a heterogeneous slobbering botch patch compound with a Radical—revolutionary tail, a pie- bald body, and muddling head without any backbone what- ever, weak-kneed and nervous—(laughter)—they would be termed most audacious profane people, so they would not do it. (Langhter.) Yet the Liberal members used terms not as complimentary by any means. The speaker indulged in his usual blatant diatribes against the Ministry, and speaking as an Irishman predicted, without qualification, that if Mr. Gladstone attempted to perform a similar tour in the North of Ireland to that accomplished by Sir Stafford Northcote he would be hooted and hissed out of the country by the loyalists, but would be fondly 'embraced by the dis- boy d. The Government had done much that it should not havi done, and had fulfilled none of the promises made be- fore they entered office.—Mr. LIONEL BROOK seconded the motion, which was carried; and the Hon. DE TArrox EGERTON. in responding, asked the audience to contrast the speeches of Sir Stafford Northcate in Ireland and the Mid- lothian speeches of the Piemier. He found fault with the Government for endeavouring to maintain cordial I jelationi with France after the conduct of that eanntey in the Egyptian war, and made a few obtuse remarks with regard to the French Republic, which, he stated, was the only one in Europe (sic.) There were members in Her Majesty's Cabinet who desired England to be governed by a Republic. but "England had existed under one monarch for 800 years," and he did not believe there was ,a tithe of the people who wished to remove the present monarchy. These historical blunders were cheered.—Mr. BROOKES, who received a hearty reception, formulated a "war cry" for for the Tories in the words "peace with honour, economy with efficiency, development, seen. ity, and certainty," and declared that the Liberal motto of "peace, retrenchment, and reform" leas a niisnomer.—Dr. STEELE moved 'That this meeting is of opinion that John Brooks, Esq., of Brook- lands, is a fit and proper person to represent Mid-Cheshire In Parliament, and pledges itself, on the retirement of Piers Egerton Warburton, Esq., to use all legitimate efforts to se- cure his triumphant eturn."—Mr. HENRY REYNOLDS, J.P., seconded the proposition in a chatty speech, and it was tarried unanimously.—Votes of thanks terminated the pro- ceedings. •

The work of the committees had come before th.e Board in a I thoroughly matured form, which had prov'al of the greatest advantage to thc.m in carrying out the'a labours. In con- clusion, he might express his gratitcation that so many of those gentlemen whom he saw arund him would meet there again upon the new Board. de also expressed regret that Mr. Brunner and Mr. liraland had not seen their way to ' again become jnemb3rs ~.,1 the Board. div.head: A. MIDNIGHT ATTACK AT FARNWORT H.
div.p: A. MIDNIGHT ATTACK AT FARN- WORT H.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., John Connolly, a labourer, of Bold, was brought up in custody, charged with unlawfully wounding Thomas Mannion, also a labourer. Inspector Wood said Mannion was a) seriously injured that he was unable to leave his bed for several days. He had Dr. Booth's certi- ficate to that effect.—lt appeared that about half-past eleven , o'clock on Saturday night Mannion and two other men were walking along the road, about a quarter of a mile from the Horn's public-house, Farnworth, when they were met by the prisoner, who was also accompanied by two other men. The prisonet's party attacked the other, and Man- bnion's companions fled, chased by their assailants. The prisoner and Mannion were left. alone and the former knocked the latter to the ground, and kicked him in a most brutal manner about the head and face. Police-constable Snowden deposed that he apprehended the prisoner about four o'clock on Sunday morning, and took him to the house where Mannion was lying. Mannion identified him as the man who had a.saulted him. Mannion was very badly bruised about the head.—The prisoner was then remanded until Friday. The prisoner was brought up at the Police Court pater- morning, before Mr. John Brock. He was defended by Mr. Knowles. The evidence given on Monday was repeated, and he prisaner was commit ted. for trial.

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST- A- WARRINGTON
div.p: CHARGE AGAINST- A- WARRINGTON
PUBLICAN.

Yesterday, at the Warrington Borough Police-court, Wm. Richardson, publican, was summoned for selling by retail intoxicating liquors without having a license for the same, contrary to section 3 of the Licensing Act, 1872, and Thos. Domville, joiner, was summoned for aiding and abetting in such unlawful sale.—The information connected with each summons was institnted by the police.—The Chief Con- stable (Mr. Hunt) said that the case arose in the following fashion. Some few years ago the King's Arms public-house, Buttermarket-street, opposite Scotland-road, was kept by a man named Bate and his wife. They died leaving a num- ber of children, and Mr. Crompton, of the Blackburn Arms, Corporation-street, wilts appointed executor to carry on the business. A man nTtned Rigby was put in to take charge, but he died last January, and the license had been trans- ferred to the widow, Ann Rigby. It was not until the pre- vious Saturday that he heard Mrs. Mgby had left the house OR September 24th, and that defendant was Richard- son, but when that fact came to his knowledge he sent to the King's Arms to ask by whose authority he was doing business.—(Richardson: I dispute that.)—The Chief Con- stable, continuing, said that he also sent a com- munication to Mr. Crompton. However, as time went on, and he heard nothing further, he gave instructions for proceedings to be taken. The police would tell the Court that on the occasion of their visit they found the defendant Domville and others drinking, and they made la note of what transpired. Mr. Hunt added.that Richardson Iliad formerly held a license in Warrington, and if he had only applied to the magistrates for temporary authority to sell on the premises in question he did not think the Bench would have objected to such a course, or even to have transferred the license.—Ann Rigby was then called, and stated that she formerly held the license of the King's Arms, Buttermarketestreet. She was not in occupation on Tueslay last, and she had not sent Richardson to manage the house. —P.C. Neill stated that on Tuesday evening,about half-past eight o'clock, he went in company with P.C. Hennessey to the King's Arms, and observed children going in with cans for beer. At five minutes to nine they entered the house and in the parlour saw the defendant Domville and another man with glasses before them. Richardson was present, and 1 witness said to him "You are selling without a license, I and you had better close the house," when Richardson re- plied "that he was not aware of it." Witness thereupon ' told him that he would be obliged to report the matter to I the Chief-Constable. As they were leaving two other men entered the house. Witness and Hennessey remained out- side a few moments, thinking that the men would not be served with drink, but as they did not come out witness re-entered and found that the men who had last gone into the place had been served with a pint each, and that Domvilla had been supplied with another glass of beer.— P.C. Hennessey corroborated.—Sergeant Spinks spoke to i having visited the King's Arms on Saturday and warned 'Richardson of his risk in conducting the house without a ' license. Richardsen then siid that the negociations were n3arly completed, and that in a few days the license would ' I be taken by Mrs. Butterworth, of the RAM'S Head, Horse- market-street.—ln defence, Richardson pleaded that he had 1 I been appointed to manage the estate until Mrs. Butterworth ' took possession. .lle had no desire to infringe the law as he , gained nothing by it. Domville had been served with a glass of beer before the policemen entered the house but not afterwards. He denied having 'nen previously cautioned. ' , —Doraville said that he we nnitA iomnr wt. of the affair. and dld not hear what took place between Richardson and the ;police officer.—The Chief Constable did not press for a heavy tine, but that it might be a caution to publicans in- ' , fringing the law in such a manner.—The magistrates tined ' Richardson in the mitigated penalty of £l, and dismissed the case against Dumville. The latter cooly asked for his 1. expenses to be allowed. bat this the Bench declined.

Alderman DAVIES proposed "The health of the Member RELEVES. for the Borough," and in the course of his observations, Turkeys ala Supreme. said : The toast is one worth listening to, and I know you Beef a la, Jardin'ere. will appreciate it thoroughly. (Applause.) If ever there Saddle of Mutton. RAM and Spinach, was a time in which politicians should cast aside their politics and take up the armour of aatrlotism it is to-day. If ever there was a time when the two great parties of the country should join hand in hand to pat down Communism, and those things which would injure our great nation it is now we should fight shoulder to shoulder. (Applause.) Therefore I think that with very great propriety the Mayor can call upon an old Conservative to propose the health of a good and worthy member ot Parliament, although he happens to be a Liberal. (Laughter and applause.) It is not at all a difficult task for me to perform. If we are to have a Liberal member for I.Varrington, I know of no man I would prefer to Mr. McMinnies. (Applause.) I don't even except you, Mr. Mayor—(laughter)—but I repeat that if we are to have a Liberal member, I sin prepared to say Mr. McMinnies is the man. But, gentlemen, you must bear this in mind—that whatever testimony I am prepared to give to the excellent merits Mr. McMinnies possesses, we, as Conservatives, will always be prepared to fight him when the time arrive% hitting him pretty well above the belt. (Laughter and applause.) I don't think I need call upon anyone in this chamber to say anything about the merits of Mr. McMinnies. There is something about him which com- mands their affection, and I do not hesitate to tell our Liberal friends in Warrington that in a great measure that kind and generous feeling—a feeling which r have no doubt they are proud of—enabled them to make him victorious at the last election. lam sure Mr. McMinnies will excuse me if I diverge from the subject of the toast, and refer to another subject. Reference has been made to night to gentlemen who have filled the office of Mayor in this town. Mr. McMinnies alluded to the first Mayor of Warrington. (Ap- plause.) Often when I have been at the meetings of the Council I have looked at the Mayer, but I have never seen one whom I thought was not doing the best he could in the interests of the borough—(applause)—but I have seen something behind the Mayor, and that is a picture—the picture of our friend Mr. Beamont, the first Mayor of War- rington. (Cheers.) lam now speaking to my brother mem- bers of the Council, and also to those outside the chamber, when I appeal to them as to whether we ought not to take advantage of a new Act of Parliament. I aria not asking you to take up an old but a new law. Let us take advan- tage of the new Act of Parliament, and do as Preston did, which stepped back and elected from amongst the people a good, worthy, able and venerable gentleman, Sir. Townley Parker, as their guild Mayor. Is it not possible for oar Corporation, as we have , Mr. Beamont still amongst us, to ask him to become our next Mayor? (Cheers again and again renewed.) There are, no doubt, many gentlemen who are ambitious, and very properly so too, to allow themselves to be nomina- ted as Mayor, but I think I am quite justified in saying that every man who is amb:tious to occupy that post would re- joic) to see Mr. Beamont again made Mayor of the borough —(applause)—and if he would consent it would indeed ee a guild year for Warrington. (Cheers.) I think it would be the means of making him even a younger man. We should not ask him to take upon. laimself any cares of office exc.otine those which were absolutely ~-,1“;..‘t rwo., Lao.. I believe, judging from your hearty expression of approval to-night, that it is the wish of the Council Mr. Beamont should be elected, and I am quite certain the suggestion would be received by acclimation oatside. Mr. McMinniee is the next speaker, and I have no doubt he wi:l take advan- tage of the opportunity to say something in support of what 1 have said. Strange to say, Mr. Beamont is the next speaker to him, an I in his remarks I hope he will accept the effer which we now make to him, and allow himself to occupy the position I have suggested. I have great pleasure in proposing the health of the member for the borough. (Cheers.) The toast was received with enthusiasm. Mr. MCMINNIES, in responding, said: I am very much obliged to vote for the kind manner in which this toast haa been received, as well as to Alderman Davies for the kind terms in which he has alluded to me. During the time I have had the tioaour of representing this borough, I have aLways endeavoured to do what I could in all matters of a local nature to promote the interests of my fellow-towns- men. (Applause.) In whatever positiodl am placed, I shall alsvelys consider it my duty thus to act, and I have only to ask you believe that what I say is any wish and desire. My inflhnce will always be at the disposal of my fellow-townsmen. I have always found the peoli'e of W,u - rington disposed to believe that those who are acting for them to the best of their ability deserve their approbation. Mr. Davies has introduced a very important consideration into the toast he Ipis proposed, and I am not, therefore, dis- posed. say anything further with respect 'o myself. I may say that the hint—l suppose I ought not to call ik more than a hint—that Mr. Davies has thrown out appeals to my affections with peculiar force. (Applause.) I had some- thing to do with the incorporation of ths bare ugh, and I know that Mr. Beauiont's conduct during his mayoralty went to compose certain differences which had arisen dur- ing the long, and in some respects angry, controversy which took place as to whether the town should be incorporated or not. I believe that the inhabitants of Warrington in that respect owe a great deal to Mr. Beamont for the trouble be Was put to in getting into order the Corporation, which had only been called into existence at the moment he assumed the chief duties of it. I repeat that Alderman Davies has intro- duced an important matter, and I do not know what Mr. Beamont will h tve to say with regard to it. I hope, at any rate, that unless he says at once, "Yes, I will accept the in- vitation of my townsmen—l will take the post which more than 30 years ago was offered to me," that he will not give us a decisive answer. to-night. (Cheers.) Ido hope he will consider what has been said, and what our memories are with reference to his mayoralty. I hope he will agree to the proposition which Mr. Davies has made. I have now no more to say except to thank you very kindly for proposing my health; and as long as I am your representative, I shall endeavour to do my duty. (Applause.) The MAYOR: Before Mr. Beamont rises to speak, I should like to add a few words to those that have fallen from the lips of Alde:man Davies and Mr. McMinnies. I fancy the feelings of my heart are very much the same as those of all sitting round this table. The feelings I entertain for Mr. Beamont are the feelings I should entertain towards my oivn father. I have an intensity of respect for Mr. Beamont—a respect that cannot be gauged—and I feel perfectly con- vinced—and I hope Mr. Beamont will forgive me for saying this—that if he will accept the office of Mayor for the next year, it will give joy, to the whole of the inhabitants of Warrington—to every man, woman, and child, of every grade and shadoof opinion. We should rejoice if the town could be governed by a gentleman honoured and respected as Mr. Beamont is. I beg of him, for the sake of the memories.of the past, to take office again, and add fresh laurels to his brow. It would, indeed, be a glory to War- ringtona n esteemed.Ao x T (Loudwhooc n h re cheers.) sr si n . ) Mr. Bm. to be governed by a gentleman so worthily respected d was received, with hearty cheers, said: I am afraid the g kind feeling which you have showu towards me has almost incapacitated me from saying what I wish to say. Ido not know whether my voice can be heard at the other end of the room. (A voice': " Ills.") Then lam very glad. I was going to say that I have been requested to propose a toast, which in point of fact I am as I ought to be most willing to propose, namely, "The Cor- poration of Warrington." (Applause.) With regard to the Corporation, it has a head and it has a body. A body without a head is very much like a ship without a rudder, or a bell without a clapper. (Laughter.) I hope, in the first p 1 ice, you will allow inc to refer to the services of past Mayors of Warrington. There are some things in this country which can never be forgotten. I recollect that when I was Mayor of Warrington, and when the mayoralty was a new office, people thought that the chief magistrate of the borough could do anything. One of the constituents came to the Mayor to ask him to keep all the public clocks at the same time—(laughter)—and the Mayor's answer was that Charles V., the great emperor, could not make twelve watches go at the same time, and how, therefore, could it be expected that the Mayor, who was not such a great man could make al/ the clocks keep time? (Laughter.) But the present Mayor of Warrington had presented them with a Mock which can correct Old Time himself almost, aad I wish to ask you if you ever had a more tintely or a more !kitting gift nude to
