After the dinner, _ _ The MAYOR gave the toasts of "The Queen" and "The Prince and Princess of Wales and the rest of the Royal Family." Mr. Councillor BROADBENT proposed "The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces," to which Captain REYNOLDS suitably responded. Mr. PErrna &runs proposed "The Bishop, Clergy, an 1 Ministers of all Denominations," and coupled with it the names of the Recto., the 41,ev. John Yonge, and the Rev. Father Feeny. The RECTOR, who, on rising to respond, was received with applause said: I rise to return you my sincere thanks for your kindness in proposing this toast, and also for coupling my name with it. The Bishop of the diocese is well known to all of you, and, therefore, I need say nothing further about him, except that he holds a high and important position in the Church. I thank you for your good wishes towards me. I need all your good wishes, for I have been a great sufferer of late, but still I thank God my health is now better. I livtj in a damp locality. Twice recently in a fortnight we have been inundated, but lam looking forward with great expectations to the Ship Canal being made, which I hope will do away with these inconveniences. (Laughter and applause.) I beg to thank the Mayor for his kind invita- tion to-night, and I am glad that during his year of office he has given us what has long been wanted in the town, namely, a good clock to keep us all in good time. We are all proud to be here to-night and to enjoy his hospitality. (Applause.) The Rev. JoHig YONGE also responded. He said: lam sure very few words will be necessary from me to assure you that the gentlemen whose names have been coupled with the toast, as representing the ministers of all denomi- nations in the town, feel very proud of the honour which has been accorded to them in drinking their healths, and wishing them prosperity in the work in which they are en- . .
. . gaaed. It is pleasant to be able to meet on an occasion like this through the kindness of the Mayor, as it shows that, whatever difference there may be between us with .regard to

some questions, there still is -an amount of friendship—exist- ing:, and that we meet with perfect cordiality. (Applause.) I long for the time when Judah shall no longer vex Ephraim, or Ephraim envy Judah, and when the ministers

_ of. all denominations will come even closer together than at present is the c Ise. (Hear, hear.) There is a great deal of work to do and the sooner we cm come more closely to- gether, and work hand in hand, the better it will be for the society in the midst of which we are placed; and the more likely we shall he to hobo on the nrnaperity nf the ennnt rsr we all love. (Applause.) The Rev. Father FEENY saki: I did not expect to have had the honour of being called upon to speak this evening, b,c ause I know perfectly Well that there are many older eccksiastical representatives in Warrington than myself. Still I am glad to add a few words to those which have been said by the Rector and Mr. Yonge. I have a kindred feel- ing with regard to the work that lies before us, as I believe it is desirable we should act in fellowship. (Applause.) I will candidly say that when I came to Warrington some seven years ago it was with some little diffidence, because I had heard some very shady opinions with reference to War- rington generally, and the difficulties the clergymen of the town had to encounter in many walks of life; but I have pleasure in stating that as regards tho Roman Catholics I have the honour to represent this evening, and as far as I am personally concerned, my opinion has very much altered. (Applause) I have always experienced great kindness, and the hand of friendship has been extended to me. It was a great pleasure to me three or four years ago to meet in this room to try with others to alleviate the great distress which then existed in the borough owing to the severe frost, a circumstance which, no doubt, all the mem- bers of the Council present will remember; and it was then I gauged the feelings of the people with regard to the clergy and the many difficult works in which they have to engage. We have to labour amongst all classes—poor and rich—and I can assure you, as Mr. Stubs has said, it is a great en. couragement to us, and carries us on in our work, when we cm feel that we have the sympathy, of the leading laymen. _ (Applause.) Therefore, on behalf of the Roman Catholic . .

community of tbe town, which now must number some seven thousand persons, I have very, great pleasure in responding to the toast, and thanking the Mayor very cor- dially for his hospitality a.ld good wishes. (Applause.) Mr. MCMINNIES, M.P., who had a very cordial reception, proposed "The health of the Mayor," and in doing so s tid : —The Mayor has succeeded a long line of predeceesors who have performed the function of chief magistrate of this borough with great acceptance and advantage to the borough, as well as with credit to themselves. My mind reverts to years ago, since which time certainly a genera- tion has elapsed. I remember gentlemen who took the office of chief magistrate of this borough and performed their .duties with great advantage to the town as well as with great honour to themselves. I remember the first Mayor— (applause)—who I am glad to see is with us this evening. (Renewed applanee.) We hope he may be able to attend these gatherings for many years to come, and I can say that while he was the first Mayor as to time, he is also first in affectionate remembrance. (Cheers.) I remsmber Mr. Allcard. a very able, and I should say, perhaps the most thorough and honest man I ever had the privilege of meeting. I remember Mr. Plerpoint, who, notwithstanding that he had a great deal of business to do in apother direction, was al- ways reedy to devote a great part of his time to the interests of the borough, and a great portion of his life to the service of his fellow-townsenen. I remember Mr. Stubs,who was very genial, very conciliatory, ever first and foremost in good works—(cheers)—and we must all feel that we owe him a debt of gratitude for the pains he took in extending the cause of edacation in the borough. I also remember Mr. Perrin, who devoted a great deal of his time with great self- sacrifice to the performance of public duties which he be- lieved contributed to the advantage of his fellow-townsmen. I remember a long line of gentlemen who have filled the post of Mayor of this borough, but time would fail to allow me to name them all. I suppose that what lam about to say will be endorsed by every one in this room, and, no doubt, out of it, that the present Mayor is in every respect a worthy successor of those who have preceded him. (Cheers.) His munificence has been remarkable. Those amongst us who desire the spread of art amongst the people will not forget his munificence to the School of Art, and I am in a position to say that, great as his munificence has already been, if it is required it will be extended. (Ap- plause.) Those of you who have a great regard for' the ex- tension of elementary education in the borough will,l have no doubt, remember that the Mayor has given to the People's College a subscription almost as large as that which I have just mentioned as having been given to the School of Art. And in various other ways the Mayor has exhibited an amount of muni6cenc3 which, I suppose, vse shall never forget. His hospitality on various occasions has been very great, and I should say his year of office from first to last has been a great success. (Applause.) Perhaps he is the only man in this room, or out of it, who rejoices that it is nearly over. - (Laughter and applause.) I drink his health ' most heartily, and congratulate him upon his year of office. We wish him many years of usefulness and happiness, and hope that, in whatever position he may °find himself hereafter of honour and usefulness, the end of his career may be as successful as his mayoralty has been. I give you "The health of his Worship the Magyor." The toast was received with musical honours.

The Mayor, who was evidently deeply affected by the warmth of the reception accorded biro, on rising to respond, said: I thank you very sincerely indeed for the kind manner in which you have received the toast of my health. I thank Mr. McMinnies for what he has said. It is indeed difficult for ma to respond to a toast proposed in such flowing lan- guage ag that which has been used by my friend. I think

the town? (Applause.) I hope it will long be remembered; I and that his name will be engraved upon it. The bell which gives the clock voice was presented in 1647 by Sir John Booth, who called himself "Rector of Warrington," but by which I think he meant not that he was the rector of the town, but the ' governor. I think that the name of the Mayor. who has made the bell more useful than it has been before ought not to be dissociated from it.—(Applause.) I remember the magnificent reception which the Mayor gave to the Mala- gasy Envoys when they were in Warrington. (Uheets ) I shall never forget his gift, which was a beautiful specimen of his manufacture, to the Queen they represented. I hope the odour of that act of kind remembrance which reached Madagascar will last far longer than the broken vise men- tioned in the poet's song, whilla "retains the scent of the odour after the roses are gone: (Applause.) I hope the progress of Madagascar will not be interfered with by the threatened invasion. I believe the body corporate of the town is worthy of the town. lam a great pedestrian, and therefore a good judge of the state of the streets. That ex- cellent old poet Horace said in Rome that the Appian Way was the best way because it was the smoothest. but I will say, Not smoother or cleaner was the Appian Way. Than are the streets of Warrington to-day. (Applause.) There is an immense amount of credit due to those who have charge of the streets. The police force, also, of Warrington within my memory consisted of a stout mar, who could not run after a thief—(laughter)—but now yoa have a little army of policemen. I hear no complaints against them, bat, on the other hand, a great deal mty be said in their favour. (Applause.) Wlaat-lago says of him- self, _

1 It is my nature's plague To spy ints abuse, and oft my • Jealousy shapes faults that are 'lot, might bs the policeman's motto. But Ido not think the police of Warrington see faults which do not exist, and I think they act with priadence'and mercy. With regard to the removal of the sewage, every town experiences a dif- ficulty, but I believe that ha Warrington an admirable method is adopted, and I believe it is the only one that will succeed. One of the characters in "Measure for Measure' says to Claudio—

Thou art not noble; For all the aecammodAtions that thou basest Are nursed by bmeness. (Laughter.) He thought that should be the motto of all who had to do with the removal of the sewage; and in the words of one who wist.el success to the English Constitu- tion, "Esto Perpctuo"--last for ever. I wish the same wis.h for the Corporation to which I now propose the toast. (Cheers.)

The Mason : But what about yourself? Mr. BEAMONT : You have put me in a dilemma, and have asked me a question which I dare not answer at the present moment. (Cheers.) May the Corporation flourish as long as it is required. (Cheers.) The EX-MAYOR humorously responded. Mr. Dux, in proposing "The Town and Trade of War- rington," said: The town is certainly one which, when you take into consideration the number of its population, bears a very high position relatively to other towns of similar s;ze. It is a town which has produced many remarkable re- presentative men, and it is foremost in many important works of education, refinement, and self-improvement. (Hear, hear.) We have, I am glad to say, an excellent School of Art, and we know of the excellent work which gas been done done by Mr. Thompson, the headmaster, whom we are glad to see present. We congratulate him ripen the result of his labours, and the success which has been achieved by his pupils. His labours henceforward are to be carried on in a locality and under a roof more worthy of his ability than the place at present occupied. In Warrington we are not behind other towns in matters of education. We possess a Literary and Philosophical Society. which is doing good work amongst the younger people of Warrington, and affords opportunities to those who have literary attainments to bring forward their views, and to write and to read papers for the society. We have also this year renewed, if not inaugurated, classes in connection with the Cambridge University Extension Scheme, and there is at the present time a course of lectures being given upon electricity and magnetism which those who have heard them will bear me out in saying are exceedingly instructive I and interesting. Mr. Beamont, in the remarks he has just I made, had referred to stich•an extent to the management of I the town that it is not neceesary for me to follow in his footsteps, and I will conclude my observations by making a brief allusion to the trade of Warrington. We wish it every success. For years past it has not been so successful as it used to be. We trust, however, that prosperity may return. It is perfectly clear that the manufacturers of Warrington must have prominently before them this point—that it is impossible for men in trade in this country to succeed un- less they possess not only habits of the greatest industry and self-denial, and adaptation to business, but absolutely a genius for the particular business in which they are engaged. Competition now is so great in almost every branch of trade that it is impossible to make any profit unless the trade is not only conducted on the most favourable conditions but also with great application and aptitude on the part of those who conduct it. What are the reasons why we have been suffering from depression in trade? They are many. Fifty years ago the manufacturers of the Continent and of America s were only in their infancy, and we had the command of al- most all the markets of the world. The continental nations from time to time made rapid progress in the arts and man- ufactures. They have borrowed our ideas, our machinery, our workmen, and now they produce in the markets of the world things which are equal to our own in quality, and which run us very hard indeed in fbn ran. Llto vv z we to sermount these difficulties? The only safe- guard and the only hope I have for any permanent revival of trade in this country is that we a'l earnestly seek out new openings and new markets for our products. I think all who have looked with any attention to what has been going on in the world must have felt that Africa is the future field—one of the future fields at all events—to which our attention ought to be direc,el, so that we May there in new and virgin soil soul our manufactures to new and numtrons customers, who may by their demand tend to re- place and put our trade in the position it occupied in the I past. (Applause.) I do not think the Chamber of Commerce of this town has yet received that support from the traders ani manufacturers it deserves, because the Chamber might be useful in many ways, and be the mouthpiece of the trade of this district. 1 have much pleasure in coupling with the toast the name of Mr. Z;bl Armitage, a gentleman and a manufacturer who employs a large number of hands, and we all trust his basiaess may prosper. If it were not for the business with which he is connected many of our women and children in the town would be without employment. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. Attell-rAuE, in reply, said: I think I can say, without betraying any secret, that the trade of Warrington requires -thata). good many gentlemen should drink its very good heala. (Laughter.) It is quiet, and has been for sonic time pest. What the causes of depression are I do not pretend to be able to say, and I cannot claim for the trade with which I am connected any exemption from the general rule.

I The MAYOR proposed, in complimentary terms, the health of the officials of the Corporation, and, in the absence of irdCie Town Clerk; wh) had left, Mr. Chorley and Mr. r.ragdin responded. The proceedings shortly afterwards terminated.

Tt:e New Corporation Gas Works at Bradford, which have cost a hundred and fifty thousand pounds, were opened by the Mayor yesterday. ANOTHER MARINE MADMAN—Dever, Friday.—Mr. Cope- man started on his raft to cross the Channel this morning. Coont Herbert Bismarck arrived at the German Embassy iu Lon:Ion yesterday morning from the Continent. Yesterday, at North Shields Police Court, John Walton, master butcher, was charged with having in his possession meat which was unfit for human food. He was also charged with selling meat unfit for human food. In the first case— that of having unsound meat in his possession—the magis- trates fined the defendast £l5 and costs, and in the second case the nominal penalty of Is and costs.

The Archbishop of Canterbury writing to the hon. seer taries of to 3 or. t fioreCommemorationCommittee,says he is obliged to them for giving him the opportunity of ex- pressinc, the unbounded respect which in common with every a'dmirer of wise benificence he entertains for Sir Moses Monteflore, and accepts with pleasure the offer to add his name t) the committee.

A police-sergeant, named John Blyth, in the Manchester county force, committed suicide yesterday morning under distressing circumstinces.. He had lately been removed against his wish from one out-diviaion to another, and he has since been in low spirits. He was seen at six o'clock yesterday morning, bat an hour later, when the constable's wife went to take breakfast to the deceased, she found him hanging from a gas jet in the corridor quite dead. THE STRIKE OF ENGINE•CLEAKERS.—The strike of the engine-cleaners employed by the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company at Manchester continues, and as great excitement prevails in the district, the gates of the works are guarded by detectives. The men state that their wages do not rise above 9s. to 15s. a week, and that they work 63 hours. The company decline to treat with their men,, and, contending that the strikers have discharged themselves, are engaging new hands.

A -SAN- FRANCISCO JOURNALIST ON EIS TRAVELS.— Alfred Wallace Kelly, a journalist of San Franaisco, was charged at Clitheroe yesterday with obtaining food and lodgings by false pretenc2s. On Wednesday the prlsoner hired a carriage at the Swan Hotel, Whalley, and drove to Stonyhurst. On returning he ordered supper for himself and six others, and nine bottles of champagne were drunk. He ran up a bill of over £lO, when he was found to be with- out cash. He was remanded for inquiries to be made. IMPENDING LEGAL CII&NGES.—The Law Journal under- stands that on the re-assembling of Parliament Sir Henry James will be prcw,sed by the Prime Minister as Speaker of the House of Commons upon the resignation of Sir Henry Brand. Upon the election of Sir Henry James by the House, Sir Fairer Herschel' will, as a matter of course, be- come Attorney-General, and the Solicitor-General will be either Mr. Davey, Q.C., or Mr. C. Russell, Q.C. Professional usages point to the former, as Equity has for some time been unrepresented among the law officers. FALL OVER A VIADUCT.—About four o'clock on Thurs- day morning, as a train of empty trucks was passing over the Charlton Viaduct, near Shepton Mallet, the driver noticed that /3 omething was wrong, and pulled up as soon as possible. He found that six of the trucks had left the line, loix of them having been precipitated over the viaduct into a field below—a depth of about fifty feet. The telegraph

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 1:', Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Mapchester, write (Oct. 25th):—

The past week has beer productive of but a very moderate volume of business, the approach and the commencement of the fortnightly settlement now In progress no doubt begetting iedifference to operate till bargains could be made for the "new time." Added to this, throughout the greater portion of the week prices have tended towards depression, led by the heavy lines whose traffic returns are taken as a criterion of the condition of the trade of the country, and the revenue returns being disappointing the dull tone has been more pronounced. After " carrytng over" yesterday a decidedly better feeling was manifest, but in some cases the higher prices marked have not been maintained. The Foreign Funds exhibit some few alterations, but with the exception of a rise of j In Peruvians and fin Egyptian Unified and a fall of in Argentine Hard Dollar Bones the changes are very slight. Mexican Railways, though only f down on the week, have deeined eeverely from the highest points reached during the period, as during the earlier days they showed much strength, and were sent as 'high as 93, from wlaieh, however, they have rapidly fallen away, closing to-day at ; or, as we have said, about f below last Thursdays close. The other classes ot investments do not present any decided feature, excepting Insurance and Telegraphs, in both of which the revisions of quotations are numerous, and a decidedly adverse majority in each case. The business doing altogether in these investments is compara- tively small and rather straggling. COAL, IRON, &C., AND MINING. The business done is meagre, and without feature. Some distinct changes in prices are to be recot (led. however., as the following will show. aigher—Staveley A If, John Brown's 1 to lf, Telegraph Con- struction and Maintenance I, Cammell's f to 1, Sheepbridge A to , and Patent Nut and Bolt I. BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. IrC, THE BURGESSES OF THE SOUTH-EAST WARD. TADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—Having been requested by a very large and influential number of the Burgesses in your Ward to allow myself to be nominated as a Candidate for the Election of a Councillor, on the Ist of November next, to represent you, I have, after due considera- tion of the responsibilities in connection with the dut!el of such undertaking. consehted to be thus nominated. In seeking your suffrages, Idoso as the nominee of no political organisation, f3r in my opinion the good I government of our Borough will be best promoted by those who cast aside politics in municipal clatters. Considering the contemplated improvements in our town, you require repre- sentatives with some experience of a practical character, and having lived in Warrington all my life, I am well known in this respect.- Should your choice fall upon me, you may be assured my best energies will be devoted to the furtherance of all improvements, with a due regard to strict economy, and you may rely upon it your Confidence will not be misplaced. lam, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, JOHN HEDGCOCK. Mill-street, Warrington, October 24th, 18133. BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE SOUTH-EAST WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—The time for which you elected us has now expired, and at the request of a large and influen- tial meeting of Ratepayers, we have again consented to offer ourselves fur re-election. Three years ago you placed us at the head of the poll, and we can assure Ton that during that time as Councilors we bate tried as much as possible to merit the confidence you then so cordially reposed in us. If you again return us to the Council Chamber as your Representatives, it will be our con- stant endeavour to watch your interests, and to give a helping I hand to anylneasure that we believe to be for the good of the town of Warrington.—Thanking you for past favours, we have the honou'r to be Ladies and Gentlemen, your obedient Servants, R. W. FRANCOMB. S. CAVEWHITTLE. Warrington, October 25th. 1883.

BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE :_•OUTH-EAST WARD. -- LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—As I have decided t ) withdraw from the contest in your Ward in favour of the two Conserva- tive candidates, MESSRS. FRANCOII B AND WHITTLE, who have been duly and legally nominated. 1 hope you will give them your hearty support. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant. THOMAS JOLLEY. Warrington, October 26, 1883.

BOROUGH OF BT. HELENS. TO THE ELECTORS OF WEST SUTTON WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.—After a very pressing invitation from a deputation of influential ratepayers, to offer myself as a candidate for West Button Ward at the forthcoming Muni- cipal Election, I have, after some hesitation, decided to accede to their request. In asking the suffrages of the Electors af this Ward, I have no other object than faithful service to your interests and those of the Borough generally. The questions affecting the sanitary conditien of the Borough, all facilities for cleanliness and recreation, such as Baths and Recreation Grounds, the support and extension of our Free Library. and all questions of an elevating tendency shall havehigy best at- tentton. Should you do me the honour of e!ectiWme as your Representative in the Council, it will be my study to show that your confidence has not been misplaced. I am. Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours respectfully, W LL1.411 LONGTON. Eccleston Cr3nge, October 22nd, 1883.

BOROUGH OF ST. HELENS. TO THE BURGESSES OF EAST SUTTON WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMSN,—Iffy term r.,f Office will expire on the Ist of November next, for which yoa kindly elected me to serve you in the Council of this Borough. At the request of a large number of Ratepayers of this Ward, I again offer myself as your Representative, and, if elected, I will to the best of my ability attend to the interests of your Ward, and the Borough generally.—Soliciting your kind support, I remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, JAMES FISHER. Olive Mount. Mill-lane, Sutton, St. Helens, October 18th, IEB3.

BOROUGH OF ST. HELENS. TO THE BURGESSES OF PARR WARD. -- LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.—In COmpliaEce to the wish of many friends, I offer myself as a Candidate to represent you the Municipal Cornell of this Borough. I have been amongst you over 16 years, and have held offices of a public nature for some time past, arid being daily amongst you, I am in a posi- tion to see wrat is required in your Ward. Should I have the good fortune t be elected I shall do my utmost to represent you with the greatest economy and efficiency. I am, your obedient servant, F. .1,, BROWN. Bishop-street. Farr, October 19th, 1883.

BOROUGH OF ST. HELENS. TO THE BURGESSES OF WINDLE WARD. -- LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—The period for which you elected me to represent you on the Town Council having almost ex- pired. I beg to again offer you my services. trusting that my conduct during my term of office has been satisfactory to you. If you do me the honour of again electing me, 1 shall endeavour to do my best to serve the interests of the Ward and Town. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen. Your obedi.nt servant. J. C. GAMBLE. Cowley Hill, St. Helens, 10th October, 1883. BOROUGH OF SAINT HELENS. TO THE BURGESSES OF HARDSILIW WARD. LADIES AND GENtLEMEN.—The term for which you electei me as one of your representatives in the Town Council having now almost expired, I beg again to place my services at 3 our disposal. I venture to trust that my cmduct in the past has met with your approval; and I assure you that should it be yoar pleasure to re-elect me on the Ist November I shall, in the discharge of the duties devolving upon me. ever have in view the welfare of the Bonsugh and the good of its inhabitants, I am, Your obedient vrvant, DUNCAN McKECRNIE. St. 6t. Helcns, 18th October. 1883. - -

BOROUGH OF ST. lIELENS. TO THE BURGESSES OF ECCLESTON WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN —I beg to thank you for the honour you have done me, in returning me again, unopposed, to ,the Town Council, and I trust that at the end of my term of office you will have no reason to regret having made me one of your representatives. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant. W. W. PILKINGTON. Glass Works, St, Helens, 25th October, 1883. BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.—THE PUBLIC HEALTH ACT, 1875. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the Mayor, Aldermen, and . Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington, in the counties of Lancaster and Chester, acting by the Council as the Urban Authority for the said borough, propose by virtue of the Public-Health Act, 1875, to put in force and to present a Petition to the Local Government Board in pursuance of the said Act, praying that they may be allowed to put in force the powers of the Lands Clauses Consolidation Acts with respect to the purchase and taking of lands otherwise than by agreement for the purpose of widening, opening, and otherwise improving the West side of Bridge-street from Bridge Foot to Friar's Gate. And NoTICE IS HEREBY FURTHER GIVEN that a plan of the proposed undertaking is deposited at the office of the Borough Surveyor, at the Town Hall, within the said borough, where the same may be inspected at all reasonable hours, and that the total quantity of lands required by the said Mayor, Alder- men, and Burgesses for widening, opening, and otherwise im- proving the said street, and for the purpose of the said under- taking is 7.000 square yards or thereabouts. pensation to tenant farmers for unexhausted improvements. The latter Bill was simply the extension of an Act passed in Lord Beaconsfield's time called the Agricultural Holdings Act, and if it had not been for that Bill the present Bill could never have come into existence. Since ever the Liberals; got into office, when they were in the plenitude of their power, the reform now spoken of had been kept back as a question of policy, and it was produced now as a clever party manceuvre and clever party cry at the next election. The manner in which they proposed to manipulate the ques- tion of reform for party ends rather than national ends, was pretty obvious from the statements and writings of the Liberal Party. Having quoted from a recent article in the Fortnightly Review, Mr. Brooks said that whatever might be the merits of the reform that was proposed, the purpose for which it had been brought forward and the manner in which it had been manipulated ought always to be remembered. (Cheers.) The usual votes of thanks followed. The programme of songs, itc., was—Pianoforte solo, "Pasquinade," Mrs. Addenbrook ; song, Kings of the main" (encored), Mr. J. M. H. Todhunter ; pianoforte solo, "Spring song," Miss Baker. Professor Trevori, conjurer, Jrc., also gave an amusing entertainment, and the proceedings closed with the singing of the Wational Anthem.

SCENE AT A FlRE.—Shortly before six o'clock yesterday , morning, people passing on their way to work noticed smoke ' issuing from the windows of a house in Gilnow-lane, Bolton, occupied by James Neild, commercial traveller. An entrance was forced through the front window, and the stairs were found in flames and the house filled with suffocat- ing smoke. It was impossible for the family to descend by the ordinary way, and Mr. Neikl getting out of the back- room window on to the scullery window rescued six of the younger children by this means. His wife threw her baby from the window, and it was caught safely by the crowd. She then jumped from the window into the street, but caught one leg inside the lower front windosv., sustaining severe lacerations from the ankle to the thigh. The fire was ultimately extinguished by buckets or water, but the furniture in the kitchen was destroyed.
